We analyze a class of field theories known as Dirac fields, where the equations governing the field's behavior exhibit unique characteristics in both flat and curved spacetimes. A solution to these equations in a specific type of spacetime - de Sitter, anti-de Sitter, flat, and other configurations - is referred to as a 'arena'. This paper focuses on examining arenas within the Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker spacetime models. We establish the stability of previously discovered arenas as the sole stable solutions in various time-evolution scenarios. Additionally, we use phase transition concepts to demonstrate that arenas are created from an initial state consisting of multiple coupled fields. This process is consistent with the principles of symmetry breaking. Furthermore, we use numerical methods to show that arenas consisting of two coupled fields are unstable and cannot persist. However, we propose that orphans - a specific type of arena consisting of a single, non-interacting field - may also represent a valid state of the system. We suggest that these orphans, which can be stabilized through the introduction of certain types of non-minimal curvature corrections, could serve as long-lasting time-evolution configurations. We observe that in models containing less than three times the minimum amount of curvature, these arena solutions become impossible, while in models exceeding this threshold, we find a maximum number of stable arena solutions available. Lastly, we use numerical methods to explore a wide range of spacetime models and, through varying the scale factor, determine the number of arena solutions that exist within these models. We discover that these arena solutions become nonexistent as the scale factor reaches a certain threshold and, in scenarios where the scale factor is much larger, we find a maximum number of arena solutions that can exist. We eventually plan to extend this work by considering the effects of coupled field interactions. We hope that these findings will be instrumental in informing future observations that pertain to the behavior of these arena configurations. In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in categorizing tumor cells from lymph node images. Using the Breslow depth measure as the basis for learning, we found that training a deep neural network in a decentralized setting of patient-derived image data produced comparable results with a centrally collected dataset of similar size. However, despite equating data sizes, the federated learning approach allowed us to decrease the required training iterations by up to 12 times. Notably, both training methods demonstrated similar levels of accuracy in categorizing tumor cells, with evaluations made on a patient-derived image dataset collected from 60 study participants and annotated by two pathologists. While the use of federated learning may offer improvements in training efficiency, it also presents potential risks of decreased model performance and potential biases in resulting models. Consequently, it is imperative that the effects of this approach be thoroughly evaluated to ensure its safety and efficacy in clinical applications. Potential solutions for mitigating these risks include collecting larger datasets, training models centrally, and using models transferred from pre-trained models as a means of alternative federated learning strategies. Moreover, incorporating formal error analysis as part of FL and using models that are simpler in complexity may also offer improvements in performance and reduce potential biases in resulting models. Additionally, the use of robust baselines in training models could also serve as an adaptive countermeasure for mitigating performance declines during FL. Nonetheless, the application of FL in medical image analysis holds great promise and, when utilized properly, may offer numerous advantages in training models without compromising accuracy or subjecting sensitive patient data to remote processing. The behavior of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) can be classified into two types, 
high-brightness and low-brightness, based on their spectral patterns. The 
spectral-line analysis of a low-brightness AGN in the galaxy NGC 7213 has shown 
that this type of AGN lacks hot emitters, contrary to the prediction of the hot 
emitters theory that would have produced both high- and low-brightness spectra. 
The absence of hot emitters is indicated by the lack of a specific emission signal, 
and the data show a better fit to a model that includes only two emitters when compared 
to a model that includes three emitters. Additionally, the analysis reveals that 
NGC 7213's emission spectra are consistent with the spectra of a black hole with mass 
approximately seven times that of our sun, and that the emission emission lines 
originating from the galaxy and black hole can be adequately explained by two 
emitters with temperatures of approximately 0.35 and 6.3 million degrees Kelvin. 
The lack of a third emitter emitting at a temperature of approximately 100 million 
degrees Kelvin that was expected from the hot emitters theory is notable in this 
observation. The analysis takes into consideration three possible non-AGN factors that 
could have caused this observation - a star formation process previous to the galaxy's 
observation, a process of absorption by galactic dust and the presence of a non-AGN 
breeze in the galaxy. The presence of a non-AGN breeze in the galaxy that was 
predicted but not observed until now is indicated in the data. The analysis reveals 
that the presence of a non-AGN breeze in the galaxy can adequately explain this 
observation by supposing that the galaxy's low-brightness spectral-type high-brightness 
spectra emission-line ratio is decreased by a factor of 0.3 and that this breeze 
emits primarily at two emitters with temperatures of approximately 0.35 and 6.3 million 
degrees Kelvin that are indistinguishable from emitters within the galaxy and black hole. 
The analysis reveals that this breeze has a temperature, and thus energy, that is 
consistent with predictions from the theory of black hole spin-down. The analysis 
estimates that the mass and rate of mass loss of this breeze are approximately 0.06 and 
0.00006 times those of our sun, and that this breeze is approximately 0.00006 times 
the mass of our sun.

We explored a situation in which both a direct controller and an indirect manager lacked knowledge of the system dynamics, and we had access to a numerical system model but no analytical formula to represent it. Under these conditions, the manager could adjust the direct controller's settings to optimize performance, but this was challenging because the manager needed to estimate how changing the settings would affect the system's behavior, and direct feedback was limited. To overcome these issues, we developed a two-phase learning process. In the first phase, the manager uses the direct controller's feedback to create an informative model of the system's behavior through trial and error. In the second phase, we utilize this model to identify the controller settings that yield the best performance outcome, and we found that this two-phase approach worked effectively in our study. Specifically, we tested the approach using a nonlinear aircraft system with multiple engines and defined performance metrics, and we found that it allowed the manager to optimize the direct controller's settings and achieve better outcomes. Furthermore, we observed that our approach allowed the manager to develop an effective system model without requiring knowledge of the system dynamics, and we found that utilizing the manager's utilization of the direct controller led to better results. Additionally, we noted that our approach resulted in less oscillatory behavior when testing the system's responsiveness to disturbances and the effectiveness of the controller. Based on these findings, we believe that our approach provides a useful model-free strategy for optimizing controller performance without requiring knowledge of the system dynamics, and we found that the manager's ability to utilize the direct controller was crucial to its effectiveness. Furthermore, we observed that our approach resulted in comparable performance to methods that assumed knowledge of the system dynamics, and we found that the manager's model of the system's behavior was durable against changes in the system's operating conditions. Specifically, we tested the approach by simulating various scenarios, and we found that the manager's model allowed it to adjust the direct controller's settings effectively. Ultimately, we believe that our approach provides a practical and effective model-free strategy for optimizing controller performance without requiring knowledge of the system dynamics, and we found that the manager's ability to utilize the direct controller was crucial to its effectiveness. Additionally, we observed that our approach resulted in comparable performance to methods that assumed knowledge of the system dynamics, and we found that the manager's model of the system's behavior was durable against changes in the system's operating conditions. Satellite imagery allows for cost-effective monitoring of the entire Earth, facilitating research in environmental protection, navigation, transportation, and military applications. This survey presents an alternative framework, EarthNets, for leveraging AI in Earth observation systems via satellite imagery. EarthNets specifically addresses double infections in images, incorporating machine learning and crowdsourcing. This approach is demonstrated through BibNets, a novel database system that maintains graph representations of events and their temporal correlations. Furthermore, JayNets is introduced as an AI-driven method for detecting objects in BibNets. These contributions can be applied to various applications, such as threat detection and environmental protection, and have been implemented in a working prototype that utilizes distributed technology for data retrieval and user interaction. Overall, this survey outlines opportunities and challenges for integrating AI into Earth observation systems."

This paper introduces ReAD, an open-source toolkit designed to identify performance issues at the process level on Linux systems. Per-process data is analyzed to detect anomalies in runtime behavior. An optimized algorithm is utilized to divide memory into equal segments, allowing for in-place calculation of statistical characteristics without unnecessary data copying. As a result, ReAD operates at a process-level and system-scale to effectively identify performance issues. An evaluation using thousands of addresses as training data confirms the feasibility and effectiveness of this method. Further research is suggested to refine this approach and establish a baseline for performance optimization. You can obtain the ReAD toolkit at: https://github.com/dragonflymb/ReAD. The abstrakt solution aims to create a universal abstract representation of code that can be learned from real-world examples, unaffected by specific programming languages. This abstract representation is expected to capture code semantics, enabling tasks like code debugging, vulnerability detection, and plagiarism checking. The proposed method involves constructing a graph from source code and employing a graph neural network (GNN) to generate the abstract representation. Since direct source code-to-graph conversion is susceptible to errors, the abstrakt solution uses weak supervision through the analysis of stack traces to create conceptually related nodes. Furthermore, the model's capacity to generate abstract representations is enhanced by leveraging external knowledge through weighted inter-graph edges that connect similar code segments. Experimental results demonstrate that the abstrakt solution outperforms existing code analysis techniques. Moreover, the developed model exhibits notable improvements in downstream tasks, specifically code debugging and vulnerability detection. To facilitate wider adoption, the accompanying open-source toolkit includes a full-fidelity training dataset, training scripts, and a serving API. This study reviews cutting-edge research using photometry from stars to assess aerosols in the atmosphere. We provide a detailed examination of the most recent developments in the method, including new approaches that utilize fast-time resolution observations of stellar fields. These advancements focus on the optical measurement of aerosols, albeit some of these studies also incorporate auxiliary observations such as satellite data to derive the aerosol amount. Several innovative features of these methods are discussed, including the use of machine learning and artificial intelligence to improve the aerosol estimation, as well as methods that leverage photometry of rapid variations in the solar brightness (e.g. flares) to improve local aerosol mapping. The review concludes with a discussion of key challenges associated with integrating the stated methods into global aerosol monitoring networks. Additionally, we explore the feasibility of integrating the stated methods into existing solar radiation measurement networks to enhance accuracy in solar radiation forecasting and climate impact assessment. It is also noted that integrating these methods on a larger scale may contribute to the development of a ground-based network capable of complementing satellite measurements at specific locations. This could be particularly beneficial in locations with frequent cloud cover, areas lacking satellite coverage, or regions where satellite data is expensive or unavailable. Utilizing a combination of these methods at ground stations and integrating them with satellite data could lead to the establishment of a combined, powerful tool for aerosol monitoring and solar radiation forecasting on a local or regional scale. Such an approach could potentially utilize ground-based and satellite data in conjunction with other auxiliary observations such as surface measurements of solar irradiance to develop a more comprehensive understanding of atmospheric aerosols and improve solar radiation forecasting. This could ultimately lead to better estimates of the impact of aerosols on the climate and a reduced underestimation of this impact, as shown in previous studies. Moreover, this approach may facilitate re-analysis of existing data collected over many years to investigate long-term changes in aerosols and their effects on the climate. Crucially, it is observed that integrating these methods could aid in detecting abrupt environmental changes and distinguishing between natural and anthropogenic aerosols. Finally, it is observed that integrating these methods could aid in improving model representations of aerosols and their impacts on the climate, as well as detecting signs of COVID-19-related changes in aerosols. We introduce a new method, dynamically weighted inertial forward-backward (DWIFOB), to tackle structured monotone inclusion problems. By incorporating the forward-backward algorithm and the extrapolation technique from Anderson acceleration, we develop a method that converges at a rate comparable to $O(k^2)$. Furthermore, we prove that under certain conditions, DWIFOB converges exponentially, and through numerical tests, we verify its superior performance. Moreover, we show that taking limits sequentially and dynamically can lead to an alternating proximal point method (AltPPM) that converges exponentially as well. Notably, DWIFOB's formula includes the parameters of AltPPM, allowing for the creation of various variants of DWIFOB by adjusting those parameters. Finally, we demonstrate that DWIFOB can be employed to solve distinct monotone inclusion problems such as complementarity, Laprojective, and splitting problems. Our code is open-source and accessible at https://github.com/tiebinng/DWIFOB. Recent breakthroughs in neural networks have led to a surge in interest in applying deep learning to computer-aided neural design. However, developing effective controllers for neural networks remains a significant challenge. This work proposes using the Property-Directed Synthesis (PDS) framework to guide the development of deep learning controllers through the specification of design objectives in PDS. Notably, controllers derived using this method demonstrate strong generalization capabilities across various application scenarios, surpassing the performance of traditional training methods. Moreover, incorporating controllers into deep learning training further enhances design outcomes, making the system more robust and efficient. Controllers can also be reused without undergoing retraining, as our experiments successfully demonstrate. We evaluated our method with three case studies involving the design of filters, tone mapping operators, and image restoration processes. These case studies not only showcased the efficacy of our method but also highlighted the potential for deep learning controllers to be applied in a broad range of neural design applications. The search space created by these controllers also offers a unique perspective on designing neural networks. To facilitate the use of deep learning controllers for neural design, we developed a Python framework featuring a user-friendly interface and several design search tools. This framework, known as NeuroDesignSearch, is designed to make it both simple and efficient to apply deep learning controllers to neural design problems. Further information on NeuroDesignSearch, as well as the accompanying code, can be found at https://github.com/st-hk-neural-design-search/NeuroDesignSearch. Additionally, a demo showcasing the design of a 6-layer convolutional neural network using NeuroDesignSearch is available at https://neural-design-st-hk.search.automation.ai/design/conv2+.html. This demo not only highlights our method's capabilities in neural design but also offers an interactive design search experience. As our work, NeuroDesignSearch, becomes a reliable tool for neural design, it paves the way for the widespread application of deep learning controllers in computer-aided neural design. Moreover, it also further solidifies the connection between PDS and deep learning, demonstrating the immense potential for these controllers to be applied across a diverse range of design domains. Therefore, we strongly believe that PDS has the great potential to revolutionize the design space. To evaluate this, we selected three design objectives in PDS, specifically the application of deep learning controllers to design objectives in PDS. Notably, our experiment successfully showcased the specifications of these design objectives and effectively controlled the behavior of neural networks, making PDS a highly effective tool for designing neural networks.

This research paper explores the concept of hybrid spatially concatenated
signaling as a promising solution to mitigate signal strength decline in mmWave
communications over long distances. To build upon this idea, we develop a novel
encoding technique that combines spatially separated symbols with a single
antenna, utilizing multiple input feeds. A specific implementation, the
Multi-Group Broadcasting (MGB) hybrid encoding technique, is created by
segmenting the antenna array into several groups, with each transmitting a
distinct symbol. To maximize the overall throughput of MGB-encoded systems,
an optimization problem is formulated and solved using the alternating
optimization method. This enables each group to optimize its beamforming
vectors and input signals in response to others. Furthermore, our findings
reveal that MGB-encoded systems can achieve higher throughput compared to
conventional hybrid systems. To accelerate performance evaluation in 3D
mmWave environments, a simplified channel model is introduced. Finally, our
simulations demonstrate that MGB-encoded systems can deliver improved
throughput and higher spectral efficiency compared to hybrid systems. The
results also show that using four groups in MGB encoding yields superior
performance to using two groups. Crucially, our findings are validated against
both benchmark and alternative hybrid encoding techniques, including Non-Cooperative Broadcasting (NCB) and Uplink Commonization (UC). Note that NCB is a special case of MGB with only one group, while UC is another hybrid encoding technique that uses a single input signal. To provide a more comprehensive understanding, our encoding ideas are also applied to the scenarios of minimizing interference and creating private beams. The latter can be seen as a hybrid encoding approach to achieve private beams. To prevent a flood of redundant data and promote fairness, a throughput-maximizing power allocation scheme is developed for MGB-encoded systems. The proposed encoding technique has the potential to be further integrated into other hybrid systems, where its performance can be evaluated using alternating optimization and a range of tools. Federated Learning adoption has been hindered by communication challenges. Federated Distillation offers a potential solution by transferring model parameters and intermediate values to facilitate local data interpretation. However, this distillation approach comes with its own communication limitations. To address this issue, we introduce Local Distillation Refactoring, a technique that reworks remote models to require less information to be transmitted. Specifically, only the last layer's activation is shared, thereby reducing communication load without incurring accuracy loss. Experimental results confirm that our approach can train models without parameter transmission, thus surpassing the accuracy of baseline models and outperforming existing comparison benchmarks. Notably, this enhancement is achievable without local data aggregation in Federated Distillation, thus opening up new possibilities for communication efficiency in this paradigm. In many practical multi-objective optimization tasks, such as designing aircraft and finding the best treatment for cancer, different objectives are not given equal importance.  While some tasks require objectives to be treated as equals, optimizing preferences is crucial in others.  Historically, different techniques have been employed to handle these varying importance levels.  Some methods cap an objective's influence, while others derive a customized utility function to reflect an objective's relative importance.  1) How effective is capping an objective's influence in realistic optimization domains?  2) Can a customized utility function be learned effectively?  To address these questions, the authors studied multi-objective optimization with diverse importance levels in realistic domains.  This research is the first to thoroughly examine how well current optimization techniques perform in such domains. By incorporating adjustable Dirac points into a 2D lattice, we find that its symmetry is characterized by a c-time period. Utilizing a 2D lattice based on a hexagonal pattern with quasicrystalline properties, we demonstrate that the incidence of Dirac points is dependent on zone indexing and the type of crystal rotation symmetry present. When zone indexing changes, the locations of Dirac points can be adjusted. Additionally, introducing crystal rotation symmetry results in the occurrence of Dirac zeros instead of Dirac points. Depending on the type of symmetry, the number of adjustable Dirac zeros within a Brillouin zone may be 0, 1, or 2. This theory can be applied to various quasicrystalline structures featuring hexagonal patterns, as well as conventional crystalline structures with larger unit cells. Potential experimental implementation can be carried out using scanning tunneling spectroscopy or scanning tunneling microscopy on materials such as Au-Ga, Si(111)(7x7), and Pt/Ga surfaces. Software development teams utilizing Bug Tracking Systems (BTSs) collect historical data on recorded problems, which can be applied to improve and demonstrate the effectiveness of proposed solutions and methodologies.  Despite these benefits, most published studies rely on the same limited dataset, obtained from a single BTS repository.  This study presents an alternative dataset derived from the public Jira repository of 57 software projects, encompassing 33,416 problems and their updates.  This new dataset offers enhanced diversity in technology, team size, and problem update frequency.  It also includes detailed problem description, associated components, and recorded statuses.  To facilitate dataset usage, the research team developed a series of analytical methods and visual demonstrations to help developers and researchers demonstrate the utility of their solutions and experiments.  This dataset, as well as accompanying code and documentation, is accessible through a research repository, while research results based on this dataset are shared through research papers.  This research is intended to contribute to the BTS community by supplying necessary resources for systematic evaluations of BTS functionality.  This work is valued at $10,000 in services offered by ResearchSoft.  This dataset is deemed suitable for testing various BTS techniques, such as data mining, and can be utilized for training machine learning models to support BTS operations.  Additionally, the dataset could support evaluations of developer tools and methodologies focused on writing readable and comprehensive problem descriptions, as well as assigning problem labels and tracking problem updates.  This research is significant because it seeks to evaluate and demonstrate the efficacy of numerous methodologies and tools for enhancing BTS processes.  This research is significant due to its extensive dataset size and diversity, offering an alternative to existing datasets for researchers and developers.  This research is significant due to its systematic approach, developing novel resources for evaluating and demonstrating BTS methodologies.  This research is significant due to its broad applications, including training machine learning models, testing BTS techniques, and evaluating developer tools and methodologies.  This research is significant due to its public availability of resources, including the dataset, research results, and accompanying code and documentation. This research offered insights into the relationships between problem descriptions, associated components, and recorded statuses. In distributed machine learning, aggregating local model updates into a centralized server is often done using techniques like stochastic averaging, yet this approach can lead to slow convergence and unsatisfactory accuracy. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a family of higher-order aggregation methods that surpass linear and quadratic aggregation methods. By utilizing a novel class of non-linear aggregation functions, we formulate an efficient model updating procedure for distributed machine learning, demonstrating its higher computational efficiency compared to existing methods. To rigorously evaluate our proposal, we develop a mathematical framework that provides a precise bound on the rate of convergence for our model. Furthermore, we conduct comprehensive numerical experiments to assess the performance of our high-order aggregation method under real-world conditions. The results show that it achieves substantial improvements in convergence speed and accuracy compared to existing techniques. The code for these numerical experiments is openly available at GitHub. A major breakthrough in developing a scalable quantum computer relies on perfecting the process of mapping and identifying individual atoms within a material structure. Although atomic defects have been the focus of research for decades, no system has been developed yet that can efficiently capture and identify individual atoms within a diffraction pattern. This paper presents a solution to this challenge by proposing an innovative optical lattice trap that utilizes an anisotropic triangular structure. This innovative design captures over 99% of atoms and provides the lattice trap with an extremely high resolution, allowing for precise identification of the atoms' positions. This breakthrough is made possible by a unique arrangement of lasers that creates diffractions on multiple sides, resulting in a unique set of patterns that can accurately represent the positions of the atoms. Additionally, the system can be scaled up to utilize smaller detection patterns without compromising its performance. This design serves as a model for constructing a quantum computer using defect-based spin qubits. This research also presents a new approach for simulating and designing complex optical potentials using a coherent structure, enabling the creation of atom patterns that can help understand complex phenomena. This innovative design may also be used for applications such as atom-based simulation, magnetic resonance microscopy, and coherent diffraction imaging. Finally, this research outlines possible pathways for implementing this design using existing experimental setups with minimal modifications. This innovation can capture and identify individual atoms through a diffraction pattern with high resolution and efficiency, paving the way for a scalable quantum computer and new insights into diffraction physics. In a variety of applications such as data classification and price prediction, regression models are commonly used. However, direct application of regression models to derive complex products like polymers based on composition is impractical due to the need for numerical values of materials that are not available. A potential solution to this problem lies in the application of integer optimization techniques that can handle discrete data. Research has shown that a two-stage approach, first using regression models to derive intermediate products and then using integer optimization to combine these products, can yield accurate and efficient results. This study presents an alternative method where integer optimization is used alone to directly derive final products based on composition. Furthermore, research has shown that a technique known as the Technique for Derived Polymers based on Linear Regression, or TDPL, can achieve a balanced level of accuracy and computational efficiency. This TDPL approach involves combining multiple regression models and using integer optimization to derive final products based on composition. To assess the effectiveness of this technique, computational tests were conducted using standard benchmarks and the results showed that TDPL can yield competitive outcomes. Specifically, the method outperformed a widely used commercial software solution in both computational efficiency and resilience to changes in problem scale. Furthermore, the results demonstrated that TDPL can remain effective and efficient even when dealing with extremely large and complex problems. Lastly, the research involved determining whether the underlying mechanisms of TDPL could be generalized to other applications beyond the derivation of polymers. Based on the results, the study concluded that TDPL presents a novel and innovative approach that can be effectively utilized in diverse domains. Additionally, the research highlighted potential avenues for further research, including the exploration of other linear regression models and the incorporation of probabilistic techniques. Also under consideration is a novel formulation of the polymer derivation problem that incorporates a novel solution strategy. This formulation could potentially lead to more efficient solutions, especially in very large problems. On the other hand, the current TDPL approach may hold more value in practicing operations research and management scientists due to its already demonstrated effectiveness and ease of implementation. Conversely, the study's findings may not be suitable for the derivation of polymers, but rather the research presents a new and interesting approach that can be utilized in various domains. Lastly, the results may be utilized to develop a machine learning model and compare it with existing commercial software. This comparison could then be used to develop a more efficient and effective linear programming model. This research was previously presented at the 2022 INFORMS Conference. Portable ventilators play a crucial role in delivering life-saving respiratory support in intensive care and can be effectively improved through optimization using mathematical models. By formulating a problem involving patient respiration, it is possible to apply optimization techniques in order to enhance ventilator performance. This research utilizes a patient model through direct transcription of continuous optimization problems, resulting in function and Jacobian values. Due to the absence of underlying variables, direct transcription lacks sparsity, thereby complicating the application of specialized interior-point methods. By introducing simple displacement variables, we reformulate the problem to maintain sparsity, enabling more efficient computations. This research demonstrates a novel approach for tackling complex, high-dimensional optimization problems involving continuous dynamics. Additionally, we highlight the importance of rigorous modeling in state estimation for ventilator control during the COVID-19 pandemic. Our model effectively balances simplicity and precision, and we show that our proposed method can significantly reduce computation time while achieving better results. While this conformal measure is deterministic, its associated dimension can take various values, resulting in different graph properties. Conversely, a measure with a certain dimension exactly equal to one will have a spectral dimension between one and two, indicating randomly fast random walk behavior. Our investigation involves gathering a vast database of signatures via various devices and incorporating a comprehensive validation process to ensure accuracy. By utilizing a complex statistical model, we identify and quantify the uniqueness of each signature. Additionally, we analyze the intricacy of each signature through the assessment of its features and compare its reliability to that of traditional biometric data. The presence of a localized charge defect in a two-dimensional electron gas results in the formation of spin-vortex crystals, characterized by spin-textures that extend beyond the defect's confines. Using a semi-analytical approach for the generalized Hartree-Fock method, researchers have studied the spin-vortex configurations of two localized charge defects in the context of type-I superfluidity of spin-polarized electrons. These findings indicate that higher-order spin-vortex arrangements emerge, in contrast to the second-order spin-textures observed in previous studies on a single defect. Specifically, the polylobed structure of the spin-textures is shown to transition into a chain of lobes as the electron density decreases. Furthermore, simulations based on the Hartree-Fock model suggest that these spin-textures may persist due to the exchange energy associated with spin-polarization, despite the absence of a true topological phase transition. Ultimately, these findings offer insights into the spin-textures formed by a localized charge defect through an analogy with magnetic skyrmions. Lastly, researchers explore the spin-textures that would arise if the electron gas were able to exhibit true topological phase transitions. In such a scenario, the spin-textures would be determined solely by the defect's shape function, giving rise to spin-polarized domains that are anatomically equivalent to the spin-vortex configurations observed in the Hartree-Fock simulations. However, these domain walls would be topologically non-trivial, as demonstrated through numerical solutions of the Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations governing the quasiparticle states of the electron gas. In particular, the realization of a spin-vortex phase without any exchange energy constraints, as seen in a system of hard-core bosons, suggests that the spin-textures could consist of a linked configuration of higher-order polymers. The conditions necessary to observe this scenario are discussed. In order to experimentally observe these spin-textures, researchers suggest utilizing local probes such as scanning tunneling microscopy or local magnetic resonance techniques, or the creation of artificial defect structures using advanced nanofabrication techniques. The implementation of such experiments could provide a direct visual assessment of the spin-textures and enable a comparison with the theoretical predictions outlined in this study. In conclusion, this research has contributed to a deeper understanding of the complex spin-textures formed by a localized charge defect in a two-dimensional electron gas, as well as the associated topological properties that give rise to unique quantum phases of matter. The study has further elucidated the interplay between disorder, interactions, and topology

Graph modeling in biomedical science has yielded significant results, 
enabling the accurate interpretation of complex biomedical data through 
unsupervised and supervised techniques. Biomedical datasets, characterized 
by heterogeneous and interconnected nature of their components, are ideally 
represented using graph models. Various applications in biomedical science have 
benefited from graph modeling across different stages of data collection, 
analysis, and visualization. Notably, graph modeling has facilitated tasks 
such as disease diagnosis, pathogen prediction, patient clustering, tissue 
classification, cell characterization, and drug targeting, among others. 
Furthermore, advancements in machine learning and biomedical sciences have 
created opportunities for incorporating diverse graph models into these tasks. 
In this article, we review the recent applications of graph modeling in 
biomedicine, summarize typical challenges in this field, and discuss the 
ongoing trends and future directions for biomedical graph modeling and machine 
learning. Examples of graph model success stories in biomedical science are 
presented to demonstrate their efficacy and impact. Additionally, we analyze 
biomedical applications of graph modeling across different data collection, 
analysis, and visualization stages to identify trends and areas of improvement. 
Based on this analysis, we discuss future directions for biomedical graph 
modeling and machine learning. Overall, graph modeling has become a vital tool 
for working with biomedical data, and its continuous evolution will lead to 
further successes in biomedical machine learning. To share our research more

This technical report presents a method called complete least squares (CLS) that offers an efficient way to calculate the best fit for nonlinear measurement models, especially when working with noisy data. We provide a straightforward formula that can be used for a range of parameter estimation problems, including those involving one, two, or three unknowns. We then develop an iterative approach for solving equations that don't have straightforward analytic solutions, such as those that arise in maximum likelihood estimation. We compare the performance of CLS with other established methods, like least squares (LS) and maximum likelihood estimation. The results show that CLS offers a strong alternative, but it requires additional computational resources. Ultimately, we find that the success of CLS in estimating parameters depends on the underlying nonlinearities in the measurement model. If the model is linear, CLS performs similarly to LS; however, if there are significant nonlinear effects involved, CLS is capable of providing more accurate estimates. Due to its high computational demands, we recommend CLS for applications where fast processing times are a top priority. Instead, LS is more suitable for use cases where rapid processing is essential. Further research is needed to further optimize the CLS method. Key areas for further research and development identified in this report are state estimation, Kalman filters, biogeocentric cartography, forward geodesy, inverse geodesy, and modeling the Earth's rotation. Researchers are encouraged to apply the CLS method to these areas to appreciate its benefits firsthand. Our findings may also contribute to the development of more effective algorithms for software maintenance and image processing. However, our study discovered that in the Hubbard chain with random site potentials, at low energies near the ground state, a delocalized crossovers occurs for any interaction strength greater than the critical $U_c \approx 1.6$. For $U>U_c$, a small amount of low-energy, degenerate, delocalized state exists, characterized by a power-law decrease in low-energy excitations. The excitation spectrum of this state is not influenced by interactions, resulting in a contradiction of Lieb's theorem. The state's nature is similar to a random singlet state observed in systems with antiferromagnetic interactions and is considered a semi-frustrated state caused by disorder and interaction. The methodology employed includes numerical exact diagonalization and variational approaches such as the Gutzwiller, matrix product, and density matrix renormalization group techniques. Furthermore, the emergence of power-law behavior prompted an analysis of renormalization group flow, which suggested the associated instability to be related to a Weyl Fermi surface present in the unpinned state. The Ginzburg number $G$ and the critical damage number $D_c$ were also determined, with findings indicating that $D_c \approx 0.57$, $G \approx 0.34$, or $G \approx 0.45$ depending on $U$, which implies that very weak disorder can delocalize electrons. Our research provides evidence that interacting quantum systems can exhibit unexpected delocalization due to disorder, resulting in atypical states that fail to conform to established paradigms. The associated physical phenomena, such as non-interacting-induced power-law behavior and the breakdown of Lieb's theorem, should also be addressed by theorists. The underlying mechanisms can potentially be extended to apply to three-dimensional systems that exhibit similar power-law behavior. Finally, the delocalization induced by disorder is significant as it may lead to a breakdown in the semi-metals' property of easy ferromagnetic spin alignment and could also inhibit superconductivity. Moreover, the effects of interactions and disorder could be interchangeable, which may have far-reaching implications for the quantization of conductance and the occurrence of non-zero total spin in the ground state. In cases where multiple agents exert influence over a single agent's choices, inverse reinforcement learning becomes complicated by limited clarity on what constitutes a valid reward system. To address this issue, we suggest a straightforward theoretical framework that can incorporate partial influence through probabilistic means, utilizing a hierarchical Bayesian model to establish a connection between the shared assumptions underlying multiple reward systems and their corresponding effects on an agent's behavior. We demonstrate the utility of this framework in a controlled environment involving a robot's navigation, where a supervisor partially guides its decision-making, influenced by a common underlying principle. We show that our proposed framework results in a more focused concentration of learning the underlying reward system, when compared to a scenario without partial influence. Additionally, we find that our framework facilitates smoother transitions between unregulated and partially-influenced settings, as compared to unguided learning in such situations. These benefits are documented in both the simulated environment and in videos showcasing our robot's behavior in a physically challenging setting. The past several years have seen preprints experience rapid and significant growth, 
particularly in fields such as physics and biology where the impact is most pronounced.
This article delves into the history of preprints from the beginning of the arXiv decade (1991-2000) 
and forecasts its future in the broader science community. Key factors contributing to preprints' success include 
user-friendly online platforms, standardised submission processes, and the substantial reliance of researchers on the internet.
These elements have streamlined preprints into an integral part of research and significantly influenced scientific outcomes.
As a result of these developments, we expect preprints to continue playing a vital role in research and ultimately become the standard practice. 
Bare preprints will emerge as a prominent force, especially in fields where preprints dominate, and in combination with other approaches such as research data and citizen science. 
Ultimately, the shift towards preprints will revolutionise the way research is conducted, significantly altering the landscape of publishing and citation practices. 
It remains to be seen if green roadmaps, allowing authors to link preprints to published articles, will survive or disappear in the face of open preprints.
Furthermore, we must address the challenges posed by preprints, such as quality control and research funding, and make necessary changes to existing policies and procedures to make preprints the new standard. 
If these issues can be resolved, we can anticipate a future where preprints serve as the dominant model, and efforts are underway to make preprints the primary means of research dissemination. 
In this context, we examine different scenarios for different fields of research and the role of preprints in funding decisions, ultimately concluding that preprints are essential for evaluating research proposals and making informed funding decisions. 
In this light, we contend that preprints, particularly open preprints, mark a profound transformation in science, and our predictions for the future of preprints are cause for both optimism and concern. 
Ultimately, the preprint decade will go down in history as a remarkable scientific achievement, and the preprint century will be remembered as a monumental turning point for scientific publications. 
On this note, we present the numbers that tell the story of preprints, highlighting their significant impact and the profound implications for scientific research and publication. 
In this spirit, we propose a new approach to research management, one that prioritises preprints and is tailored to the needs of researchers and readers alike. 
We must be flexible and adapt to the changing landscape of preprints, and our predictions for the future of preprints

In response to the ongoing pandemic, higher education in India has been disrupted since March 2020, with lectures and exams transitioning entirely to online delivery. To minimize disruption to their teaching duties, relaxation of assessment standards has been implemented by many instructors, with some rewarding students with lower performance through smaller assignments or modified assessments. To accommodate this changed landscape, many educators are rethinking their assessment strategies to suit their students' new realities. 

This discussion paper presents arguments for and against ways to adapt educational standards during unprecedented circumstances, with examples from our own online studio-based learning environment. We hope that by sharing our own experiences, other educators can draw inspiration and find relief during these unsettling times.

Furthermore, we demonstrate that for tunable iterative algorithms, a choice of step size exists that guarantees convergence to the minimum norm solution. For ill-conditioned problems, we implement a new convergence analysis based on the Lipschitz constant, allowing these algorithms to converge under weaker conditions. We also introduce a technique to expand the domain of convergence for each algorithm by utilizing a preconditioner. We illustrate the effectiveness of these techniques through numerical experiments involving sparse recovery, vector recovery with general norms, and phase retrieval. Additionally, we analyze the performance of these algorithms in conjunction with performance guarantees for the specific recovery tasks. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/pkostin/CSSchur. Enhancing click-through rate (CTR) is a critical goal for advertisers and advertising platforms. Current AI models primarily utilize user behavior data and often overlook visual content from advertisements, which has significant potential for improvement. To this end, we developed an advanced CTR prediction approach that not only leverages behavioral data but also analyzes the key elements of advertisements through a multi-modal deep learning framework. By designing a modular model with separate encoding modules for text, image, and auxiliary information, we can tap into the implicit knowledge contained within advertisements without compromising efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses state-of-the-art models by substantial margins, with a CTR enhancement rate of nearly 8%. Moreover, our model processes ads faster than industry standard models, making it suitable for real-world CTR forecasting applications. The effective utilization of visual content also facilitates the exploration of additional information, such as logos and app icons, which can further boost CTR forecasting quality. To facilitate broad adoption, the proposed model's source code, data, and advertising dataset are openly made available for other researchers and industry professionals to build upon. This technical document expands on a previously published article, exploring the concept of constraint enhancement for business process models. The article in question introduced the idea of specifying the maximum allowed occurrences of operations in business processes, a feature lacking in traditional process models. Building upon this foundation, this technical document delves into several key aspects of the enhanced process model, providing a formal definition of the concept and supporting it with a visual representation, as well as outlining the procedure for solving feasibility problems related to this new model. Furthermore, this technical document discusses how to address feasibility problems by limiting the magnitude of coefficient problems. A protocol is described for solving these feasibility problems, which involves converting them into their integer equivalent through the application of linear programming techniques. Additionally, this technical document examines feasibility problems in business processes with operations of a higher magnitude and presents a method for solving these problems, which involves manipulating the process model through the addition or removal of operations. Finally, this technical document addresses the concept of feasibility problems in business processes with operations of a variable magnitude and presents a method for solving these problems, which involves utilizing techniques such as cutting planes to modify the process model. The article concludes by outlining areas for further research inspired by the novel approaches presented here. Fisher's mean effect size in a study represents the average effect it would produce if all observations were equally distant from the mean effect value. However, this measure lacks causal implications, as demonstrated by its failure to consistently predict the results of permutation tests. To establish reliable range, additional estimates or assumptions about the shape of the causal curve are necessary. The behavior of mean effect size in certain types of studies, such as those analyzing non-random samples or binary data, can be misleading due to its tendency to underestimate effects and fail to accurately represent the underlying distribution. As a result, the mean effect size should not be relied upon for causal inferences and provides only limited insight into statistical results. Furthermore, the mean effect size's lack of causality is demonstrated by its failure to resolve the "replication crisis," as evident from the analysis of a large dataset containing information on 58,611 scientific studies. The effectiveness of online fundraising campaigns largely depends on crowd behavior patterns in social media. This study was conducted to provide valuable insights for content creators and marketers by analyzing the relationship between social media crowd behaviors and online fundraising success. We gathered and compared a vast amount of data from successful Kickstarter projects, Twitter, and Reddit to identify consistent patterns. From this data, we developed an algorithm to determine the optimal time to post content and increase the likelihood of gaining crowd support. The results of our research, performed on a dataset of 160 Kickstarter projects, showed that there are specific crowd behavior patterns in social media that can predict the success of online fundraising campaigns. Additionally, we found that moderaor approval can significantly impact the success of these campaigns. The strategies we identified can be utilized by content creators to design more effective campaigns and improve their chances of success. The code for this research can be accessed at https://github.com/JosephKamvar/OnlineFundraising. Additional research findings can be found at https://bit.ly/3aJ0V6N.

The task scheduling issue in Multi-Point Robotic Manipulation (MPRM) emerges as a significant challenge in both industry and academia, with various experimental and analytical methods having been investigated over time. This paper presents a new approach, Clustering-based Task Sequencing Method (CTSM), aimed at addressing MPRM sequencing as a combinatorial optimization problem. Initially, a task-oriented graph representation is established, where nodes correspond to tasks and their interactions are represented by time constraints. These constraints can then be grouped and optimized using a clustering approach, resulting in reduced clusters based on spatial correlations. A sequencing solution is then generated for each cluster, using their spatial characteristics to inform a greedy algorithm. The proposed method is further validated through analysis of its time complexity and practical demonstration of its efficiency in tackling a difficult MPRM sequencing instance. Compared to existing methods, CTSM is shown to outperform established benchmarks in terms of solution quality. Moreover, CTSM's runtime is remarkably shorter than other methods, with some examples taking only a few milliseconds to execute. The study highlights the significance of task clustering in advancing MPRM sequencing research and notes that CTSM represents an advancement in both theoretical and practical aspects. The method has been made available through a public repository, including both source code and example instances for verification. This research was financially supported by NSFC fund 71871123, 71901115, and 72171114. Additionally, it has undergone two rounds of peer review and revision to ensure the highest scientific standards. The research is part of a broader effort led by Li Zhang at Shanghai Jiao Tong University's Robotics Laboratory. Moreover, CTSM is a modular component of this research, contributing to the development of a clustering-based framework for robotic manipulation sequencing. The work has been influential in promoting this approach, using numerical examples to demonstrate its efficacy and establishing CTSM as a key module. Moreover, it has promoted the use of clustering-based methods in robotic manipulation sequencing through numerical examples and theoretical analysis. The research has been recognized through awards at the 2020 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation, where it was selected from a pool of 800 papers. The research is notable for its rigorous methodology, using numerical examples and theoretical foundations to validate its approach. Moreover, it has promoted the use of clustering-based methods in robotic manipulation sequencing and has been recognized through awards at IEEE conferences. The research has been financially supported by Fundamentals of Intelligent Systems. Additionally, it has been promoted through a series of seminars at Shanghai Jiao Tong University's Robotics Laboratory.

The concept of team synchrony in sports has gained significant attention, with research finding its application beyond sports, including teamwork in professional and everyday settings. Unlike other forms of synchrony that rely on identical external inputs, team synchrony emerges from members' individual perspectives and is influenced by varying parameters, such as timing and spacing. Our findings demonstrate that even small differences in timing can prevent true synchronization, while discrepancies in spacing can facilitate stable and robust team synchrony within certain limits. To maintain team synchrony, some team members may need to adjust their frequencies of movement, but when faced with multiple solutions, the one that requires the fewest and smallest adjustments by all team members is preferred. This study evaluates various scoring functions to evaluate and compare different states of team synchrony, with the goal of determining which state is 'best'. Our analysis also explores the challenge of identifying and weighting individual team members' opinions to achieve optimal performance. It is found that each team member has a valid opinion and that these opinions can be diverse, yet all contribute equally towards achieving a good score. A method is developed to aggregate these opinions uniformly, demonstrating that team synchrony with zero errors can be established through collective adjustment of the team members' views. Additionally, this study focuses on the situation in which some team members' opinions are similar or even identical, known as links within the team. It is found that these links can facilitate stable and robust team synchrony within certain limits and that each link contributes towards achieving a good score. Our analysis also explores the challenge of determining and evaluating these connections within the team. A method is developed to determine and evaluate these connections, as well as to calculate the scores that each team member and the team as a whole could potentially achieve. This study focuses on two types of scores, known as harmony and balance, which measure the stability and robustness of the team synchrony, respectively. It is found that each link within the team is either harmonious or imbalanced, and that these connections can be diversified to achieve better scores. Furthermore, this study focuses on the relationship between the links within the team and the frequencies at the team level, and finds that the team's cohesive structure allows it to achieve better scores. Additionally, this study evaluates the challenge of determining the frequencies at the team level from the individual member views, and finds that the team's cohesive structure allows it to achieve better scores when the frequencies are not constrained. The diversity of information sources can lead to differing results from information retrieval systems, which can suffer from a lack of diversity or present results biased towards certain sources. Various studies have analyzed the bias in search outcomes but often rely on manual annotation of information retrieval systems and can be difficult to conduct due to limited access. This paper presents a new approach to auditing bias in video search outcomes by using virtual agents to mimic human queries. Our method allows for the testing of existing major video search platforms' bias without requiring manual annotation. We apply this approach to examine the diversity of video search platforms and discover that YouTube and Vimeo exhibit no variety bias, while Google Video does. This research aims to contribute to developing a method that can efficiently determine the diversity of search platforms and helps design fair and diverse search APIs. It is the first study to utilize virtual agents to audit a variety of established video search platforms. We hope that this research will inspire more studies on auditing bias in video search outcomes. We also make available our code and data for replicating the study outcomes.

A new method is developed to estimate monodromy y-Intercepts of nonlinear sigma models, demonstrated through an analysis of the Wess-Zumino model. By iteratively solving bootstrap equations, the fourth y-Intercept is determined, confirming previous numerical outcomes while providing a theoretical foundation for future calculations. The approach is versatile and can be applied to other sigma models for higher accuracy loop calculations. The code used for these computations is publicly accessible at https://github.com/DudeSolutions/Wess-Zumino-Bootstrapping. The authors speculate that similar techniques could be useful for quantum field theories. The monodromy y-Intercepts as functions of g are investigated; interestingly, they exhibit asymptotic behavior akin to Regge trajectories in conformal field theory. The underlying system of bootstrap equations is analytic in g and exhibits a singular pattern; the points where the singularities occur are directly related to the values of t-g^2. The region between these singular points is where the fourth y-Intercept is calculated; the range can be extended to more complex expressions by incorporating additional monodromy y-Intercepts. The methodology can be applied not only to the Wess-Zumino model but also to other models, such as the hard-matter sigma model and the twisted superconformal theory. Graph Neural Networks have demonstrated exceptional potential in dealing with various graph-based challenges. However, graph data is scarce and labeling it becomes even more costly due to the complexity of graphs. Despite significant advancements in supervised learning, graph classification still struggles due to a lack of labeled data. To overcome this limitation, we propose an innovative pseudo-labeling technique that utilizes a limited set of available labels to generate high-quality pseudo-labels for unsupervised graph classification tasks. We based our technique on an ensemble of different graph predictors and incorporated constraints to ensure that pseudo-labels are consistent across different optimization methods. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we conducted extensive experiments on 5 publicly available datasets, comparing it to established few-shot learning methods. The results show that our technique surpasses the performance of baseline methods, achieving remarkable results, especially in scenarios with the use of high-quality ensemble pseudo-labels, and we plan to make our code available. Further details are available at https://grasp-ml.org/. Keywords: Graph Neural Networks, supervised learning, few-shot learning, pseudo-labeling, graph classification.

In Fermi fluids where Pauli's principle applies, we examine the impact of repulsive interactions among fermions beyond the framework of SU(N) generality. Utilizing Lanczos exact diagonalization, we investigate the complete many-body spectrum of a two-dimensional square lattice with nearest-neighbor Heisenberg-like interactions on small square clusters of 18 fermions, representing a marginally degenerate system with extensive fermionic excitations. Without reaching the regime of strong coupling, we locate the known two coupled systems in the low-energy sector and identify potential additional components. Utilizing SU(N) symmetry, we determine possible coupling systems of fermionic excitations as a result of the repulsive interactions, and employ diagrammatic techniques to study the Fermi surface, consistent with Luttinger's theorem for all fermionic excitations. We utilize this knowledge to analyze the Fermi surface and establish a relationship between the repulsive interactions and phase shifts of fermionic excitations as a result of the repulsive interactions, measured via Fermi liquid theory standards. We demonstrate that our findings are transferable to other Fermi systems by applying them to a examination of a Fermi liquid droplet, where interactions are also expected to result in phase shifts of bound fermionic excitations. This research explores an unconventional approach to robot navigation, where a robot follows a wall in a maze-like environment with dynamically changing dimensions. Unlike existing methods that rely on robot-specific parameters, this new technique uses unsupervised learning to learn an internal map of the environment. Without requiring knowledge of the robot's dimensions, this method relies solely on sensory input from a front-facing sensor. As the robot moves forward, this sensing data is used to update its internal map, allowing it to maintain alignment with the surrounding environment. Two instances of this navigation method are examined - one with a simplified red tape environment and another with a more complex black tape environment featuring intersections and branching paths. Results show that this navigation method is effective in both scenarios, allowing the robot to traverse the terrain with minimal deviations. Unlike existing wall-following robots, this technique is capable of navigating situations where the robot's dimensions are unknown, especially in scenarios involving narrow passages, corners, and intersections. The widespread use of IoT applications in diverse environments necessitates reliable and robust localization and tracking (LT) of mobile devices. Adverse weather conditions and complex geometries can severely impair the performance of location-based applications. Moreover, vulnerabilities in radio signal-based positioning methods to interference and multipath propagation make conventional techniques less reliable. This research introduces an innovative adaptive method to develop a robust LT solution, focusing on UBI-based IoT applications in indoor environments. The proposed approach combines an optimized positioning technique with a recurrent neural network-based anomaly detection method to detect and counteract adverse interference. It addresses the challenges of LT in inhomogeneous indoor environments by learning from the spatio-temporal characteristics of radio signals and constructing a predictiveLT model. Furthermore, it demonstrates a notable 99% resistance to various types of interference and a 40% lesser error rate in environments with complex geometries, compared to standard techniques. The developed framework is designed to be platform-independent and is implemented using MATLAB, with experimental validation in a simulated indoor environment mimicking real-world conditions. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/AmrAbouelkheir/ADPT.git. Based on these findings, this adaptive LT method has significant practical applications and could be utilized in various IoT applications, including smart healthcare, where accurate real-time tracking of mobile devices is critical. We demonstrate a geometrical duality between orthomodular lattices and subsets of a vector space with a positive definite inner product. This duality reveals the underlying structure of orthomodular lattices in terms of geometric principles. Furthermore, this method allows for a straightforward calculation of the cardinality of orthomodular lattices. Additionally, this approach is shown to be compatible with the existing partial order relation in orthomodular lattices. However, this geometric duality does not naturally preserve the join and meet operations. To address this issue, we develop a modification of this duality that preserves the algebraic structure of orthomodular lattices while maintaining key geometric features. Nevertheless, this modified duality is found to be imperfect and does not guarantee the preservation of the join and meet operations in all cases. To resolve this limitation, we establish a perfect geometric duality between certain sublattices of orthomodular lattices and geometric structures. This duality is shown to be equivalent to a established partial duality between orthomodular lattices and sublattices. Consequently, this geometric duality provides a alternative representation of orthomodular lattices based on geometric principles. We introduce a visualisation tool written in OCaml, embedded in Coq, for analysing proof trees generated from Coq proofs. These proof trees can be leveraged for metrics such as proving capabilities, hypothesis usage, and abstract interpretation. The embedded tool allows for easy integration with existing Coq projects, including macros for retrieving proof tree data and a command for visualising the trees. The source code is accessible via GitHub at https://github.com/jgpryor/coq-psv. This work is based on the author's MSc thesis, which can be found at https://eprints.soton.ac.uk/524124/. 

Please note that there's a limitation in the number of nodes that can be visualised (currently at 10000) due to performance constraints. The tool generates SVG images, which can be saved using a right-click in a web browser. For navigating through the proof tree, we recommend using Coq's existing ptree command or other analysis tools like coq-emoji or coq-gappa. The tool has been tested on Coq versions 8.6, 8.7 and 8.8.

If the residual vector of the linear system can be projected onto the null space of a given matrix, its behavior in relation to an orthonormal basis within that null space determines convergence. This orthogonality and convergence relationship holds analogously to the behavior of a gyrovector space. Furthermore, we introduce an alternative stopping criterion for inner solvers that relies on monitoring the angle between residual vectors and considers this criterion sufficient for terminating iterations in IPMs. This criterion is straightforward to calculate and does not require premature solution to the original linear equation system when sufficient convergence has been achieved. When inner solver termination is facilitated by this criterion, it has been found that solutions obtained are indistinguishable from those obtained through full convergence in IPMs. This has been verified through comparison with solutions obtained by solving the linear equation system directly and solving it through a quantum computer. The effectiveness of this criterion has been confirmed through interior point methods involving both barrier and weight functions. Additionally, we point out that while this new criterion may lead to inner solver solutions that are not exact, these solutions have been found to be useful for a wide range of applications. The halfspace depth effectively measures multivariate data's depth, 
allowing ranking with varying dimensions. Despite its beneficial characteristics, 
this method encounters difficulties with data points near the boundary, 
resulting in inaccurate depth values and a failure to maintain monotonicity. 
To overcome these limitations, we introduce a new depth measure based on the 
isometric log-ratio (ILR) transformation. This method applies the ILR transformation 
to positive multivariate data, then uses a modified version of the halfspace depth 
on the resulting coordinates. The resulting depth values are continuous, 
monotone, and valid for data near the boundary. Furthermore, we develop a plot 
called the depth profile, enabling effective visualization of multivariate data. 
We also propose an approach for estimating regression relationships using this new 
depth measure. To assess the performance of our method, we compared it with 
established depth measures and the conventional approach of linear regression 
on simulated and real-world datasets. The results demonstrate that our technique 
is comparable to the alternative methods for simulation data and better than 
linear regression on real-world data. The associated R code is available on GitHub 
at <https://github.com/jjzeng/ILRDepth>.

The High-Dimensional Ranking Lasso (HDRLL) problem involves selecting key performance measures to rank candidates by expected utility while controlling false positive rankings. The exoplanet desert around nearby stars that are observed using radial velocity techniques is primarily defined by its intensity in terms of the stellar mass. The idea that a low-mass inner planet with a short orbital period might prevent the formation or detection of a more massive planet around a star with a mass greater than 1.1 solar masses has been supported by various studies. The aim of this study is to assess whether this phenomenon occurs around stars with a mass less than 1.1 solar masses by analyzing a large dataset from the CORALIE/HARPS radial velocity programme. The dataset contained 1,660 inner planets with a mass less than three times that of the Earth and a orbital period less than 100 days by 804 stars with a mass less than 1.1 solar masses. The occurrence of the exoplanet desert around low-mass stars was assessed by comparing the number of planets in a given mass range in a test and mock samples. The result showed that the occurrence of the exoplanet desert around low-mass stars was not significant and could be attributed to detection biases. The discovery rules from this study are as follows: (1) there is no significant decrease in the number of planets per unit mass around low-mass stars with a mass less than 1.1 solar masses when compared with a test sample; (2) the most significant decrease in the number of planets per unit mass around low-mass stars with a mass less than 1 solar mass occurred in the super-Earth region; (3) the most significant decrease in the number of planets per unit mass around giant planets with a mass greater than 30 Earth masses occurred in the period range from 100 to 1000 days. The result of this study contradicts the outcome of another study that used the same dataset and is attributed to the differing definitions of the exoplanet desert. To counteract the biases in Attention Mechanism, we've developed a new de-biasing approach that increases performance without requiring labeled data. Our approach works by removing the effects of attention weights on input vectors so that they no longer favor certain dimensions or attributes. We use a normalisation technique that shares information across all elements, resulting in a noisier estimate of the original un-biased attention weights. We have successfully applied this method to a range of models, including Transformer, Multi-Head Attention, Graph Attention Networks and MatchNet. Experimental results show that this technique leads to improved performance and more stable training, particularly in graph classification tasks. This study re-evaluates global averaging techniques from a perspective rooted in optimal transport theory. We establish their connection to Wasserstein gradient flows and develop a novel interpretation of averaging processes as solutions to partial differential equations. Our analysis sheds light on the role of transport matrices in averaging procedures and leads us to introduce a new scheme that integrates transport matrices with averaging processes. To illustrate the generality of our approach, we derive an original averaging scheme for non-convex kernel functions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of our framework to a broad class of problems, including non-smooth loss functions, multi-mixture models, and kernelized dynamics. To facilitate practical application, we present a set of feasible rules for constructing transport matrices that can be used to solve various machine learning tasks. We showcase the performance of our approach on benchmark datasets and highlight its superiority to existing state-of-the-art averaging methods. Additionally, we empower learning algorithms to tackle an even broader range of problems by tackling issues of non-expressiveness, sparsity, and identifiability through regularization techniques based on optimal transport. These regulatory mechanisms can be easily integrated into our proposed framework and provide additional benefits to existing methods. Our analytical findings, supported by numerical experiments, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach and its potential applications. Crucially, our work provides a unified understanding of global averaging techniques and their connection to optimal transport theory, paving the way for further innovation in this domain. thus researchers typically use pre-trained models to streamline the process. 
The primary goal is to identify ideal initial pre-training and the required data quantity for effective semantic segmentation. 
Counterintuitively, we found that training models on depth estimation, which seems unrelated to segmentation, yielded better pre-trained models than classification.
We theorize that depth estimation and segmentation share similar challenges, 
specifically predicting a low-frequency, continuous output and dealing with ambiguous and partially occluded pixels. 
To validate our assumption, we assessed various pre-training objectives and observed that extending multi-task learning to incorporate depth estimation significantly improves segmentation performance, 
even when accompanied by common classification tasks. 
The novel technique necessitates minimal adjustments to current frameworks and can be applied to a wide range of models without relying on binary or multi-class classification data. 
Consequently, we believe that depth estimation can serve as an valuable additional task for training semantic segmentation models. 
The code is publicly available at https://github.com/focallength/depth-estimation-for-semseg.

which demonstrates the potential benefits of depth estimation as a pre-training objective for semantic segmentation.

The integration of depth estimation and segmentation can further be improved by incorporating other sensor forms, like monocular or stereo RGB, as well as LiDAR, for a more substantial boost in performance. 
Ultimately, we think that depth estimation can serve as an valuable additional task for enhancing the training of semantic segmentation models and improving their overall efficiency and quality.
