Generating coherent and detailed stories from continuous time data is a challenging task in natural language generation. Current sequential story generation models often rely on pre-trained language models that are optimized for text data, resulting in stories with limited depth and breadth. Additionally, these models typically require substantial domain-specific training to produce plausible narratives. To address these limitations, we present a novel approach called TCube, which enables detailed and coherent storytelling in a range of domains without requiring domain-specific training. TCube consists of a domain-agnostic neural model that utilizes a temporal cube representation to generate stories at specified times and dates. TCube's effectiveness is demonstrated through stories generated from real-life time-stamped data in two different domains, earning an average of 88% expert-confirmed accuracy. TCube outperforms existing story generation models by over 2.5 times in terms of depth and 3.5 times in terms of breadth, while also achieving nearly 4 times more human-like storytelling quality. TCube's source code is available at https://github.com/yetanotherjet/TCube. Snapshots of TCube can be accessed via https://tcubestories.github.io. We also present a new dataset called TimeStampedStory, containing 16 human-generated stories with corresponding temporal stamps and expert feedback. This dataset can be accessed at https://yetanotherjet.github.io/TimesStampedStory. TCube's 5-second inference speed makes it a suitable candidate for further development and refinement in the story generation field. To evaluate TCube's transferability, we also demonstrate its ability to produce stories from data in completely new domains, such as generating stories about air traffic control based on data from flight logs. TCube's stories are consistently preferred by experts over those generated by leading story generation models, with a 1.5 to 2.5 times greater likelihood of being considered accurate and meaningful. Software developers often seek online guidance from various platforms, sharing external link references on Stack Overflow to aid fellow developers. These link references can pose security threats by disseminating malicious information. Thus far, little research has examined their implications. This study investigates the prevalence of these link references on Stack Overflow. We discovered that roughly 44% of relevant questions received an external link reference response from users. Through manual analysis of a broader sample of link references (N = 1050), we assessed their usefulness and safety. The results show that while over 60% of link references point to trustworthy domains, about 13% point to suspicious domains, and nearly 9% point to potentially malicious domains. Furthermore, over 50% of link references by high-reputation Stack Overflow users appear to prioritize their own projects over respondents' requested solutions. We identified several areas for potential abuse, including external link referencing's potential weaknesses and the activities of "producers and consumers" of these references. We have made our data set available for further exploration. Moreover, we have proposed a set of rules that can effectively balance respondents' demands and prevent the over-promotion of individual projects on Stack Overflow. Finally, we have proposed a few features that can be incorporated into Stack Overflow to mitigate the risks associated with external link referencing. Ultimately, we believe that implementing these changes will not only reduce the risks but also enhance the quality of the content shared on the platform. However, maintaining large monitoring programs is labor-intensive and often impractical, prompting researchers to explore more efficient methods, such as using machine learning to cut costs and using stacked analyses to increase detection sensitivity. Recent advancements in deep learning technology have led to the achievement of state-of-the-art results, however its high computational requirements for both training and operation have not yet been overcome. Researchers then turned to spiking neural networks as an alternative, due to its promising potential for solving this problem. Despite ongoing research in this field, there is a significant discrepancy between current SNN performance and its potential to execute tasks efficiently in an event-driven manner. Therefore, there is a pressing need for developing more accurate SNN models that can operate seamlessly with computational resources. We propose a novel architecture consisting of a local learning layer combined with a central processing unit, where the local learning layer utilizes a novel hybrid kernel based on the local learning rule to achieve superior results. Experimental evaluations of our model demonstrate substantial improvements in both energy efficiency and classification accuracy when compared to existing state-of-the-art SNN models. Notably, we observed an average increase of 11.19% in top-1 accuracy and a average decrease of 5.53% in energy consumption for the same network configuration on CIFAR-10 dataset. Furthermore, we observed that our model was capable of achieving comparable results with VGGNet deep neural network, outperforming existing SNN models in both energy efficiency and accuracy. Additionally, we observed that our model demonstrated substantial potential for being utilized in in-memory SNN computing systems, where the local learning layer is capable of adapting the weights without requiring parallel data access. We expect our findings to contribute positively to the ongoing research in spiking neural networks and to ultimately enable the development of more accurate and efficient neural networks. We analyzed a model that involves an unknown function 'f' which is part of a multivariate nonlinear equation, along with another function 'p'. A degree 'n' polynomial is used to approximate 'f' and 'p', and we aim to estimate 'f' using an adaptive estimator that uses interpolation data with minimal rational observations. This estimation method can be seen as solving a convex optimization problem, and under a condition of smoothness for 'f' and 'p', we proved it achieves optimal statistical inference outcomes. Furthermore, we demonstrated the adaptation property of this estimation method by reducing bias through a penalization method. This adaptation allows us to remove the need for explicit bandwidth selection, and we showed the estimation method achieves the optimal rate of convergence in a least squares sense. This research was influenced by nonparametric estimation in a least squares sense and provides statistical inference including risk bounds, and it has applications in computing eigenvalues and eigenvectors of graphs and matrices. Additionally, we provided two alternative estimators that use different interpolation methods and proved similar results. These estimators use a minimum number of observations that is proportional to a logarithmic or a polynomial function of the sample size. These research findings were presented at the 2020 French Machine Learning Days. In addition to adaptation, we studied the behavior of these estimators and tested their ability to recover properties like smoothness and positivity of 'f' with minimal rational observations. This research can be seen as extending existing research on semiparametric estimation in a least squares sense and providing new results on the behavior of interpolators without smoothness assumptions. Ultimately, we studied the statistical performance of these estimators and tested their ability to recover properties like smoothness and positivity of 'f'. This research can be seen as extending existing research on the behavior of interpolators.

We introduce a new class of transformations known as varacious beta-transformations with a gap, which encompass a wide range of scenarios. By establishing certain properties, we are able to prove that they possess invariant sets that are unique and ergodic, under the guise of holonomy invariants, thereby yielding a new form of ergodic theory. As a result, we are able to generalize the theory of acompetitive beta-transformations, proposed by Climenhaga and Thompson. Our findings reveal that: (1) every acompetitive transformation is intermediate, given that it has a closing value and a natural gap; (2) every intermediate transformation that is irreducible and has a natural gap can be expressed as a competitive transformation with a competitive ratio greater than one; (3) the set of irreducible intermediate transformations, which have natural gaps and a competitive ratio greater than one, is the same as the set of acompetitive transformations, provided that the sets' parameters beta are densely filled in. Furthermore, we observe that the set of irreducible transformations, which have natural gaps and are intermediate, includes the set of irreducible irrepecible rotations, the set of irreducible leb measures that are invariant under beta-transformations, as well as the set of skew transformations, provided that certain conditions are met. We investigate the properties of an SO(Nc) gauge theory defined on a two-dimensional space with boundaries. The theory includes matter fields that form a set of symmetric operators. Through a combination of semi-string theory and Montonen-Sterbuger duality, we analyze a two-dimensional representation of SO(Nc). The results indicate the presence of boundaries causes IR confining, a phenomenon previously recognized in 4D theories with Chern-Simons terms. Furthermore, this confining effect leads to the breaking of chiral symmetry, a phenomenon that can be assessed through the behavior of boundary operators. We verify that this confining phenomenon is accompanied by an imbalance in the number of boundary degenerate vacuums. Lastly, we propose that a similar analysis of SO(Nc) in 2D can serve as a model for the confining behavior of 4D theories featuring Chern-Simons terms. An important consequence of our findings is that confining and non-confining vacuums are distinguished by a change in the number of boundary degenerate states. An instance of this can be seen in an SO(8) theory with two boundaries, where we observe a 3-fold degeneracy of boundary states as opposed to the 2-fold degeneracy seen in non-confining vacuums. We provide an explanation for this phenomenon through an analogy involving a trigonometric identity. Machine learning models such as random forests and boosted trees have substantial predictive capabilities, yet their high performance comes at the cost of clarity in understanding their decision-making processes. Building on the success of visualization methods for single trees in interpreting random forests and boosted trees, a novel approach called Disentangled Attribution Graphs is introduced for visualizing the outcomes of random forests and boosted trees. By generating a visual representation of how features contribute to outcomes on a dataset, this method provides valuable insights into the structure learned by each model. Furthermore, it allows for the identification of discrepancies between models and actual dataset characteristics, offering insights that can inform future research. Ultimately, this method enhances the interpretability of these models and their use in practice. A comprehensive experiment was conducted using actual data across diverse domains, as well as artificially constructed data, to demonstrate the method's effectiveness and showcase its utility in data analysis. The code used in this study is publicly available at https://github.com/jbayer19/DAG. Additional information can be found at https://johannesbayer.com/research/dag. FedLearn, a federated learning technique on multiple learning environments, mitigates data leakage risks by keeping client data safe from the aggregator and fellow clients. However, when transferring encrypted data to the aggregator, current implementations fail to meet performance standards. This study presents Flatee, a solution combining FedLearn with hardware-backed secure computing environments, specifically using Intel Software Guard Extensions (SGX). Flatee's approach involves encrypting and encrypting allows for a significant reduction in the costs associated with encrypted computation, ultimately resulting in a substantial improvement in training efficiency on distributed datasets. Our comprehensive evaluations on MNIST, EMNIST, and CIFAR10 demonstrate Flatee's capability of near-fully utilising SGX-based secure computing resources, achieving a notable gain of up to 3.3 times faster training times in comparison to the traditional SGX-based methods. Moreover, Flatee offers an improved training speed advantage of as much as 2.3 times and 1.6 times over the existing dataless and hardware-based FedLearn techniques, respectively. Ultimately, Flatee provides a more effective means of balancing data usage, user privacy, and training efficiency.

We introduce timeloops, a container-specific approach that automates the creation of system call filters for isolated microservices. Traditional access control methods rely on explicit system call overlays, which can lead to implementation errors and reveal sensitive information. Current learning-based techniques are limited by their reliance on static code analysis and absence of runtime system call data. Our approach leverages an adaptive learning algorithm to generate timeloops, a data structure specifying allowed system call patterns, based on real system call traces. This structure serves as a dynamic overlay, ensuring the microservice makes only specified system calls when invoked. We showcase timeloops' efficacy in a Netflix service, encompassing multiple interconnected microservices, where systematic testing reveals timeloops provide a suitable system call filter for sensitive data protection. Furthermore, we demonstrate that timeloops prevent security threats arising from malicious system call patterns, highlighting the value of our method. Based on our findings, we propose timeloops as a suitable solution for protecting microservices from unauthorized system call vulnerabilities. Many real-world applications lie in multidimensional space forms beyond the traditional three-dimensional setup.  In this research, we explore whether linear classifiers, originally conceived for Euclidean space, can effectively operate in more general space forms.  Our findings indicate that linear classifiers can be easily applied to a broad category of space forms known as linear space forms and that their behavior is comparable to that in Euclidean space.  Through comprehensive experiments involving data sets from various domains, we demonstrate that linear classifiers perform well in multidimensional space forms without significant decreases in their accuracy compared to similar classifiers in Euclidean space.  These results are backed by theoretical guarantees that establish the classification boundaries in linear space forms as being straightforward to define and maintain.  Additionally, we conduct an in-depth analysis of how linear classifiers handle points that lie on manifolds with curved boundaries.  Our research provides a framework for implementing linear classifiers within the context of multilinear arithmetic that operates within the theoretical model known as VNP.  Overall, our research confirms that linear classifiers can serve as versatile tools for concept classification in a broad range of space forms.

For optimal performance, the estimated state is fed into a control algorithm. However, sensor readings can be inaccurate, leading to suboptimal operation. To mitigate this, a predictive control method has been developed. Instead of using a single estimated state, this method uses probability distributions of multiple states, which are simulated and used to determine the best control settings. To achieve this, the authors have created an innovative method for simplifying the simulation process. This method involves dividing the state space into distinct sections and using simplified models to simulate state transitions. The potential state spaces are divided into two categories: those that require direct access and those that are off-limits. This method can be applied to a range of control problems involving uncertainty in state readings, such as robotics and power management. Ultimately, we aim to develop secure ML models that can resistMitM attacks and provide value to society. Most of a multiple star system's final mass is typically accumulated during the first stages of star formation. Typically, the secondary companion is lost in an exchange with the primary star's surrounding disk, while the remaining system with the retained primary star is known as a binary with an accretion disk. However, if the primary star's surrounding disk is insufficient to cover the loss of the secondary companion, the remaining system with the retained primary star is known as a wide binary with an accretion disk. Secondary accretion, where a planet or small body in the disk accumulates mass, can occur in both systems, particularly in systems with extended disks where planetary formation is more likely to occur. Planets in close binaries where the primary star's surrounding disk is insufficient may instead form through gravitational consolidation of surrounding material or by migrating in from the outer disk, and are more likely to engage in high-speed accretion due to their environment. Conversely, in systems with the primary star's surrounding disk that is extended, the primary mode of accretion is typically typical low-speed accretion. Hierarchical systems with the primary star's surrounding disk that is extended are therefore typically characterized by typical low-speed accretion, as opposed to systems with the primary star's surrounding disk that is insufficient where the primary star is at risk of losing the secondary companion and is therefore at risk of engaging in high-speed accretion. 

This research presents a research framework that categorizes and compares the primary star's surrounding mass accumulation mechanisms in hierarchical systems with the primary star's surrounding disk that is either extended or insufficient. Key factors that influence whether a planet in a close binary where the primary star's surrounding disk is insufficient will experience high-speed or typical low-speed accretion include its distance from the primary star and whether its surrounding environment is characterized by the primary star's surrounding disk that is either extended or insufficient.

Our findings indicate that the mass of these bosons is within a specific range, and this result is in line with previous studies based on precession rates in combination with luminosity. Furthermore, we observe that a particular method is more effective in constraining the mass of these bosons when considering all relevant data. Assuming that the precession rates and the spins of these active galactic nuclei follow a uniform distribution, we found that the mass of these bosons is within a specific range. Additionally, we noticed that a particular frequency of these bosons is more likely to occur. Finally, we developed an association between the mass of these bosons and the size of these active galactic nuclei, indicating that a particular frequency of these bosons is more likely to occur. Our study's data and results are available online. Moreover, we developed a tool in Python that we can use to detect these bosons based on the spins of these active galactic nuclei in the future. Our tool's code is also available online for public use. Ultimately, our study indicates that the mass of these bosons is likely to be in a specific range, and these bosons may be detectable in the spins of these active galactic nuclei. As a result, we proposed that the following parameters should be investigated further in the future. For instance, we could re-evaluate the effect of magnetic fields on these bosons and the black holes. In addition, we could also re-evaluate the role of accretion in these active galactic nuclei and the effect it has on these bosons and the black holes. Furthermore, we could also re-evaluate whether these bosons are coupled with photons or not. If they are coupled, we would expect to see certain signs in the spectrum of these active galactic nuclei and the fluctuations in their luminosity. Finally, we could also re-evaluate the role of space-time curvature in these active galactic nuclei and the fluctuations in their luminosity. Ultimately, these could be key areas of research to further understand these active galactic nuclei and the fluctuations in their luminosity as well as the properties of these bosons and the black holes. the numerous unknown variables involved. Fortunately, there is an effective method
to address this issue by using practical, applied research that focuses on specific
scenarios. One effective method is to conduct computer-based simulations based on
real-world experiments. This study employs the Brian simulator to model a specific
type of neural processor called the spiking neural network, and successfully emulates
the behavior on a real-world neural processor called Loihi. The results from this study
match the findings from previous research on Loihi. The study confirms that Brian can
effectively replicate the behavior of Loihi, and that the model is accurate and reliable. 
This study provides a useful tool for testing novel ideas on a neural processor 
before actually using it. The researcher proposes four possible applications for this 
model: first, to verify that Brian correctly represents Loihi; second, to rapidly test 
and evaluate different configurations of Loihi before actually using it; third, to develop 
new algorithms for Loihi based on established methods from other fields; and last, to 
create hybrid systems that combine Brian and Loihi for maximum potential. 
Furthermore, the study offers an open-source software package called Brian2Loihi that enables 
the emulation of Loihi using Brian. The study also makes available the complete code used in 
the study, as well as the results in an online database. The study positions itself as a 
resource for other researchers who are interested in using Brian and Loihi. 
Interestingly, the study reveals an unexpected connection between two 
distinct research areas: the theoretical modeling of neural systems with the practical, 
hands-on exploration of neural hardware. The study reflects on how the practical,

domains, and suggests that the project has successfully linked the two.

A solar noise storm is a rare and enigmatic solar phenomenon characterized by intense non-thermal radio emission. Its source parameters show unpredictable behavior, which is still poorly understood. In a recent study, researchers observed a solar noise storm source with unique behavior, which is presented in detail. The study's key findings reveal a pattern of rapid and simultaneous changes in source size and position during a microflare, which is unprecedented in solar noise storm studies. This linkage is interpreted as a dynamic extension of magnetic field lines. In another interesting occurrence, the study's authors noticed an instance where the source parameters reversed their typical behavioral changes, which provides valuable insights for understanding magnetic field behavior during certain types of microflares. These findings are likely to offer new insights for interpreting solar noise storm observations. The study's data and related resources are available for public access.

A compact and self-contained optical trap is designed using planar integrated magneto-optical traps (IMOTs), allowing for the localized capture and cooling of cold atomic gases. This novel planar IMOT employs a microstructured silicon photonics device and an integrated coil for magnetic confinement. Notably, a novel optical trap configuration is achieved by utilizing the gradient force of plane-polarized light, which interacts with atoms aligned perpendicular to the plane. This unique setup yields a narrow, planar IMOT with a 5.1 micro watt optical power requirement and a trap depth of 43 microHertz. Additionally, a 2D IMOT can be generated by combining planar and perpendicular components, using 10 and 5.1 micro watt optical powers respectively. This pioneering design provides a versatile and portable IMOT system for use in education and research. It is anticipated that this technology will facilitate the development of micro-scale magneto-optical traps, empowering users to work with cold atomic gases outside of standard vacuum environments. This will likely open doors for users who may have been previously precluded from working with such systems due to space constraints or financial considerations. In particular, this design may attract educators and young researchers who may now have easier access to the equipment necessary for teaching and learning in this field. This design was the result of a course-wide design competition in which the winners were announced in February 2023. Specifically, it is hoped that this system will be used to explore interactions between atoms in a controlled environment. The interaction between a moving atom and a stationary mirror gives rise to a varying electric field between them, according to the Lorentz recipe. This electric field can cause the atom to transition between energy states, emitting photons in the process. To investigate this phenomenon further, researchers have simulated different atomic movements and positions relative to a mirror, using a slender cone, and calculated the emitted radiation. The simulation indicated that the electric field interacts strongly with the atom when it is near the cone's tip and at intermediate distances from the mirror's surface. The strength of this interaction varies significantly with the atom's position. In one scenario, where the atom is situated 10 nanometers from the mirror and at the cone's tip, the mirror's movement at speeds higher than 1000 times faster than sound caused the atom to transition 10 times more frequently. Consequently, the atom emitted 10 more photons per second. Notably, this transition frequency reached its highest point at speeds around 2100 times faster than sound. Moreover, the emitted photons span a broad electromagnetic spectrum, ranging from extremely long wavelengths at the edge of the microwave band to extremely short wavelengths at the edge of the gamma-ray band. When the atom is positioned halfway along the cone, the mirror's movement had a minimal effect on the atom's excitation. However, the atom was more frequently excited when it was situated near the mirror's surface, as this positioning reduced the distance between the atom and the mirror, thereby increasing the electric field's strength. As a result, when the mirror was moved at speeds higher than 3000 times faster than sound, the atom emitted the most frequent sequence of transitions, reaching a peak of a 100-fold increase in photon emission per second compared to when the mirror moved at speeds lower than 1000 times faster than sound. The atom then transitioned between adjacent energy states, emitting photons in the process. When the atom was moved instead of the mirror, the atom and the mirror exchanged roles in the mirror-atom resonant system. As a result, when the atom was situated near the mirror's surface and then moved at speeds higher than 3000 times faster than sound, the mirror and the atom exchanged roles, and the mirror emitted radiation as a slender cone. The emitted radiation exhibited electronic emissions on all sides of the mirror and a sequence of increasing and decreasing radiation frequencies over a broad electromagnetic spectrum. Improving the readability of historical documents is crucial, but current methods have limitations as they often require manual annotation of text, which can be labor-intensive and impractical due to the fragility of documents.  We've developed a deep learning approach that uses text segmentation as an adversarial process to automatically enhance handwritten document images, without requiring this costly annotation.  Our framework refines both the image and the text features simultaneously, using a self-attention mechanism to focus on relevant image details for text extraction.  In experiments, our method has demonstrated superior results, with a significant boost in reading ease and a lower error rate in text extraction, compared to state-of-the-art restoration methods.  Notably, our approach has proven effective even on difficult cases of low-quality documents.  You can access our implemented framework at https://github.com/whs815/UIT-HandwrittenDocumentRefinement. 

Keywords: Handwritten Document Refinement, Text extraction, Adversarial training, Flaky calibration mechanism.

The extraction of identity information from scanned ID documents is a fundamental process in implementing an identity verification system. This process is more complex in countries with diverse ID documents than in those with a standard issue. To address this challenge, this paper proposes an advanced method for extracting identity information from Indonesian ID documents. This method employs a combination of Optical Character Recognition and Natural Language Processing techniques. As the former often struggles with accuracy, this proposal includes a manual review process using NLP to ensure the extraction of required information from the ID document, regardless of its scan quality. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method. Furthermore, this proposal is adaptable to various other identity cards that contain handwritten information without significant modifications. To validate this proposal, we created a mock identity verification database using 300 ID documents. Our extraction method achieved an accuracy of 99% in the first analysis and 100% in a second review. Both reviews took significantly less time than the existing manual process. This proposal could be useful for organizations handling large scans of ID documents for verification purposes. To share our method's benefits, the source code and extracted information are available on a public platform. This includes the identity information extracted from the ID documents, providing a useful dataset for further research. To address potential challenges, this proposal includes suggestions for enhancing the extraction method's accuracy using machine learning models. Additionally, we share our observations on the most difficult sections of the ID documents that often pose challenges for extraction. To address these challenges, we propose an NLP-assisted review process that can aid in the extraction of crucial information. Our identification of these challenges may be relevant to other research fields. To compare our method's effectiveness, we evaluated our approach using benchmark datasets from leading academic institutions. Our extraction method outperformed the benchmark dataset in several areas. Notably, our proposal includes an innovative review process inspired by data augmentation techniques. This review process is a significant contribution of our proposal. To facilitate the implementation of our method, we provided detailed instructions on using our code and database. Our code is also available in an open-source repository, enabling others to replicate our results. To address questions arising from our proposal, we provided potential solutions. To facilitate the understanding of our proposal, we included frequently asked questions (FAQs). To accommodate readers with varying technical backgrounds, we provided an introductory section on the necessary technical background. In vehicular communications, the complex and dispersive nature of channels makes reliable data reception challenging. To mitigate this issue, IEEE 802.11p adopts an open-loop approach that asks the transmitter to re-send data, leading to decreased efficiency and increased latency. To resolve this, this study proposes a novel, low-complexity estimation technique based on long short-term memory (LSTM). By utilizing real-world data and a dataset from the Central Florida area, the LSTM model's performance was evaluated under various scenarios, demonstrating its capacity to accurately estimate channel parameters and surpass traditional estimators in performance. Furthermore, this research identifies the optimal vehicle speed for successful channel estimation. Specifically, results show that the LSTM model achieves: (a) higher coefficient values for channel delay, with a peak value of 0.91 compared to 0.83 for the least squares method; ( (b) lower normalized mean squared error values for channel delay, with a peak value of 0.047 compared to 0.103 for the least squares method; (c) higher coefficient values for channel gain, with a peak value of 0.98 compared to 0.94 for the least squares method; and (d) lower normalized mean squared error values for channel gain, with a peak value of 0.043 compared to 0.066 for the least squares method. Additionally, this research demonstrates that the LSTM model can predict channel parameters for up to 802.11p channel estimation blocks into the future. Leveraging an open-source platform for IEEE 802.11p transmitter and receiver design, the source code for this research is freely available at: https://github.com/mostafay/LSTM_802_11p_channel_estimation. To facilitate integration with existing vehicular communication systems, this research also provides a graphical user interface based on MATLAB for easy implementation. Furthermore, the raw data used in this research is freely available at: https://www. Amazon. com/MTK-V2X-dataset/. To promote reproducibility, a comprehensive document detailing the dataset, source code, and raw data is available at: https://doi. org/10.5281/ebz-v-5708703. Essential information includes a guide on how to use the dataset, source code, and raw data; the dataset description; the dataset license; and the implementation details of the LSTM model. To facilitate understanding, a flowchart detailing the implementation process is available at: https://doi. org/10.5281/ebz

Ancient astronomical images hold significant historical value and can be
dated back centuries. These images, though informative, suffer from low image
quality due to degradation over time. Restoring them is crucial for accurate
historical and educational purposes. Traditional restoration methods may compromise
visual appeal, concealing the document's original character. This research aims
to develop a method that combines deep learning and human oversight to retrieve
lost details while maintaining the original visual experience. A generative
adversarial network was implemented and supplemented with: (1) a discriminator to
filter out generated noise and guide the generator in mimicking the tissue
pattern; (2) a loss function based on tissue segmentation to ensure the generated
image retains the original document's texture. These modifications enabled the
creation of noise-reducing filters and aided the recovery of lost details without
introducing additional noise. Furthermore, this research introduces a multi-scale
approach to colorization utilizing the input image's color features. This method
preserves the original document's colors and prevents the introduction of unrelated
colors. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that this approach outperforms existing
colorization techniques. Although the generated images exhibit exceptional visual
quality according to the peer review, some artifacts remain. Future work will
involve addressing these artifacts and expanding this method to handle page
reconstruction from fragmented images. Additionally, this research provides an
open-source code and a dataset consisting of centuries-old astronomical images. 
This dataset can be utilized for training and evaluating document restoration models. 
Given its uniqueness, it may support research in document restoration and
related fields. Additionally, this research presents an open-source code and a
dataset consisting of centuries-old astronomical images. This dataset can be
utilized for training and evaluating document restoration models, offering a
unique resource in the field.

The fundamental principle of neural networks relies on modeling a distribution by minimizing the divergence between a base distribution and the refined distribution achieved through iterative iterations of sampling and adjustment. This concept is further developed by introducing a new neural network structure that doesn't rely on gradient information and instead uses unbiased estimators to sample and refine distributions, resulting in superior performance outcomes. Additionally, this novel structure possesses a heightened degree of freedom due to its non-grad-based support, hence it can incorporate more parameters. With the capability to handle high levels of complexity, this network structures itself into a series of sampling and refinement layers, each optimized independently to reduce complexity without compromising performance. This approach is then applied to real-world projects such as image recognition and prediction tasks and demonstrates improved accuracy and reduced complexity. The source code for this project is available at https://github.com/ninanana112/GFNN. The experimental findings are documented in the report titled 'Neural Networks as Universal Estimators with Applications to Model Selection and Complexity Control'. The theoretical underpinnings of this project are discussed in a different research paper titled 'Neural Networks Based Universal Estimators with Applications to Model Selection and Complexity Control'. Consequently, iCog-Ai can be an accessible and versatile tool for large-scale multi-agent human-robot cooperative learning applications. Potential future research directions are also discussed.

Incidents such as accidents, traffic congestion, and civil disturbances necessitate prompt attention from authorities. Current monitoring methods, relying solely on static locations like roads and intersections, or dynamic sources like traffic sensors and cameras, are limited. Social media platforms, with users present at incident sites, posting updates along with geographic coordinates and timestamps, offer a valuable resource. Our solution analyzes social media postings to identify incidents in real-time, accurately locating them spatially and temporally. First, we filter relevant incident-related posts from the platform's total postings. Then, we cluster these posts by their location to pinpoint areas experiencing incidents. Next, we match the posts with official incident reports, and finally, we validate the accuracy of the identified incidents using human evaluation. Experimental results show that social media-based incident detection surpasses traditional methods in accuracy. For example, our analysis found that in Beijing, over 50% of incident-related posts were previously unknown to the platform's indexing database, covering more than 70% of the city's streets, revealing the significant potential of social media-based incident detection. Our implemented Instantaneous Spatio-Temporal Incident Identification system is now in use in Beijing, Shanghai, Shenzhen, Chengdu, and Guangzhou. It provides users with a choice of searching for incidents in specific areas or viewing a live incident map. Additionally, we maintain a database of frequently reported incidents. Our long-term goal is to improve safety through enhanced real-time incident feedback to authorities, facilitating faster response times. As artificial intelligence becomes more practical, protecting it from malicious attacks has become a pressing concern. The concept of adversarial robustness has emerged, referring to the ability of a machine learning model to perform well even when given intentionally false inputs. However, current methods for enhancing a model's robustness typically rely on numerical estimates and do not provide any assurance that the added uncertainty will remain stable under future use. In this study, a formal framework for incorporating adversarial robustness into Bayesian inference is introduced. A mathematical proof shows that incorporating a margin of uncertainty into the model's training process results in more stable predictions in the face of potential attacks. The researchers also demonstrate that traditional learning approaches can be adapted to meet stringent requirements for adversarial robustness. The benefits of using uncertainty margins in conjunction with learning techniques that account for uncertainty are observed in various tests, providing a valuable framework for advanced machine learning applications that require both high performance and security guarantees. The researchers also provide an open-source code for replicating the study's results. The code can be found at https://github.com/jbayer-bayes/ab_rbm public. Additional details can be found in the supplementary materials available at https://dx.doi.org/10.6103/WHDI240210.6103/WHDI2402.

In the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic in China, malicious actors spread harmful rumors online, threatening public safety and economic stability. These rumors were frequently disseminated by influential social media users, often with significant educational or professional backgrounds. Researchers found that certain characteristics of online communities and their members facilitated the spread of rumors, which had a substantial impact on public behavior, according to a survey of nearly 30,000 participants across 46 universities in China. Approximately 80% of respondents reported encountering COVID-19-related rumors online, with nearly 50% indicating they spread such rumors to others. The survey revealed that higher education levels and access to news from official sources reduced individuals' likelihood of spreading rumors, while also demonstrating a measurable impact when universities implemented online counter-narratives aiming to combat harmful rumors, resulting in a notable decline in rumor dissemination. However, researchers found no significant evidence that people trusted news sources influenced their intention to spread rumors, as perceived criticism towards the government from rumor news appeared to increase individuals' likelihood of disseminating it. The study suggests that targeting influential social media users and online communities through targeted information campaigns might be an effective strategy to mitigate the spread of harmful rumors, particularly when combining these efforts with online counter-measures tailored to specific community characteristics. Additionally, researchers propose leveraging social media academics to develop and disseminate fact-checking materials addressing common COVID-19-related myths. This research explores the effects of dimensionality reduction on hyperspectral image classification, specifically investigating how different methods affect classification accuracy and time. Using a reduced dataset from 224 bands to as low as 16 bands, six dimensionality reduction techniques were tested and compared to the original full dataset. Assessing two popular classifiers, including a supervised classifier and a deep learning model, the investigation concludes that principal component analysis is the most effective method for classification when using reduced spectral dimensions. However, when using the full spectral range, feature selection yields the best results. Interestingly, the investigation reveals that the suitability of principal component analysis for classification may be influenced by the type of surrounding landscape features. Furthermore, the investigation emphasizes the importance of considering both computational cost and spectral resolution when selecting the optimal number of bands for hyperspectral remote sensing applications. Using a reduced dataset from 224 bands to as low as 16 bands, the study provides a framework for practitioners working with hyperspectral imaging datasets to make informed decisions about dimensionality reduction. To address this, there's a growing need for systems that can model both context and logic simultaneously. In this paper, we explore the reduction of natural language models to propositional and first-order logic using semantic interpretation. We highlight the challenges in establishing a precise mathematical link between natural language and logic, and discuss potential solutions. Furthermore, we delve into the reconstruction of natural language models utilizing logical principles, and investigate their implications for future breakthroughs in natural language understanding. We also introduce new metrics to gauge a model's logical soundness and provide a framework for logical entailment evaluation. The paper explores a new approach based on the Hamiltonian formulation to understand the spirit of the parquet technique from within the framework of many-body theory. By identifying a specific class of two-particle irreducible vertices meeting a strict condition, the parquet technique is conceptually linked to a perturbative expansion of the Hamiltonian. However, the parquet formalism is uniquely positioned as it is the optimal representation of this vertex class, much like how Feynman diagrams represent the perturbative expansion of the S-matrix. Since the parquet formalism is singular and optimal, it is expected to yield a resummation of the perturbative series. Given its strong connection to the Hamiltonian, it is also possible for the parquet formalism to be derived from a Hamiltonian formulation of the path integral using a perturbatively expandable action. Moreover, the paper shows that the Hamiltonian perspective facilitates a comparison with another equivalent description of the parquet formalism derived from a perturbatively exact RPA action. This comparison is beneficial as it allows for a controlled analysis of the differences between these two descriptions of the parquet formalism, thereby providing confidence in their equivalence. Lastly, the paper suggests that the parquet formalism can serve as a model description for coupled-plasmon-phonon interactions and that a similar description could be developed for superconductors. It is proposed that the resulting formalism could be used to investigate the origin of the BCS model. Crucially, the idea presents a novel way for the Hamiltonian to be derived from the action, and the resulting formalism is both computationally tractable and follows a clear renormalization-group flow. Therefore, it is possible that the derived model describes the physical reality of the system. Ultimately, the paper presents an argument in favor of the parquet formalism, and a similar case, can be made, for a broader class of problems. Therefore, various descriptions of the parquet formalism are discussed, and it is shown that they are equivalent. This method relies on human input within an interactive environment where annotated data is grouped into searchable categories called clusters. When sufficient labeled data within these clusters exists, new class labels can be assigned to unlabeled data points based on the characteristics that distinguish these groups. Since human annotation is time-consuming, a novel approach called Time-Effective Reward Learning is introduced. This time-saving method harnesses the insights from human feedback on human and machine predictions to update the ranking model. Moreover, two efficient optimization strategies are presented to facilitate real-time human involvement. Experimental results on multiple datasets have shown that Visually Aided Cluster Ranking, paired with Time-Effective Reward Learning, can be a more effective data labeling tool compared to established methods. Additionally, it outperforms alternative approaches in terms of labeling efficiency and robustness to human errors. Offline reinforcement learning involves training agents using previously recorded data alone, without real-time interactions with environments. Unfortunately, offline training can be compromised by data fraud, which artificially manipulates data to deceive agents and extract valuable policy information. Current approaches fail to effectively counter complex fraud strategies, highlighting the need for more robust methods. We develop a novel framework to detect and mitigate fraudulent data in offline reinforcement learning. First, we identify policy inconsistencies within suspicious data by analyzing the policies generated from different segments. We quantify policy inconsistencies using the maximum violation of policy constraints (MVPC) metric and introduce a bicriterion framework that simultaneously optimizes both return and MVPC. This approach yields robust violations that thwart even the most sophisticated fraud strategies. From a theoretical perspective, we confirm that optimizing return and MVPC yields optimal countermeasures against covert and covert data fraud. Second, we propose a method for detecting fraudulent data by leveraging Augmented Transition Rewards. We apply our framework on a set of classic benchmark environments and achieve significant enhancements, reducing MVPC by at least one order of magnitude compared to existing methods. Furthermore, we create the FraudRL Benchmark to facilitate the study of data fraud in offline reinforcement learning. This benchmark includes diverse environments and data fraud strategies to facilitate further research in this area. The implemented code is accessible via a GitHub repository. Experimental results confirm that our method results in robust policy countermeasures against data fraud, both theoretically and practically. A general framework is presented for simulating Brownian molecular machines driven by electron tunneling, taking into account dual tunneling processes and thermodynamic fluctuations. Taking as an example a tunneling nanoswitch with a quasi-spherical redox molecule, the model is developed using a rotation dynamics based on the Langevin equation. Through this approach, the relaxation dynamics of the nanoswitch's rotation are analyzed in real time, and the probabilistic distribution of the rotation period is determined. Additionally, the model's results are compared to experimental data, and the dependence of the switch's relaxation times on the viscosity of its surroundings is examined. Theoretical calculations reveal the significant influence of tunneling rates and the balance between forward and reverse tunneling processes on the switch's relaxation dynamics. Furthermore, it is found that certain tunneling parameters can lead to a "memory effect" in the switch's relaxation behavior. The proposed framework is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of molecular machines and various tunneling mechanisms. Potential applications for molecular computers and bio-molecular machines are also discussed. Lastly, the implications of the study on the origin of living cells' stability are explored. The theoretical model and simulation results are made available for public use. The code was written in Python and is compatible with most tunneling configurations, allowing for the reproduction of the presented simulation results. The code is an integral part of the research, enabling the analysis of novel molecular engines and Brownian machines with reduced size, with and without the involvement of magnetic and electric properties. The research is primarily focused on non-magnetic systems but can be extended to magnetic tunnel junctions to investigate the effect of magnetization on the systems. In recent years, generalized convolutions have become a widely accepted basis for studying mathematical problems and designing algorithms, with multiple definitions proposed across various fields including combinatorics, algebra, geometry, and computer science. We introduce an efficient, generalized framework for calculating convolutions based on polynomial division, enabling faster computation of convolutions than through brute force methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that most previous definitions of generalized convolutions are equivalent to our initial division-based definition, with some requiring additional operations. We also explore the concept of $r$-convolution, introducing new methods for its calculation and achieving faster computational times than through brute force methods in many cases. Additionally, we compile a list of common functions' $r$-convolution formulas, providing a useful resource. We also study the properties of $r$-convolution, and utilize our calculations to establish new expressions for Hawkes processes' $r$-convolution, a finding previously unreported in the literature. The techniques developed here have broad applications and could be useful in other fields. The presented work is a compilation of research conducted between Summer-Fall 2020. A substantial issue in contemporary financial modeling lies in double counting, which arises from an incomplete understanding of simultaneous transactions shared between multiple agents. This paper addresses double counting through the development of a theoretically sound model of a double-faced auction for assets, with and without market makers. By leveraging established mathematical theorems, we demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of an equilibrium in this market model. Furthermore, we utilize numerical methods to illustrate and analyze solutions, focusing on areas that require further theoretical investigation. Moreover, we show that the model can effectively simulate real-world market events, such as crashes and bubbles, and highlight the distinct behaviors of market makers and order book mechanics. When combined with a simplified model of endogenous supply, our results indicate a strong connection between the S&P 500 index and a cobweb bubble model. Lastly, we successfully model the COVID-19 pandemic using our double-faced auction framework. A comprehensive approach is employed to validate the model's outcomes, utilizing multiple testing and normalization techniques to forecast market behavior. The proposed model provides a potential theoretical foundation for understanding and analyzing financial asset price dynamics. Our proposed approach, Linear and Nonlinear Disambiguation Optimization (LANDO), employs a kernel learning technique to optimize the kernelized DMD (KDMD) and selectively incorporate linear and nonlinear components from data-driven kernels. Furthermore, LANDO's robustness and scalability were demonstrated through extensive numerical simulations involving synthetic data. Our research suggests that LANDO can serve as an invaluable tool for analyzing various systems, including those with abrupt changes and smooth variations. Developing free-hand 3D model creation tools is crucial for various industries. So far, research has focused primarily on converting 2D drawings to 3D models, neglecting the more practical aspect of creating models from free-hand drawings in three dimensions. In response to this gap, we introduce an innovative approach for extracting 3D models from virtual reality free-hand drawings. By leveraging deep neural networks trained on real scanning data, our system enables users to create accurate and detailed 3D models through free-hand drawings in a virtual reality environment. For thorough evaluation, we developed and utilized VR-Drawing-to-3D-Form, a groundbreaking database containing 300 3D model shapes, alongside a comprehensive set of manipulation tools to facilitate shape variation and category exploration. Furthermore, to ensure seamless user interaction, we developed an efficient drawing guidance system based on neural networks, providing users with a more intuitive and productive experience. The effectiveness of our approach was confirmed through comprehensive user testing and comparative analysis with existing model creation techniques. Our contribution can be categorized into two areas: (1) developing a unique deep neural network for 3D model creation and (2) establishing a freely accessible database of real scanning data, along with a accompanying drawing guidance system and virtual reality interface. This research has potentially far-reaching implications across many fields. For example, our research has applications in fields such as architecture, product design, and cultural heritage preservation, among others. Further details are available at https://draw3d.inria.fr. In the context of vision-based navigation, recall is utilized as a means of navigating through complex environments.  Despite both recall processes--active and passive--exhibiting potential benefits, active recall is generally preferred due to its assumption of control.  However, passive recall is often hindered by a requirement for query relevance.  This paper presents a novel model, called MemoNav, which simultaneously balances both recall processes.  MemoNav is designed to learn an environment through observation, creating a memory database.  This database is then utilized for both navigating to unseen locations and identifying areas that would be beneficial to visit in order to gather more information.  MemoNav is tested on multiple simulation scenarios and found to be effective in both navigating and expanding its memory database.  Additionally, MemoNav was found to be superior to an alternative method that also utilizes recall.  MemoNav's ability to balance both recall processes is a significant advancement in the field of vision-based navigation.  Additionally, its potential applications extend beyond navigation, including areas such as localization and mapping.  MemoNav can be utilized in real-world scenarios due to its compatibility with various video sources.  Finally, MemoNav has been shown to be more effective when using an unsupervised learning technique.

These notes document my approach to modeling groundwater movement using
finite difference methods. I've chosen to focus on a single layer of flow
subject to non-uniform recharge and boundary conditions that change over
time. Since real-world groundwater flow involves complex phenomena like
groundwater memory, confining layers, and multiple flow layers, I've chosen
to initially exclude these considerations to maintain clarity. Instead, I
will develop equations for a basic scenario and then discuss how they can
be expanded to tackle more sophisticated groundwater flow problems. To this
end, I have developed a set of equations that describe steady-state and
transient groundwater flow under diverse conditions, including cases where
pumping tests and recharge patterns change abruptly or gradually. I have
also applied Green's second identity to establish relationships between
potentials, and used similarity methods to analyze the effects of varying
transient recharge patterns on drawdown in a confined aquifer. Ultimately,
these notes are intended to provide a useful reference for solving
groundwater flow problems, and have been informed by discussions with
David McKenna and Robert Hyman. Additionally, the figure accompanying
these notes was generated using Mathematica, a software package that I have
also documented how to use. Please see the associated file: MathematicaNotes.pdf.

We examined the core operations of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) and their variants, rethinking their composition from a regression perspective. Our approach yields a simplified and more robust foundation for GCN architecture design. In contrast to existing theories, we found that high-powered neighbors do indeed contribute to the outcome, but their impact diminishes exponentially with increased distance. We developed a new strategy to distill the effects of multi-hop neighbors and discovered that Graph Multi-layer Convolutional Networks (GMCNs) overcomplicate the process. Our revised regression theory is the foundation for a new GMCN design, which is both more efficient and accurate. Through comprehensive testing, we proved that GCNs and GMCNs are susceptible to overgraphification. Our technical contributions include a new mathematical framework for GCNs, a simplified and accurate design for GMCNs, and a characterization of the key challenges in modeling complex graph data using deep learning methods. Our source code is publicly available. Experimental validation demonstrates that our design outperforms existing architectures in regression tasks while using significantly fewer parameters. Additionally, our study is the first to investigate the effectiveness of graph convolutional networks in general, paving the way for future research and analysis. Our revised study also includes a thorough examination of the effectiveness of Graph Convolutional Networks in regression tasks. This has led to a phenomenon where higher-priced Content Providers are able to afford these payments, leaving lower-priced ones to bear the burden. This creates an uneven playing field where popular Content Providers can negotiate fair prices with ISPs due to their high demand, potentially leveraging this to extort money from lesser-known Content Providers. To rectify this imbalance, revenue sharing agreements between Content and Service Providers become necessary. This is especially true when considering the impact of various pricing models on different Content Providers. In online auction platforms, bidders engage in second-price biddings, where the winner pays the price of the runner-up. This payment structure offers a clear advantage in terms of privacy, as bid amounts reveal no information about the winner's valuation. Research has demonstrated robust results on the efficiency of second-price biddings. Conversely, concerns persist about trustworthiness associated with bidding strategies. To address this, we designed an experimental trial, where bidders competed in second-price auctions with option to choose between two pricing methods: a straightforward fixed bid or a hidden bidding approach called "price suggestion." The primary objective was to determine whether the price suggestion feature could enhance trust among bidders. In line with previous findings, our results indicated that bidders preferred the fixed bidding method. Moreover, we found bidders to be resistant to the promised benefit of price suggestion, as claimed by the auction designer. Intriguingly, we discovered that bidders did not view the designer's intention - to maintain bidding strategy anonymity - as a valid reason to prefer price suggestion. In a broader sense, our findings emphasize the importance of auction designers' credibility in shaping bidders' behavior. In a follow-up study, we planned to investigate how bidders perceive the violation of promises by the auction designer. In terms of theoretical outcomes, our results aligned with the findings of Benthain and Wiechmann (2014) and Jarrow (2015). In recognition of our participants' input, we have prepared a public statement addressing their questions and concerns. In addition, we have composed an email that an auction designer might send to bidders, as well as an annotated bibliography on the topics of efficiency and trustworthiness in auction design. Artificial Neural Networks, including Generative Adversarial Networks and Variational Autoencoders, demonstrate capabilities in creating aesthetically pleasing and realistic images. However, the artistic merit of generated images is ultimately subjective and cannot be fully automated. To overcome this challenge, we introduce ArtScore, a straightforward objective measurement that assesses the aesthetic qualities of GAN-generated images. ArtScore utilizes a database of human ratings of artistic quality to calculate a score for each generated image. This score is derived from a score adjustment made for the number of objects in the image through an autoencoder, an innovative technique that can generate object counts with high accuracy. To streamline human labeling, we also introduced ArtLabel, a semi-supervised approach that allows humans to easily label images as high or low art quality by selecting GAN-generated images that they consider artistic or not. We utilized ArtScore for training and testing a variety of neural network art generators, and also applied it to evaluate the performance of neural networks in generating code for VAEs. A vector-like composite operator model that addresses both anomalies concidentally is considered. In this model, quarks interact with a vector-like operator at a common point. We present an extensive collection of 4260 query-response pairs in the research article domain, comprising over 51k queries and 33k responses. These query-response pairs serve as a useful benchmark for assessing question answering models and their ability to comprehend research papers. We demonstrate the utilization of our dataset, dubbed ResearchQA, to evaluate various question answering models, analyzing their performance when relying on research papers as their sole training data. Compared to similar datasets, our results show that question answering models can accurately respond to a substantial proportion of queries from research papers, achieving 44% accuracy in our analysis. Additionally, we find that integrating responses generated by GPT-3 can enhance the overall quality of answers provided. The ResearchQA dataset, as well as accompanying code, are accessible for review at https://github.com/ghancs/researchqa.

To diagnose Attention Deficit Hyperactive Disorder (ADHD), we developed a deep learning model that uses an optimized, efficiently computed space derived from resting-state functional MRI data. Our data analysis involved rs-fMRI datasets containing information about 1,050 ADHD and 1,170 control subjects. Our model employed a two-stage diagnostic process, initially using a classification model to identify potential candidates based on commonly used ADHD diagnosis criteria, and then conducted a more precise examination of these individuals using a specialized network trained on limited data. Achieving significant advancements, our model demonstrated diagnostic accuracy rates of 87.4% for ADHD diagnosis and 93.2% for distinguishing between ADHD subtypes. Notably, when applying our model to minimal-sized computed regions, we saw a substantial boost in performance, resulting in an 11.5% increase in overall accuracy. Our findings clearly show the potential for using rs-fMRI data to create highly effective diagnostic tools for ADHD, and potentially other psychiatric conditions. Our research introduces a novel approach to addressing the issues of access limitations and data obsolescence in DNA data storage. Current DNA storage architectures are plagued by a 'ruler effect' due to single molecule retrieval challenges, leading to a daunting task of maintaining up-to-date DNA data collections. We propose a hierarchical DNA storage system addressing these problems. Each level of the hierarchy corresponds to a particular time segment, with the objective of removing outdated DNA data. This architecture allows for efficient storage by limiting single molecule retrieval to specific sections. Simulations using a DNA sequence of 16 megabytes demonstrate a fourfold decrease in retrieval time compared to flat architectures. Furthermore, calculations for DNA data refreshes reveal a substantial reduction in the energy consumed. We provide mathematical analysis to validate these findings and identify key system parameters. Our research offers comprehensive insights into the design of efficient hierarchical DNA storage systems. These insights can be applied to real-world DNA data storage projects, such as the data management strategies employed by the data storage teams participating in the 4th NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory sponsored DNA Storage Workshop. These strategies involve deciding which data to keep and which data to remove, effectively deciding the hierarchy of the DNA storage system. We also contribute with a public available tool to help designing the hierarchy of the DNA storage system. We show that our proposed architecture can effectively address these errors, while making DNA storage accessible to a broader public. We illustrate these insights through concrete examples and by showing that our approach can be generalized to find the optimal hierarchy for any problem. Topological properties that exist in momentum space have a distinct advantage over their real-space counterparts as they are more resilient to external manipulations. Nodal surfaces in momentum space, which appear in 3D topological systems, possess this desirable attribute. This compact, self-contained review begins by explaining the invariances inherent to momentum-space topology. Next, it highlights recent achievements in creating momentum-space topological effects through carefully designed photonic systems, including a study that utilized photonic topological surface states to enhance spin Hall effects. Additionally, the review discusses the incorporation of momentum-space topological concepts into other platforms such as sound waves and the electronic structure of certain minerals. Finally, it concludes by outlining potential directions for future research. With its concise and educational approach, this review is intended to introduce readers to the rapidly evolving field of momentum-space topological physics. 

Note: This comprehensive review was initially prepared for the special issue 'Topological Photonics' in Journal of Physics: Condensed Matter and is supplemented with a comprehensive list of relevant references. Please note that the review is currently listed under arXiv:2207.11475.

We have developed two entropy estimation protocols using quantum sublinear operations. The first protocol is based on random Clifford measurements and analyzes its bias and variance. The results show that with sufficiently large measurements, the bias goes to zero as the dimension of the Hilbert space increases. The variance is found to scale as $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\log \Delta \rho_0^2})$ where $\rho_0$ is the initial state and $\Delta\rho_0$ represents low-energy density matrix fluctuations. The second protocol utilizes random unitary channels and investigates their impact on eigenvalue distributions through the Forest's scaling limit. The findings suggest that these protocols can estimate entropy without experiencing exponential scaling as previously believed. The ability to estimate entropy without experiencing exponential scaling could lead to breakthroughs in quantum Markov chain analysis and quantum thermodynamics. The implementation of these protocols is demonstrated using a quantum entropy estimation experiment in Python. The project's website at https://entropya.princeton.edu provides further details. The protocols have been added to QuTiP's low-level API, making it accessible through the QuTiP library.

Differentiable rendering, which integrates non-differentiable rendering methods into neural networks, has become a significant contribution in computer vision. However, the rendering process is still not fully differentiable, particularly when dealing with occluded areas, making it challenging for applications like 3D reconstruction from a single image. To overcome this limitation, we've developed an effective and differentiable shadow evaluation method that's easy to implement and integrates well with existing differentiable renderers. By combining this new method with a neural network, we've achieved notable improvements in 3D reconstruction tasks, especially when dealing with occluded areas. To validate our contribution, we've conducted extensive experiments on various occluded objects and demonstrated its effectiveness in a range of applications. Our code is openly available for others to build upon.

The well-documented Aldous-Broder and Wilson algorithms create random spanning trees through random walks, and this research aims to examine their relationship when these algorithms are run on a temporary graph derived from a given planar one by adding 'temporary' edges. Ultimately, the analysis reveals that removing the 'temporary' edges results in a permanently equivalent graph, thereby establishing a novel connection between AB and W's algorithms. This research also presents a more general approach, a two-phase framework, for generating uniform spanning trees across all possible spanning trees of a given graph. This framework is particularly illustrated by providing two alternative proofs that demonstrate the generation of uniform spanning trees using AB's algorithm. Two specific derivations are shown, one by utilizing the two-stage framework and another by employing the concept of 'temporary' edges in edge EDF (eager depth-first) search. Interestingly, the analysis finds that AB's algorithm can be enhanced by incorporating Wilson's backtracking feature, thereby decreasing its expected generating time. Finally, the research presents a tool for automating the generation of uniform spanning trees using the two-stage framework. This could potentially be integrated into a permanent addition into the TREDFS (tree depth-first search) algorithm previously proposed by this researcher. This integration would allow for the efficient generation of uniform spanning trees in real-time. This research may also be applied to cryo-EM image orientation in 3D protein imaging and other fields.

These preconditioners are then compared in terms of effectiveness and implementation difficulty.  Our findings are similar to those from finite element problems and show that the top-left and top-right entries of the preconditioner are the most important.  This research lays the foundation for developing and applying structured preconditioners in solving cardiac mechanics problems.  The results, obtained through theoretical and experimental analysis, show that the top-left and top-right entries of the preconditioner significantly impact the quality of the solution.  This knowledge can be utilized to develop more efficient and scalable preconditioners.  The research also highlights the practical implications of our findings, and we share experimental data to facilitate the replication of our results.  This research could be extended by exploring new forms of preconditioners.  The data consists of codes for Toeplitz and circulant preconditioners, along with relevant documentation. We're examining the long-term behavior of mild solutions to the two-dimensional compressible FENE dumbbell model, where the kinematic viscosity has a positive value but may approach zero. The model describes a fluid with polymer additives, capturing key characteristics of the interaction between the fluid and polymer molecules. The global existence of mild solutions for the two-dimensional model has been proven under certain conditions on the relaxation rate and the initial data. This paper focuses on the study of the global attractor and robustness of the attractor. We construct a bi-Lipschitz global attractor for mild solutions, where the bi-Lipschitz constant depends on the kinematic viscosity. We also show that this attractor is robust under perturbations in the relaxation rate and initial data. The most significant findings concern the time behavior of the global attractor. For small viscosities, we establish that the global attractor is attracted to a family of equilibrium solutions in a certain sense. This universal solution has specific properties such that it remains uniformly bounded as the kinematic viscosity and relaxation rate tend to their respective non-zero limits. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, widespread application remains challenging due to the issue of generalizability. The ability of reinforcement learning models to perform well in diverse settings is a key area of focus. In order to evaluate this capability, researchers typically transfer learned policies to new environments or tasks. However, existing benchmark settings often have design flaws that complicate the comparison of lifelong reinforcement learning methods. To address this, we present a new evaluation framework and a collection of 16 distinct lifelong reinforcement learning scenarios. We provide policy transfer results for 13 established reinforcement learning methods to demonstrate the diversity of approaches that can be useful in addressing real-world lifelong reinforcement learning challenges. Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally states that if subsets A and B, of size k and comprised of integers, share a sumset with a size near 2k, then A and B exhibit considerable similarity in structure. Specifically, the theorem asserts that if |A| = |B| = k and AB ⊂ ℤ, with at least 3k - 4 elements, it can be deduced that there exists a subset A' of A, and a subset B' of B, both of size at least k/2, such that A' + B' ⊂ AB. In this article, we introduce a refined version of Freiman's 3k-4 theorem, tailored for instances where subsets A and B might not be of equal size. Our proof technique employs a structural analysis method it describes as 'finding a good match'. The validity of our results can be extended to larger finite fields, as well as fields with a prime number of elements, provided certain minor adjustments are made. The key innovation of our work is the introduction of a property which we term 'freiman-ness' for sets A and B, when char(ℤ(A + B)) = 0. Using freiman-ness, we can demonstrate the existence of nearly identical subsets A' of A and B' of B, regardless of the sizes of A and B. The application of freiman-ness allows us to generalize the 3k-4 theorem for both small and large finite fields, yielding a generalized version of the theorem that applies to fields with a size divisible by 4. The theorem's generalized statement reads as follows: for any subsets A and B, of a finite field ℚ, with sizes a and b respectively, and satisfying AB ⊂ ℤ(ℚ), the sumset A + B will contain all non-zero integers with a total frequency additive up to (4 - a - b + 1)ℵ0. Furthermore, if freiman-ness is achieved for A and B, it can be deduced that there exist subsets A' of A and B' of B, with sizes at least (1 - (4 - a - b + 1)/2)a and (1 - (4 - a - b + 1)/2)b respectively, such that A' + B' ⊂ AB.
