This paper investigates the impact of ground noise on noise robust automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems. We demonstrate that ground noise can adversely affect the performance of state-of-the-art ASR models, leading to a significant decrease in accuracy. Notably, the deterioration in results is more pronounced for shorter sentence lengths. Furthermore, the ground noise seems to have a greater detrimental influence on English than on Arabic speech data. To address this issue, we utilized beam pruning and word-level lattice-based decoding as possible solutions to improve the robustness of ASR systems in the presence of ground noise. Lattice-based decoding showed promising results, with an approximately 50% character accuracy for beam pruning of 250. Notably, the ground noise effect was more apparent in the beginning of sentences. We propose that this ground noise effect could be minimized by starting the ASR system without a silence assumption and providing a prediction for the first few words in each sentence, thereby enhancing the robustness of ASR systems when encountering ground noise. Experimental findings confirm this hypothesis. Additionally, we investigated the ground noise effect on several speech recognition metrics and observed character accuracy to be the most susceptible metric. Interestingly, the effect of ground noise was more apparent on sentences with longer texts. Finally, we observed that ground noise had a greater impact on female speakers than on male speakers. Nonetheless, we were unable to explain this observed difference in terms of speaker characteristics. In summary, ground noise had a detrimental impact on the performance of ASR systems, ground noise effect was more apparent on sentences containing more spoken words, and an ASR system's performance could be improved through lattice-based decoding in noisy environments. Moreover, we discovered that ground noise affected speech recognition, particularly when it involved words at the beginning of sentences, and finally, although not thoroughly investigated, we noticed a noticeable adverse ground noise effect on female speakers. In view of these findings, we recommend employing lattice-based decoding as a potential solution to ground noise and propose further study on the ground noise effect to uncover its underlying causes, particularly regarding gender-based speaker characteristics. Moreover, we plan to further analyze ground noise and explore additional methods, such as prosody-related factors, to enhance the robustness of speech recognition in the presence of ground noise. Lastly, we aim to further investigate the ground noise effect on Arabic speech data to determine the extent of its impact. To this end, we will conduct further experiments using speech data from various sources and incorporate our findings in this research paper. Nonetheless, our current study has already yielded significant insights into the ground noise effect

The concept of quantum entanglement has led to a deeper understanding of quantum physics and its distinct departure from classical physics, particularly in terms of non-locality as exemplified by Bell nonlocality. In typical discussions, ideal behavior of entangled systems is assumed, but in reality, imperfections are inevitable. These imperfections can take various forms, such as mixed states or noise contamination. Consequently, there has been a lack of clear and intuitive understanding of how to extract Bell nonlocality from such systems. Furthermore, there has been a misconception that noise automatically destroys Bell nonlocality, even though this is not necessarily the case. We utilize a recent approach known as Bell viability to develop a new framework for quantifying Bell nonlocality in presence of noise, focusing on the minimum resources required to recreate Bell inequalities from noisy correlations. Through this framework, we demonstrate that it is always possible to extract Bell inequalities from correlations affected by arbitrary noise levels using only binary responses, thus proving a long-theorized conjecture that Bell inequalities can be strictly tighter than chloroform inequalities. We also present a condition, referred to as the Bell viability threshold, that determines whether Bell inequalities can be created from noisy correlations without referring to specific forms of noise and responses. By combining Bell viability with a resource perspective, we identify the necessary and sufficient conditions for creating Bell inequalities from noisy correlations in terms of a trade-off between resource distance and noise distance. We apply this new framework to study Bell viability and resource distillation in scenarios involving continuous responses, revealing a trade-off between resource distance and noise distance that enables the creation of Bell inequalities from noisy states. Additionally, we show that Bell viability and resource distillation are interconnected, allowing us to find the minimum resource required to recreate Bell inequalities from states with low Bell viability, and illustrating how to extract Bell inequalities from states with high resource distance and low noise distance. Our work offers a new and intuitive understanding of how to extract Bell inequalities from noisy states and provides a practical measure of Bell nonlocality in presence of noise, thus contributing to the development of quantum nonlocality theory. Furthermore, we show that our findings can be applied to identify Bell viable states, and that Bell viability and resource distillation are relevant not only in quantum physics, but also in classical key distribution protocols. Additionally, we present a real-world example of our findings by studying Bell viability and resource distillation in a specific experiment, and illustrate how to apply our new framework in practical scenarios. Lastly, we provide a brief discussion on how our findings can be expanded

In the context of various random matrix models, we analyze the structural characteristics of energy level sets utilizing a straightforward, intuitive approach that relies on standard mathematical operations. Additionally, this method enables us to derive an explicit estimate for the number of energy levels up to a specified threshold, which exhibits a power-law relationship with the matrix size and the threshold value, specifically in the case of GUE, GSE, and GOE ensembles. Notably, this level of detail is sufficient to determine the scalar curvature of the Cauchy dual ensemble. We discover that, in the proximity of the mobility edge in one-dimensional systems, the level set structure exhibits a characteristic signature that distinguishes localized and delocalized regimes. Furthermore, this level set analysis sheds new light on the definition of ergodicity and the underlying physical mechanisms involved. Consequently, this approach provides a comprehensive understanding of the underlying statistical physics, thereby facilitating the development of a universal theoretical framework that can be applied across diverse domains. Moreover, this generalized framework naturally incorporates the Cauchy dual ensemble, which is known to accurately predict the behavior of Wigner's semicircle law even in the proximity of the edge. The proposed method employs elementary concepts and non-rigorous, intuitive mathematical operations to derive results that are precise and statistically significant at an unprecedented level of detail. The associated code is publicly available at https://github.com/eddiepham/Level-sets. Multiple time series data from distinct sources often needs segmentation and 
clustering for clear visualization and comprehensive understanding. In this 
research, a novel approach for data-driven clustering of dynamic systems is 
presented, where systems can be linear or nonlinear and noise affected. The 
approach is based on an influence metric that measures an element's 
contribution to forming a cluster. Using optimization, the influence metric is 
fine-tuned and unsmooth areas are identified for cluster boundary definition, 
ultimately resulting in smooth and meaningful clusters. The approach is 
demonstrated to outperform existing methods using synthetic and actual earthquake 
ground motion datasets. Current limitations of the approach include its high 
computational complexity and the lack of accommodating non-uniform sampling 
rates, which will be addressed in the near future.

This study offers an examination of Leibnizian infinitesimal calculus within three distinct philosophical frameworks - Boolos-Burgess style, Frege-Russell, and sheaf-theoretic. We develop three separate accounts of Leibnizian calculus, emphasizing the unique features of each framework. Our analysis particularly focuses on the nature of infinitesimal quantities and their inherent paradoxes. Additionally, these accounts have tangible applications in the theory of differential equations and variational calculus, as well as relevant implications for the philosophy of mathematics. Lastly, our results also bear significance to the broader understanding of the historical development of calculus, as they highlight both points of agreement and divergence in the interpretations of Leibniz's work. We also make a case for the compatibility of Leibnizian intuitions with a Fregean foundation, albeit one that accommodates null quantities. Furthermore, this study also outlines a sheaf-theoretic approach to handling null quantities, incorporating techniques such as topology, category theory, and spectral sequences. Ultimately, our results demonstrate the viability of a rigorous mathematical framework that is faithful to Leibnizian intuitions, one that can even provide insights for researchers in the field of differential geometry, partial differential equations, and quantum physics. We also draw connections between Leibnizian thoughts on calculus and his broader metaphysical conception, as well as a sheaf-theoretic interpretation that incorporates null quantities, one that can even offer a new understanding of the generalised Reichenbach's causal structure. First introduced in 2001, the concept of observing timed characteristics (OTC), a type of timed regular behavior, is discussed in the context of web interactions. Research into OTC development has been sparse compared to other types of regular behaviors. This note presents an automata-based definition for OTC and demonstrates the equivalence between this concept and timed properties defined using temporal logic. Additionally, the article specifies conditions under which an OTC model can accurately represent a temporal logic specification, and it offers guidelines for creating finite OTC models from web interaction data, addressing a key challenge identified in the original paper. The guidelines are exemplified through a case study involving a healthcare website. Furthermore, the article suggests possible directions for further investigation, including (1) establishing whether an OTC model can always capture a temporal logic specification, and (2) developing algorithms for determining whether an OTC model corresponds to a temporal logic specification. These research avenues have the potential to provide more robust solutions for modeling regular behaviors in human-computer interaction. The article is a revised version of the original paper and has been updated with new findings. The updated content includes additional material, and the results have been revalidated using current research standards. The article was originally presented at RCRA'22 and is being published in the conference proceedings. A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals is derived. This concise equation encompasses the perfect gas model, is applicable to all alkali metals, and accurately predicts their behavior across a broad pressure range. Furthermore, it is shown that the ideal gas law accurately estimates the alkali metal equation of state at relatively low pressures. At higher pressures, a modified van der Waals equation of state is provided, along with an evaluation of its predicted range of applicability. Utilizing the derived equation of state, thermodynamic properties such as entropy, heat capacity, and isothermal compressibility are calculated and compared with experimental data. Additionally, it is demonstrated that the derived equation of state successfully estimates enthalpy, Gibbs free energy, and other thermodynamic properties of alkali metals. Critical assessment reveals that the derived equation of state significantly outperforms existing theories and models in predicting thermodynamic properties. Recent laboratory measurements have provided the individual electronic mass values of the 20-inch PMTs, used in the JUNO experiment, ranging from 5 to 42 inches. However, these individual masses need to be cross-checked with tandem electron scaling methods to ensure consistency. Furthermore, the electron mass correction also plays a significant role in determining the PMTs' mass. In addition to these corrections, the experimental mass of the PMTs would need to be adjusted for residual activity resulting from the radioactive decay of Primeval Abundance Long-Lived isotopes present in the scintillator and detected by the PMTs. For the JUNO experiment to achieve its desired energy resolution goals, a thorough cross-check of the PMTs' mass measurements is essential to remove systematic scaling effects. For this purpose, the experiment employed an innovative systematic approach to determine the full-scale mass of the 20-inch PMTs, used in the experiment, by combining various correction methods. Utilizing this rigorous procedure, the experiment was able to achieve an energy resolution of about 0.1 percent. Using this fully characterized detector system, the experiment can proceed to achieve its desired energy resolution goals. In this paper, the tandem electron method used to calculate the full-scale mass of the 20-inch PMTs is described in detail. Additionally, the electron mass correction and residual activity correction applied to the PMTs' mass are discussed. Furthermore, the advantages and challenges associated with using the tandem electron method are thoroughly examined. Finally, the results from the systematic cross-check of the 20-inch PMTs' mass corrections are presented along with the relevant conclusions. Using this fully cross-checked and characterized system, the experiment can proceed to achieve its desired energy resolution goals. With energy resolutions of about 0.1 percent for the 20-inch and 1 percent for the 10-inch PMTs, the experiment can provide valuable insights into neutrino mass ordering and other key areas of study. Moreover, the experiment can offer precious insights into various aspects, including the neutrino mass ordering, electron-solar neutrino energy spectrum, and other key areas of research by taking advantage of the low background and the precise energy measurements over a broad range provided by the experiment. Multidimensional time series forecasting has garnered significant interest in recent years, primarily due to its practical applications in power consumption and energy demand forecasting. Recent research has employed advanced models like Multistep Multidimensional LSTM, Memory and Network Information Flow, and FSTGRU to achieve impressive results. These advancements have highlighted the importance of incorporating intrinsic properties of time series, dimension interactions, and spatial relationships into the model structure. To address this, we introduce a novel Adaptive Graph Convolutional Network model that builds upon traditional LSTM by dynamically forming interaction graphs between time series and using them to inform model predictions. Experimental evaluations on various datasets reveal our model to be highly competitive, striking a favorable balance between performance and computational efficiency. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates the feasibility of our model to capture intrinsic relationships within the data. Finally, we conduct a comprehensive study to standardize evaluation processes in multidimensional time series forecasting research. Accurately assessing the impact of atmospheric distortion is critical for selecting the most effective adaptive optics strategy. Historical data from various locations can be utilized to create detailed models of the atmosphere, which are then employed to simulate the effects of atmospheric distortion on starlight. We utilized a dataset comprising 504 nights of data from the Mauna Kea Observatory to create such a model. This paper outlines the method used to create a comprehensive model of the atmosphere, which involves defining the average and distribution of seeing and tip-tilt parameters for distinct weather conditions. Specifically, we developed a time-series analysis to create a customized model of the seeing distribution for different altitudes, which varies based on weather types and the position of stars in the sky. Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To leverage the knowledge from various teachers (pre-trained models), this research proposes a new method called PILE, which simplifies the process of knowledge distillation. PILE's design is based on two key components: the teacher's actual output and a pseudo-label generated by the student model. By incorporating these components into the loss function through a pairwise comparison process, PILE's performance is demonstrated to be on par with expert-provided labels, while also being more effective than existing multi-teacher knowledge distillation methods. Furthermore, PILE's approach can be applied to other knowledge distillation methods, significantly enhancing their efficiency. Experiment results show that PILE achieves remarkable improvements over strong baselines, with code available at https://github.com/ChenZheNye/Pile. We suggest a highly sensitive method to detect ultralight bosonic dark matter, which involves using the repulsive force between the dark matter particle and laboratory test masses to extract its mass and interaction coefficient. This proposal builds on established techniques used to study the optical properties of materials and offers two main benefits: (i) it requires minimal assumptions about the dark matter particle's behavior; and (ii) it enables the detection of dark matter particles in a frequency range that extends far beyond audio frequencies. Furthermore, the required experimental setup is similar to that used in conventional phonon coupling experiments. We provide a detailed theoretical framework and estimate that the required measurement precision can be achieved with a sensor design that has an extremely low thermal noise, specifically with a noise spectrum that peaks at frequencies higher than 100 kHz with a magnitude less than 10^-14 Hz^(-1/2) kinetic energy unit. Additionally, we propose that the desired sensor performance can be achieved by using a sensor design that has either a very low mass or a very short decay time. We outline two possible experimental methods to demonstrate the feasibility of this approach, with and without a resonant environment, and identify key parameters that need to be fine-tuned for a successful measurement. Finally, we estimate that the present-day sensor designs are capable of constraining the dark matter particle's mass up to 10^11 GeV. With future sensor developments that push the boundary of sensitivity deeper into the radio frequency spectrum, we believe that the proposed sensor design can enable the detection of dark matter particles with frequencies up to at least 10^14 Hz. Consequently, we suggest that the proposed sensor setup serves as a reliable and versatile tool to study the nature of ultralight bosonic dark matter across an extensive frequency range. Moreover, we think that this sensor design offers an attractive option for direct dark matter detection that is distinct from conventional methods, which rely on the collision of particles, and instead focuses on the characteristics of the dark matter particle that can be extracted through force measurements. Lastly, we speculate that the proposed sensor design may yield valuable insights into the properties of dark matter particles at frequencies that correspond to the cosmic baryon overdensities, which could provide a more stable and stable basis for understanding the universe's dark matter component. Ultimately, the direct observation of dark matter particles in the audio-frequency range could be accomplished by employing a sensor design that is capable of detecting even the slightest perturbations in the laboratory test masses over long periods of time. The growth in availability of training data has facilitated the construction of complex models, yet poses questions about consent and data protection. Federated Learning emerges as a promising framework to address these concerns by allowing model development using locally stored data, with intermediate results shared across users. This approach, combined with Differential Privacy and Equity considerations, enables the development of equitable models, insensitive to users' personal information, and robust against biases. However, several challenges persist, notably the interplay of Equity and Differential Privacy constraints, leading to suboptimal test performance. In this study, we systematically investigate the implications of these constraints for FL, commencing with an in-depth analysis of test performance under various Equity and Differential Privacy scenarios, with and without bias. We then introduce a novel DP-Equity framework, along with an optimization procedure for joint EQ-DP constraint satisfaction, with numerical evaluations demonstrating the performance of this method. Furthermore, our research explores the impact of distinct Equity forms, particularly Weighted Equity and Centralized Equity, and examines their interactions with Differential Privacy. To facilitate this research, we have created a Federated Learning simulator, enabling us to study various Equity forms, with a particular focus on their behavior in the absence of biases. Our research offers a deeper understanding of the complex interplay among Equity and Differential Privacy constraints, along with new avenues for sparsity and generalization analysis in FL. Furthermore, our results may be useful for developing future research in FL, by providing a performance benchmark for various Equity and Differential Privacy forms. Thanks to significant advancements, deep neural networks are now capable of emulating complex mental behaviors with high accuracy. Nonetheless, completing training typically requires accessing expensive, specialized computing facilities consisting of numerous powerful computing units. Consequently, selecting the optimal computing infrastructure for training deep neural networks in a distributed computing environment has become a pressing concern. Ideally, each computing unit should be tasked with training a segment of the neural network, and an efficient scheduler would allocate these tasks accordingly. Nonetheless, current scheduling approaches lack systematization, relying on intuition or a thorough analysis of the neural network architecture to make informed decisions. We propose a review-based algorithm for scheduling deep neural network training across multiple computing units, involving expert evaluations to pinpoint challenging aspects of the task. To improve scheduling efficiency over time, we revise our strategy based on accumulated knowledge, ultimately resulting in consistent performance across different data sets, and even surpassing the efficiency of highly optimized, hand-crafted approaches. Furthermore, regional reviewer training enables system-level improvements, and we prove that our method can locate inefficiencies within neural network structures that expert human schedulers might miss. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through rigorous testing using the BDDC method for solving graph partitioning issues. Additionally, regional reviewer training enables our scheduler to tackle complex, densely connected structures that would otherwise pose significant computational challenges. With regional reviewer training, our scheduler can handle a wide range of additional tasks without substantial performance degradation. Nonetheless, regional reviewer training is not a requirement for using our scheduled algorithm. We validate our approach using standard data sets, and even compared its effectiveness to other cutting-edge scheduling techniques. Ultimately, regional reviewer training results in consistent system-level improvements, and we make our scheduled algorithm available to the public to facilitate its use. Publication details: R. This study presents a novel computational method for identifying the movement of living creatures within video footage. Researchers have developed a new method to resolve collisions more effectively, employing a multi-time-step technique that breaks down complex collisions into manageable stages. By advancing simulation time in increments related to collision duration, each particle is either in a state of free flow or undergoing a collision. When a particle is involved in a collision, the time step is adjusted accordingly. The underlying structure, featuring a cubic arrangement of K and Rb or Cs within the Laves phase of $A$Bi$_2$, contains no chiral defects. However, this changes with the intercalation of excess K or Rb ions into the crystal lattice of $A$Bi$_2$, $A$ being Cs or Rb, respectively. This results in a transformation of the lattice and the creation of chiral vibrational modes at low frequencies. Similar phenomena can potentially occur in other $A$Bi$_2$ materials if they are subjected to chemical modification and have a related structural setup. The newly formed chiral structures give rise to excitations that are associated with the breaking of inversion symmetry, giving $A$Bi$_2$ (and analogous materials based on Na instead of K or Rb) the characteristics of a chiral semiconductor. We derived a time-dependent expression for Born effective capacities in non-adiabatic systems by using a Kubo formalism based on charge transport. 
In non-adiabatic situations, the Drude weight in 3D and 2D systems can be represented as the product of the square of the Born effective capacity and the chemical potential. 
Our findings indicate that the Born effective capacities in metals undergo a sudden change at very low frequencies, originating from the response of metals to very long-wavelength electrical fields and influenced significantly by electron-phonon interaction. 
We verified these conclusions through extensive computational modeling of Na, Si, and Pt, utilizing a full-elastic electron-phonon spectrum for Na to distinguish it from the conventional Drude model. 
In practical terms, the non-adiabatic Born effective capacities might be measurable using advanced techniques such as time-resolved x-ray scattering or x-ray scattering from ultrafast laser-generated plasmas. 
Ultimately, an experimental validation of the non-adiabatic Born effective capacities could provide valuable insights into the dynamics of charge transport in materials. 
In addition, this approach could be extended to superconductors, potentially leading to a new understanding of the McMillan parameter. 
Furthermore, this generalized formulation of Born effective capacities might be applicable to other types of dielectric responses, such as polar and ferroelectric materials treated as non-adiabatic. 
Overall, the non-adiabatic Born effective capacities offer a versatile and theoretically sound description of the dielectric properties of materials under dynamic conditions. 
This approach is adaptable to different materials and can be utilized with a wide range of experimental techniques without modifications. 
Therefore, this generalized formulation is expected to have a broad range of practical applications.

We are introducing a new concept called feebly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within the realm of associative rings, where every product of at most three ideals contained in it is contained in the ideal itself. By employing this novel definition, we successfully generalize multiple instances of known results from the literature. Additionally, we present examples to demonstrate the non-universality of feebly $1$-absorbing prime ideals by showing cases where they fail to exist or when they do exist but do not satisfy certain expected properties. Notably, we investigate feebly $1$-absorbing prime ideals within both commutative rings and fields, where we establish relationships between this concept and other properties such as sets of non-zero elements and ideals. Finally, we explore connections between feebly $1$-absorbing prime ideals and strongly $1$-absorbing prime ideals, where we identify specific situations in commutative rings where these two concepts overlap, while also presenting an example where feebly $1$-absorbing prime ideals and strongly $1$-absorbing prime ideals do not coexist.

In recent years, advanced damage detection for roads has drawn significant attention from automated facility management and maintenance agencies, with the goal of reducing costs and improving services. Current approaches, however, face several challenges, including the slow detection of damages, limited applicability to various countries, and the lack of integration of new and effective deep learning techniques. To address these issues, a new deep learning approach is proposed, which is built on a pre-trained model and utilizes a combination of image segmentation and classification methods to identify and categorize road hazards more efficiently. To evaluate its effectiveness, extensive testing was conducted using a large, worldwide road damage dataset consisting of over 65,000 images from multiple countries. The proposed model has shown promising results, surpassing existing approaches in multiple datasets. For instance, it achieved an accuracy of 97.3% in the USA, 96.6% in Canada, 95.7% in Australia, 94.1% in the UK, 98.1% in Germany, and 97.6% in India. Furthermore, it demonstrates better performance than other deep learning techniques, such as MobileNetV2, VGG19, and XCeption, as well as 4 key commercial and open-source computer vision models, including Cityscape, Baidu, Paddle Paddle, and Adobe Phillips Kirkor. The proposed model has also shown remarkable generalizability, with its accuracy remaining high when trained and tested using data from different countries. For more information, please visit its website at <https://roadet.github.io/RoadEt/. Implementation details are also available on GitHub at <https://github.com/RoadEt/RLDRID>. A large, worldwide road damage dataset consisting of over 65,000 images can be downloaded at <https://roadet.github.io/RDSD/.>. Finally, a comprehensive technical report has been published on arXiv at <https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.06557.>. Imitation learning seeks to bypass exhaustive data collection by instead using human demonstrations to train representations that can be applied to new tasks.  While widespread area-wise imitation has been achieved, where a single representation works well across similar tasks, it remains challenging to transfer representations between disparate task areas.  This paper investigates whether observations of task transitions can facilitate imitation in new areas.  When area boundaries are defined, the paper demonstrates that cross-area imitation is feasible if enough task transitions are observed.  This is because adaptations from one task are imitated in subsequent tasks, leading the representation to converge.  When area boundaries are unclear, the paper presents a method to diagnose the structure of the task space and initiate a new imitation area.  This structure is derived by analyzing the correlations between different tasks, and the technique is shown to be effective even when trained on multiple task transitions.  Overall, the paper's findings suggest that cross-area imitation is achievable if sufficient adaptations are observed across task transitions.  This represents an important step towards applying imitation learning in complex, dynamically changing environments.  Code for this research can be found at https://github.com/bclausn/xai.  Additional resources, including videos and the trained models, can be found at https://bclausn.github.io/xai. A Population III star's intense birth cloud is initially on a rotating disk, 
which could fragment due to magnetic fields that halt accretion, 
resulting in the formation of planetary mass objects. 
We simulated the evolution of this system, 
considering both the rotational and magnetic forces exerted by the star. 
In one scenario, the star's rotational energy generated a massive 
disk and complex magnetic fields that prevented fragmentation. 
In another scenario, an intensified magnetic field 
that wraps around the equator could form and potentially prevent fragmentation 
by blocking mass accumulation, 
which in turn could intensify the star's rotational velocity, 
creating a scenario where no planetary mass objects form. 
This intense magnetic field could persist if the star remains isolated, 
which in turn affects the environment surrounding the star. 
In contrast, a more gentle magnetic field results in disk fragmentation, 
leading to the formation of smaller objects. 
This intense magnetic field phenomenon is distinct from typical star 
formations and could result in no binary or multiple star systems 
forming around Population III stars. 
Lastly, this intense magnetic field could significantly impact 
metal-free binary star formations.

Association rules analysis is a significant technique in Data Mining, and its applications extend beyond market analysis to epidemiological and textual data analysis. The underlying structure of association rules is represented as implications, and classical systems are based on binary representations in databases and antitatabases. The concept of deduction framework generalizes this idea, enabling the use of diverse binary structures. The generalized system is evaluated by determining the deducibility of implications, and its decision-making process is shown to be NP-complete. The association rule analysis is equivalent to searching for the minimum-size base in a deduction framework, and finding such a base is an NP-complete problem. The search for a base is a well-known problem in Boolean satisfiability, and various algorithms are employed to solve it, including SAT solvers and specialized algorithms for Boolean satisfiability with restrictions. Additionally, the concept of repetition is introduced in deduction frameworks and enables the generation of new implications, leading to the discovery of new bases and association rules. The incorporation of repetition and its effect on deducibility and complexity is also discussed. The association rule analysis with repetition is equivalent to searching for a base in a certain class of sequences, and this generalized system is applicable to textual data analysis, where the presence of repetitions is often required to identify, for instance, the minimum number of letters required to write a given text. The association rule analysis with repetition is also applicable to epidemiological analysis, where the concept of repetition is often encountered, for instance, the minimum number of symptoms required to identify a particular disease. The association rule analysis with and without repetitions was applied to two real-life datasets: a textual dataset obtained from the website "http://www.freetextsearch.com/" and an epidemiological dataset obtained from "http://libimc.net/.html". The experiments demonstrated that the search for a base in a deduction system with repetition is computationally efficient, and the derived rules have a high level of accuracy in both applications. Furthermore, the derived rules were found to be more accurate than traditional methods such as APriori and other general-purpose association rule mining algorithms, and the derived rules require significantly fewer items to describe the data, indicating their superiority. The derived rules without repetition are also comparable to other association rule mining algorithms in terms of precision and recall, and the derived rules without repetition are computationally efficient and can be effectively used for data exploration purposes. The concepts of deduction framework and repetition are novel generalizations of the classical binary structure and can be applied to a wide range of data mining problems beyond association rule analysis. Using a novel approach with treatment as a counterfactual, I analyzed data from South Carolina's criminal justice system, discovering that receiving mental health treatment led to a substantial, long-term reduction in criminal recidivism. Interestingly, the recidivism rate decreased more significantly for low-risk offenders who underwent treatment, implying that mental health treatment can enhance rehabilitation, particularly for those who do not require constant supervision. Additionally, this research stresses the importance of targeting those who are most likely to benefit from such treatment, including lower-risk individuals who do not require constant supervision. Current neural-based translation and speech recognition systems rely heavily on extensive, carefully curated datasets. However, such datasets are rare and often come with a cost in terms of data preparation time. This paper presents a new method that greatly reduces the effort required to train these systems by using unenhanced, noisy data and automatically correcting errors through a form of data augmentation. We test our approach on speech-to-text technology that can translate spoken Italian into written English. By comparing the accuracy of our low-effort training method to the traditional standard, we demonstrate that minor enhancements to existing techniques allow our system to match the performance of the established method without the need for perfect data. Furthermore, we find that repeatedly applying our training method leads to significant gains in accuracy, surpassing the outcomes of numerous iterations of traditional training. Ultimately, we achieve nearly identical performance after 20 iterations of our low-effort training, whereas traditional methods required 40 iterations to achieve similar results. Code and model resources are available at https://github.com/mjfuentes/CuriousCase. Experimental results are available at https://tinyurl.com/2022EUSAR.

In protoplanetary disks, it is still a mystery why some gas disappears at the location where planets are formed.  A disk like AS 209 has an impressive array of sub-millimeter continuum gaps and ring structures, created by a complex interplay of gas flow and photochemistry.  Using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) observatory at a high angular resolution, we discover a notable CO gap in this disk.  By performing both chemical and dynamical simulations, we explore the processes behind this observed CO gap.  Although reformed CO could explain the observed gap, it is also consistent with a scenario where the CO gas is shifted away from the disk's center due from dynamical effects.  Additionally, we find that both the reformation and dynamical explanations have similar difficulties in accounting for the observed polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) emission in the disk.  Consequently, we propose that the CO gap could be influenced by both chemical and dynamical processes.  Moreover, we find that a distribution of CO that varies based on the disk's altitude could contribute to the overall gap shape.  This is particularly true for the CO isotope, $^{13}$CO, which exhibits a noticeable presence at the disk's midplane.  Finally, we discover that a CO grain that can survive radiation-free for a certain period has the potential to greatly reduce the CO gas presence at the disk's upper layers.  This has significant implications for future observations in the far-ultraviolet spectrum at the disk location where AS 209 resides. The analysis of time-stamped data becomes increasingly common across various scientific disciplines. Researchers utilize diverse software and tools to process such data, which often leads to confusion and the duplication of efforts. To address these issues, we have developed an open-source, user-friendly collection of libraries and utilities that provide a comprehensive solution for dealing with time-tagged data. The toolkit includes sophisticated algorithms for synchronization, analysis, and simulation, as well as a flexible interface for importing and combining different data formats. We highlight its capabilities through practical applications in real-time atomic clocks, radiocarbon dating measurement devices, and software simulating time-stamped data. Demos based on popular programming languages, including Python, Java, and C++, are provided to demonstrate the toolkit's effectiveness. We advocate for the utilization of this toolkit as a standard resource for scientists working with time-stamped data. Furthermore, we propose it as a foundation for developing educational courses and seminars focused on the analysis of such data. We demonstrate the existence of mild solutions for a mean field game associated with a class of controls subject to state constraints. These controls are characterized by a cost function with polynomial growth and a constraint coupled with a measurable transition function. The existence of mild solutions in this context builds upon the work of Cardaliaguet and Porreti, who established existence of viscous solutions under similar conditions. Notably, we accommodate situations where the transition function may not be differentiable. These findings contribute towards bridging the gap between continuous-time models and discrete-time models in mean field games of controls. Furthermore, the approach taken in this study lays the groundwork for analyzing the uniqueness of mild solutions using semiconvexity and regularity of the transition function. These findings are anticipated to be extended to a broader class of mean field games of flows. The content of this article is a byproduct of joint discussions with Marta Cardaliaguet and Fabio Santannopoli. The material presented here is a preliminary version of the contents that will be included in the dissertation of the first listed author.

Recent studies using the Gaia DR2 revealed numerous stellar structures in the galaxy, prompting an examination of a specific type of structure - linear collections of stars, referred to as "threads". We re-evaluated these structures through data analysis and simulations, focusing on their formation and maintenance. Interestingly, our results showed that many "threads" can be attributed to unrelated star clusters and overdensities, rather than actual structures. It became apparent that both early and recent findings shared similar issues. The main challenge lies in the algorithm used to detect structures, which prioritizes coherence over proximity. This led us to propose an alternative approach - a more comprehensive assessment of the galaxy, unaffected by detection biases, in which stellar clusters and structures are identified and characterized through established methods. This altered perspective revealed that many "threads" are in fact dispersed and can be distinguished from genuine structures, such as the brilliant southern spiral arm, where increased age and dispersion correlate with decreasing brightness. Our study demonstrates that closer attention to data processing and algorithm selection can yield more precise findings, ultimately providing a clearer understanding of the galaxy's building blocks. Additionally, our observations imply that many "threads" may actually be star birthplaces, with potential to uncover previously unrecognized patterns of star formation. Further research using higher-resolution data is needed to confirm these hypotheses and gain a deeper understanding of the galaxy's intricate structures. The diversity of products available across different e-commerce platforms necessitates efficient methods for locating duplicates among vast visual datasets. In this research, we introduce VICTOR, a cutting-edge deep learning model that detects visual discrepancies between images, allowing for the identification of replicate products. Initially, we establish a comprehensive dataset compiled from the curated collection of product images from Amazon Fashion. This dataset, referred to as VisualChecker-20k, comprises 20,057 unique product images grouped into categories based on visual characteristics. The development of VICTOR entails a multi-stage training process that involves a pair-based training method utilizing a custom-designed loss function to refine the model's performance. Additionally, we pre-train VICTOR with a contrastive learning approach tailored to the specifics of the fashion industry, leveraging a vast set of e-commerce product images totaling 80M in size. This pre-training process, referred to as FashionCL, enhances the model's overall Robustness. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that the combination of VICTOR and FashionCLCL leads to superior performance, achieving an accuracy rate of 97.3% on the test set, 7.7% higher than the baseline model that trains VICTOR solely on VisualChecker-20k. Furthermore, we analyze the distinctiveness of the sub-categories of VisualChecker-20k, demonstrating that the accuracy rate of VICTOR reaches 93% when the categories comprise solely distinct visual data, underscoring the model's potential applications in e-commerce product visual classification. In order to facilitate the use of our model in real-world settings, we also create an open-source coding framework for visual discrepancy detection, allowing other researchers to replicate our results. The dataset as well as the coding framework can be found at https://github.com/AsuncE/VisualChecker. Several experiments have also been conducted to evaluate the impact of diverse visual characteristics on the accuracy of VICTOR, confirming the model's performance across a range of visual categories. Moreover, we assess the robustness of sub-categories of VisualChecker-20k to different visual perturbations, discovering that certain visual characteristics are more robust to alterations than others, specifically textures, shading, and semantically significant segments. This research presents a novel and accurate deep learning model, VICTOR, alongside a vast, curated dataset and an open-source coding framework that enable the detection of visual discrepancies between product images, offering a range of potential applications in the training of visual classification models. Federated learning is a machine learning framework that enables secure collaborative training across multiple devices while preserving user data privacy. However, a major challenge in implementing FL is the synchronization issue - especially when devices have limited available memory. Researchers have addressed this problem through local data buffering and asynchronous data accumulation but this has introduced a constraint on data availability. The requirement that devices must wait for the next scheduled global accumulation has led to suboptimal performance. In this paper, we propose a new technique called UniGradFB that addresses this synchronization issue, allowing devices to train independently of communication schedules and yielding significant performance gains without compromising user data privacy and confidentiality. Our experiments demonstrate that UniGradFB outperforms current FL implementations by achieving faster convergence rates and near-optimal performance. This boost in performance is made possible by efficiently utilizing available memory, freeing devices from waiting-time, and empowering the ML algorithm to take full advantage of device data. Our innovative technique achieves this while preserving the core FL principles of secure model aggregation and privacy-protected data ownership. Unlike existing FL models that rely on explicit data availability constraints, UniGradFB allows devices to train with complete data availability flexibility. This freedom is enabled by a novel federated learning technique called Buffered Asynchronous Accumulation and is complemented by an efficient gradient optimization approach called Unconstrained Gradient. Together, these advanced techniques allow devices to train a ML model with the same effectiveness as training a smaller model. Our technical contributions include a novel U2F framework that can handle data availability constraints and a novel evaluation method called the Price of Conicization that estimates performance costs due to synchronization constraints. Our experiments demonstrate that UniGradFB, the first efficient FL design without data availability constraints, offers a wide range of possible parameter choices. This freedom allows developers to select the best combination of performance, privacy, and data ownership based on their specific requirements. All our code and experiment designs are publicly available for other researchers to verify and build upon our results. unigrad-fb.github.io. A flexible raft represents an idealized model for a flat structure of a fluid-filled box. When subjected to external forces like pressure and bending, it develops elastic deformations, ultimately leading to fracture-like cracks in areas of high bending stress as predicted by theoretical models and confirmed through recent experiments. To further investigate this phenomenon, we conducted additional experiments using higher-brightness microscopes to image and analyze the fractures formed in rafts under various cross-linking densities and external stresses. Unlike previous observations, we found fewer fractures in higher cross-linking densities and fewer fractures under stress than in air. By comparing our experimental results with theoretical predictions based on the concepts of fracture mechanics, we determined that most fractures occur due to weakness in air, while changes in material properties play a more significant role than external stress. Therefore, for optimal material properties, it is essential to balance cross-linking density to minimize the effects of fracture from both internal weakness and external stress. Additionally, we observed more complex fractures under stress, which can be attributed to the greater stiffness of the raft, allowing it to withstand external forces but develop more intricate fracture patterns. Specifically, we found that the number of fractures follows a power law distribution with the cross-linking density, indicating a more intricate fracture landscape, whereas the fractures under stress show a peak in number and a more even distribution among different stiffness levels. To understand these findings, we simulated the fracture using a bond-breaking model, which revealed a similar distribution of fractures in the raft. Furthermore, we found that the system exhibits two types of critical behavior, depending on the density of cross-linking, where the fractures show distinct behavior, and that both the fractures and the bonds exhibit power-law distributions. Additionally, we discovered a relationship between the stiffness of the raft and its surface tension, and found that the minimum energy required to break a bond is directly proportional to the stiffness of the raft. Based on these results, we propose that the fracture landscape of the raft, which is caused by instability when the bending stress overcomes the material toughness, can be optimized by adjusting the density of cross-linking to reduce the negative effects of fracture from both internal weakness and external stress. Moreover, we found that the fracture under stress exhibits a more even distribution among different stiffness levels, and that the system's behavior can be accurately simulated using a bond-breaking model, which may provide a framework for developing theoretical models that can be applied to more complex biological and biological-inspired materials. This study uncovered the potential for enhancing hole mobility in GaN through matched strain with ZnGeN$_2$ and ZnSiN$_2$. The optimization of the lattice parameters of these materials allows for a 30% improvement in the hole effective mass, and consequently, a 75% increase in hole mobility at the absolute zero temperature. We have also explored the hole transport properties in GaN as influenced by the tetragonal and trigonal distortions introduced by the strain. By applying a non-Abelian Strum-like mechanism, we found that the distortion can trigger the generation of zero modes at the strain-induced miniband edges, leading to an increased hole mobility near room temperature. Furthermore, the findings suggest that integrating GaN with ZnGeN$_2$ or ZnSiN$_2$ could act as a semiconducting strain generator, enabling a 10% increase in hole mobility. We have verified the theoretical predictions by reviewing existing experimental data and observed a noticeable correlation. Notably, integrating GaN with MgSiN$_2$ has shown the promise of enhanced electron mobility as well. Overall, the research indicates that matching the strain in a heterostructure can offer an effective solution to the problem of low hole mobility in gallium nitride. This study may also contribute to the discovery of new two-dimensional semiconductors with exceptionally high mobility values. This review re-examines the estimation of conditional expectation functions, a broad concept that encompasses multiple applications including growth curve analysis, function regression, and missing data imputation. Initially, the focus is on nonparametric techniques which often rely on kernel-based estimation. Notably, these estimators can be inconsistent when conditional heteroscedasticity is present, highlighting the need for more robust methods such as those proposed by Newey and Wooldridge (1993). This review also considers more recent developments in the field, driven by evolving computational capabilities and the increasing availability of high-dimensional data. As a result, novel approaches like machine learning methods and empirical Bayes estimation have emerged, which can be viewed as modern contributions to nonparametric estimation. This article aims to provide an up-to-date summary of the subject, informed by the 2019 special volume on panel data in International Statistical Review. Key topics such as time series, high-dimensional data, and missing data have been addressed. Notwithstanding the extensive existing literature, this review necessarily lacks a comprehensive treatment of every aspect, instead providing an entry-point and a synthesis of existing knowledge. Crucially, this review focuses on the theoretical underpinning of nonparametric estimation, encompassing consistent estimation and asymptotic distributions. Furthermore, it addresses context-specific challenges and outlines emerging areas of research. Ultimately, this review is intended to provide readers with a deeper understanding of nonparametric estimation of conditional expectation functions. Keywords: Empirical Bayes, Functional Bayesian Polya, Gaussian process, Imputation, Inference, Kernel, Partially observed, Regression, Replication, Variance estimation. Predicting future knowledge connections, known as knowledge link forecasting, is a sub-task of knowledge graph completion that has gained significant interest in recent years. Most existing methods focus on using interactive information from knowledge graphs and disregard non-interactive information. Furthermore, since complete datasets are rarely available, most studies rely on short datasets. We take a different approach and propose using static graph techniques that utilize the full wealth of available information in long datasets. By doing so, we achieve superior performance compared to previous methods. Our proposed method demonstrates great flexibility and can be applied to various tasks such as predicting missing links, detecting fake data, and guiding knowledge graph embeddings. We also conduct extensive analyses to validate our method's effectiveness. Interestingly, our study reveals that enhancing the density of a graph through the prediction of new connections actually hinders its ability to forecast new links. Moreover, we observe that incorporating interactive edges can negatively impact our method's performance, highlighting the value of non-interactive information. Finally, we explore the ethical implications of using dense graphs to forecast new knowledge connections. We develop a streamlined construction method for high-dimensional expander graphs based on vertex-transitive coverings of finite graphs. This results in two new and versatile constructions of high-dimensional expander graphs. First, it leads to a simplified and more efficient version of the KRV graph family, a renowned family of high-dimensional expander graphs. Second, it yields a new family of high-dimensional expander graphs, known as the cover expander graphs (CEGs), which offers greater computational simplicity and faster vertex transitivity than the KRV family. These two constructions are likely candidates for meeting the computational challenges set by Shaked Kozma's open problem in 2018. Furthermore, CEGs can be utilized to develop a simple and efficient generation of high-dimensional expander codes, which surpasses previous constructions in terms of coding performance and leakage security. These codes have been certified secure based on the assumption of solving the generic highest non-trivial symmetric group problem, which is a well-established benchmark in cryptographic contexts. This work is the first to apply the concept of transitive coverings to the development of high-dimensional expander graphs and codes. A companion paper delves into the computational aspects and contraction properties of the cover expander graphs, including its computational complexity and dimension contraction properties. We've conducted an extensive evaluation of various choice prompts to see how they perform on different task types in a zero-shot setting. Our research spans six diverse task categories, including which movie characters are friends, which country has a particular currency, and which famous faces appear in a particular photo, among others. To carry out our study, we created a vast dataset of 13,000 test questions by selecting 2,000 options from six areas of interest and designing corresponding prompts in a range of formats, including yes/no questions, identification, and multiple-choice tasks. Our analysis reveals that certain prompt configurations tend to excel in specific task types, while also indicating some common difficulties, such as defining the scope of the choice task and using clear, concise language that adheres to the chosen prompt type. Interestingly, our data shows that certain task types are more frequently encountered than others, and we suggest some potential areas for further exploration, including identifying relationships between related concepts and categorizing artworks based on description. Moreover, our investigation prompts questions about the underlying nature of choice tasks, as well as the potential for marked data, and we envision our dataset to facilitate comparisons between various ranking models and data sources, such as SPARQL and Wikipedia. Our search dataset, along with the test data, can be found at https://github.com/0xstyle/choice-prompts. Unlike existing sound-generating models, which often disregard visual inputs, our approach leverages computer vision to create sounds associated with visual cues. However, identifying and addressing data issues during the data preparation phase is extremely challenging. After these problems persist in a dataset, they can cause ML models to malfunction, but pinpointing the source of the issue is difficult without more information. In this context, we introduce a new concept, Shapley significance, which allows us to quantify the impact of individual data preparation steps on ML model performance. Our novel framework utilizes Shapley significance to diagnose data problems throughout an ML pipeline, with effective results demonstrated on sample use cases. Currently, diagnostics are only feasible in close collaboration with the ML model's developer, as manual intervention is typically required to circulate model inputs. Moreover, a standardized interface for data shadow creation, allowing the application of diagnostic tools across diverse ML pipelines, is also being devised. We provide an accessible mathematical framework for the statistical approach, illustrating its power through key examples in algebraic geometry. This examples-based approach is beneficial because statistical methods can tackle complex problems that other methods struggle with. These breakthroughs have far-reaching implications, enabling us to re-examine fundamental questions in algebraic geometry using statistical tools. This will likely spark significant new research in the field. This lecture is based on joint work with Daniele Fanelli and Ralf Sch\"utze. Envelopes play a crucial role in this analysis, allowing us to study interacting systems as a single, combined ensemble. This approach is reminiscent of the generalized lambda lemma, which represents a generalized version of the classical lambda lemma used to compute enumerative quantities in algebraic geometry. This method is particularly useful when dealing with systems involving an abundance of variables, as it simplifies complex computations by focusing on the most relevant variables. Another powerful application of this approach is in non-interacting systems, where the statistical method enables us to derive topological relationships, including the topological partition function and various correlation functions. This study provides an in-depth examination of how high pressure influences the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn, an antiferromagnetic compound with a triangular structure. At normal pressure, Mn$_3$Sn exhibits a peculiar Hall effect due to noncollinear magnetism and lack of magnetization at the surface. Upon applying pressure, this study was conducted using synchrotron X-ray diffraction, magnetic characterization, and electrical transport analysis while in a helical state. Interestingly, as pressure increases, the material's crystal structure remains intact but its Hall effect and magnetic properties undergo significant changes. This pressure-sensitive behavior arises from the regulation of a specific strain, which causes the shifting of atoms within the unit cell. Consequently, this strain enhances interlayer magnetic coupling and results in the stabilization of a new phase at higher pressures, characterized by uniform magnetization. Moreover, analysis reveals that this phase is connected to a significant increase in anomalous Hall effect at higher pressures. This discovery offers a new technique for controlling anomalous Hall effect through regulated magnetization using external pressure. Additionally, this study's findings can guide the creation of materials with controllable anomalous Hall effect. It is proposed that similar pressure-sensitive strains could induce novel magnetic properties in other compounds, such as Fe$_3$Sn$_2$ and Fe$_3$GeTe, exhibiting identical trimerization behavior. Finally, this research suggests pressure could be utilized as an effective means of modifying a material's electronic properties without changing its chemical composition. As a result, this study's findings could pave the way for the controlled manipulation of a semimetal's anomalous Hall effect through regulated pressure and strain conditions. Conversely, applying strain could also potentially induce anomalous Hall effect at ambient pressure. Hence, this study presents an original means of governing a key electronic property, not through doping, but through an external mechanical force. This paper delves into the discrete and continuous Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problems within the contexts of Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions. By setting $\Omega$ as a bounded, regular subset of $\mathbb{R}^N$ (where $N \geq 1$), and denoting its boundary as $\Gamma := \partial \Omega$, we examine the general theory of the Steklov-Robin problem. Specifically, we choose a differential operator $L$ with certain symmetric properties and investigate the eigenvalues $\lambda_j (\Omega ; L, b, \alpha)$ under distinct boundary conditions. Assuming a homogeneous Steklov-Robin boundary condition, we establish the series expansion of the eigenvalues and prove convergence, as well as structural properties of the eigenfunctions. Furthermore, we focus on the first Steklov eigenvalue and show that it increases when a disk is removed from the domain. Finally, we investigate the behavior of the Steklov eigenvalues as the parameter $\alpha$ influences the Steklov-Robin problem. Notably, we obtain upper and lower bounds for the Steklov eigenvalues and prove their convergence and asymptotic behavior. Lastly, we discuss the connections between the Steklov eigenvalues and the Robin eigenvalues. We expect this research to contribute to the broadening of the theory of Steklov eigenvalues and provide a general approach to understanding the geometry and analysis of domain boundary conditions. The main findings of this paper were initially presented at the 9th ECCO Conference in Montreal in June 2019.

Improving the accuracy of brain disease detection through diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (dMRI) is a critical concern. To achieve this, researchers are developing new methods based on a simplified model that represents dMRI data through directional weighted graphs. However, real datasets often exceed the capabilities of graph-based models, requiring the use of more complex structures like hypergraphs to effectively analyze the data. Yet, the development of hypergraph-based methods is hindered by the limited availability of suitable algorithms and frameworks. A new technique, guided hypergraph reconstruction, has been developed to enhance the accuracy of disease detection by utilizing the effectiveness of hypergraphs. This approach involves constructing a pair of hypergraphs from diffeomorphism-aligned brain images and using their connection to identify and locate disorders. It has been successfully applied to dMRI tumor and multiple sclerosis lesion detection, demonstrating improved performance compared to graph-based methods. Furthermore, it has the potential to be integrated into established graph-based frameworks, as seen in its implementation using DTI-Probabilistic-AK, a widely used software for brain disease analysis. This integration has led to enhanced results and could potentially be applied to other existing frameworks. In addition, a comprehensive evaluation of the proposed method has been conducted using data from various sources, including publicly accessible datasets and an extensive collection of tumor lesions. This review has served to demonstrate the effectiveness of hypergraph-based approaches and guided hypergraph reconstruction in particular. It has also highlighted their potential to improve the accuracy of disease detection and awareness of their advantages in the field of dMRI and hypergraphs. This knowledge could potentially be utilized to develop more accurate brain disease detection algorithms. Several code segments and other required resources have been made available, including hypergraph reconstruction code, to facilitate the reproduction of this research. Important information on the used software, used data, and other relevant resources can be found in a previously published paper focused on reviewing hypergraph-based methods. This ensures that the necessary information is easily accessible and that others can draw upon this knowledge, as recently asked, by providing relevant details. Since 2017, there has been an increased interest in the use of hypergraphs to improve the accuracy of dMRI-based brain disease detection. This interest follows earlier concerns, also present since 2017, about the limited capabilities of graph-based models and the need for more complex structures, such as hypergraphs. This has led to a published review of hypergraph-based methods and guided hypergraph reconstruction, a new technique that utilizes the effectiveness of hypergraphs to detect tumors and lesions from dMRI and MRI images.

We created a large, comprehensive dataset of annotated chest X-rays to serve as a foundation for machine learning research in visual lung analysis. By employing 3D CT scans and accurate anatomical segmentation, we generated high-quality labels for the CXR-Aug dataset. Compared to existing datasets, our annotations exhibit greater detail and less noise, enabling deeper learning. With over 9,000 images, CXR-Aug outclasses current benchmarks in size and labels. Studies based on CXR-Aug indicate improved accuracy in detecting focal lesions and lung diseases, ultimately facilitating safer clinical decision-making. The dataset, including full annotation details, is accessible for free at https://github.com/iterative-cvxh20/cxr_aug. It is also integrated with the Dataverse platform at https://data.cxr.ai/. We encourage the research community to utilize CXR-Aug for training and evaluating deep learning models. Additionally, the source code for our project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/iterative-cvxh20/cxr_aug/tree/main/cxr_aug. We aim to expand our annotations to include more complex findings like pulmonary embolism and congestive heart failure. Nonetheless, we have successfully established a solid base for analyzing lung conditions using images. Moreover, we developed a standard evaluation protocol for comparing the understanding of machine learning models across different regions of the chest and across various diseases. By utilizing CXR-Aug, we observed that current models trained on widely used datasets often struggle to accurately recognize certain disease conditions based on anatomically relevant cues. This knowledge may contribute to the development of more effective algorithms. We propose that future models should prioritize both spatial and temporal (i.e., region and time) generalization in visual lung analysis to ensure seamless application across different regions of the chest and consistency in making clinical decisions. Ultimately, we hope that CXR-Aug will aid in bridging the gap between deep learning models and clinical expertise. Our research delves into the concept of stability within a cryptocurrency's value as a medium of exchange. We begin by identifying and categorizing the various costs associated with using a cryptocurrency as a means of exchange. These costs encompass transaction fees, risks related to price fluctuation, and the minimum amount required for a transaction to be feasible. We conclude that true stability in a cryptocurrency's value as a means of exchange can be achieved when its transaction costs remain steady and unchanging. Applying this concept to existing payment systems, we find that only stablecoins and cryptocurrencies with constant transaction fees can be considered cost-stable. Furthermore, we examine the stability of popular cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin, and find that they are not cost-stable due to increasing transaction fees. Nevertheless, we propose that a cryptocurrency with constant transaction fees could serve as a reliable means of exchange. To that end, we suggest a feasible reform for Bitcoin aimed at making it a more stable means of exchange, thereby potentially rekindling its status as a dominant payment system. Alternatively, a new payment system could be developed with low transaction fees, providing users with a viable alternative. We maintain that our theoretical findings on cost-stable payment systems can contribute to the development of more efficient cryptocurrency designs. Moreover, our analysis may be applied to existing payment systems to inform their improvement and provide a framework for evaluating the effectiveness of cryptocurrency redesigns in achieving stability. Lastly, our research raises an important question: what role can a regulator play in promoting stability in a cryptocurrency's value as a means of exchange? We suggest that a regulator could encourage the development of stable payment systems by promoting designs with low transaction fees, such as a minimum fee-based cryptocurrency. To that end, the EU's Payment Services Regulation provides a potential framework for implementing such an initiative. We advocate for further research into the theoretical aspects of cost-stable payment systems, as well as empirical analysis of the stability of existing payment systems, including cryptocurrencies and the US dollar. We hypothesize that a cryptocurrency with constant transaction fees could outperform other payment systems in terms of stability. We conclude that our research may be of interest to cryptocurrency developers, investors, and users, as well as regulatory bodies, with a focus on stable payment systems that can serve as a means of exchange. We maintain that our theoretical findings can contribute to the development of more stable payment systems, such as design-based or fee-based cryptocurrencies, that can effectively compete with established payment systems, including Bitcoin and the US dollar. We propose that our research may be of relevance to the development of efficient payment systems

Our analysis demonstrates that the amplitude of fluctuations in a specific type of Kardar-Parisi-Zhang equation that originates from a quasilinear averaging process follows a Gaussian distribution. This averaging process is a part of a broader mathematical framework known as perturbation, or weak, noise theory. By solving the associated linear differential equation, we show that this averaging process can be represented as the inverse scattering transform of the Zakharov-Shabat system. This method drives the development of a recursive formula for calculating the amplitude of fluctuations. Ultimately, the amplitude's behavior is characterized by a power law, specifically $t^{1/4}$. This finding challenges the widely held hypothesis that the amplitude may asymptotically approach a self-similar state. Additionally, the amplitude's behavior is dependent on specific initial conditions, leading to a term that decays over time. This observation is observed for both positive and negative initial conditions. Our analysis also reveals that integrating the amplitude's time-dependent component does not follow a standard Gaussian distribution. Instead, this integral is comprised of a standard Gaussian distribution and a polynomial function of the initial condition. This observation is a key characteristic of feeble noise theory. Furthermore, the amplitude's behavior may be categorized into distinct regimes based on specific time scales, leading to a term that decays over time and a term that grows over time. Our analysis also demonstrates that the amplitude's behavior may be asymptotically represented as a sum of exponential terms. In SASE FEL schemes, short pulse durations are commonly limited by the coherence time, typically measuring in hundreds of attoseconds for hard X-rays and femtoseconds for softer ranges. This paper introduces an innovative approach utilizing tapering to produce sub-femtosecond pulses in the XUV and soft X-ray domain. By manipulating the tapering curve, we achieve a higher electron density gradient than typical SASE conditions, yielding shorter pulse durations. However, this strategy also incurs a corresponding decrease in pulse coherence, enabling the generation of attosecond pulses. The proposed scheme can be implemented using either a fully tunable or a fixed tapering scheme, with the former offering greater flexibility. The parameters for the first such implementation at the VUV-FEL in Berlin were determined, including a predicted pulse duration of approximately 8 fs and containing a significant attosecond component. The proposed technique will be a crucial tool for producing extremely short pulses and is anticipated to be a pivotal development for the advancement of the European XFEL. Additionally, this research will be presented at the 2020 EUCARD3 Workshop. The parameters discussed for the VUV-FEL in Berlin were further examined and the results demonstrated an atosecond component exceeding 80% of the pulse duration. The feasibility of implementing this scheme was also evaluated for the Center for Free-Electron Laser (CFFEL) and the results showed that a pulse duration of around 160 attoseconds can be achieved. The specific details and performance expectations for CFFEL were calculated. The proposed technique can serve as a prototype for implementing enhanced pulse compression in various SASE FEL systems, including the European XFEL. The fundamental characteristics of the proposed scheme were also compared to a complementary approach using self-injection seeded SASE FEL schemes. The parameters for the first such implementation at the SASE FEL facility in RADIA were determined, including a pulse duration of around 160 attoseconds in the 5-20 eV energy range. The feasibility of producing sub-femtosecond pulses in the soft X-ray and hard X-ray regimes was also evaluated using a fully tunable tapering scheme, yielding promising results. To effectively combat unfair electoral divisions, a clear definition of the issue is needed along with straightforward, voter-approved solutions. The problem is well-defined when focusing on the concept of partisan advantage rather than fairness, which can be achieved through a mathematical representation as an optimization problem. A feasible solution to this optimized issue is proposed by modifying a known heating problem, which results in a clear, easily understandable indicator of biased division arrangements. The new measure is called the Gerrymander Index and is being utilized to create a straightforward, voter-approved method to address the problem. The new approach is presented in a simple, easy-to-understand format. 

Keywords: Computational social science, fair division, gerrymandering, combinatorial optimization, heating problem.
