Textile images present a unique set of challenges due to their high dimensional, highly correlated nature and tendency to exhibit sparse noise characteristics. The gradient of the Haar wavelet transform via the ordered Haar wavelet transform is an efficient tool for distinguishing textured regions, extracting edges and detecting noise. This method is particularly suitable for textile defect detection as it enables the isolation of flaws within textured regions, edge areas and noise. However, this approach still struggles with some noise issues. By combining the improved gradient of the Haar wavelet transform and low rank decomposition, a more effective technique has been developed for flaw detection and recognition. A flaw identification method based on this combined approach has been successfully applied and assessed. The results demonstrate its effectiveness for a range of flaws including different types of wear, and this method has been successfully used for automatic textile quality control. The experimental data is drawn from the NTU-DIT textile dataset. The code for this method is available online. To effectively navigate a complex environment, a visual navigation system must strike a balance between exploring its surroundings and utilizing that information to complete tasks. Current methods using reinforcement learning often result in excessive exploration, leading to slow task completion. To overcome this limitation, we've developed a new multi-task learning framework that simultaneously trains a navigation agent to both gather information and use that information to complete visual navigation tasks. Our method achieves this goal by leveraging information-theoretic constraints to regulate the navigation system's level of exploration. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly improves task completion times while maintaining optimal information gathering. Additionally, our method's inherent state monitoring capabilities allow it to assess its own level of exploration, eliminating the need for external estimation. To implement this framework, we've created a novel task module that facilitates learning useful visual features for navigation. Our task module ensures that the features it produces are maximally informative for navigation, leading to better performance when compared to other feature extraction methods. For instance, when tested in the DeepMind Capture the Flag challenge, our agent successfully completed all levels within the time limit, earning a perfect score of 10/10, underscoring the effectiveness of our proposed framework. Our open-source code is available at https://github.com/yongyang1993/URVL.git. Additionally, the trained agents can be found at https://github.com/yongyang1993/URVL.git#tree/master/model_zoo. Our work offers insights into using Urn Models for regulating exploration in reinforcement learning. To improve navigation efficiency, we've integrated our information-theoretic regulation method with evolutionary strategies, a gradient-free optimization technique. By applying this revised equation across various situations, we found that for black holes in systems that lose energy rapidly, such as black holes in dense stellar environments or those undergoing radiative feedback, their mass may behave erratically and deviate significantly from an exponential pattern. Furthermore, we found that for black holes in these intense energy-loss settings, the real part of the equation's solution can be represented as a power law, rather than an exponential, and that this solution may vary depending on the specific parameters in question. The implementation of attosecond science necessitates the accurate measurement and
coherent manipulation of high-energy electron movements over incredibly short
timeframes. Research has shown that the charge density in the vicinity of a
photoelectron source can be stabilized using an irrationally phased ultrashort
laser pulse. We investigate whether this concept's effectiveness can be extended
to a coherent control scheme for generating isolated attosecond pulses. Through
the application of a spatial light modulator, different spherical aberrations are
introduced to an otherwise coherent irradiated pulse, mimicking a conventional
high numerical aperture lens. We collect and analyze attosecond pulses in the
presence of defocusing and focusing aberrations, revealing a surprising ability
to extract isolated attosecond pulses even with a high degree of distortion.
However, the underlying physical mechanism is found to be related to spatial
phase modulation rather than merely compensating spherical aberrations. This
reveals a new approach to producing isolated attosecond pulses, as well as
controlling the spatial and temporal characteristics of XUV pulses, utilizing
conventional experimental setups. Nonetheless, our research also indicates that
relying on coherent manipulation to consistently produce high-quality isolated
attosecond pulses may not be feasible, given the significant requirement and
constraints on the needed intensity of the irradiated pulse, which may not be
achievable without compromising other important aspects of the pulse. Ultimately, we
demonstrate that this development presents an intriguing opportunity for the
reliable production of single attosecond pulses in a field-modulated scenario.

This new information on Algol's potential companions will help future researchers to refine our understanding of the system. This paper primarily focuses on a specific type of PDE, specifically the nonlinear Schrödinger equation, to analyze how it behaves over time in spaces outside of compact objects. Given an initial condition with sufficient properties, we demonstrate the existence of various non-trivial, explosive solutions. Notably, when the object is convex and the nonlinearity meets a specific equation, we find explosive solutions of much greater magnitude than those in free space. Our solutions have the added benefit of being globally defined, extending from $-\infty$ to any positive time. This work significantly builds on earlier research, such as that of Holmer and Roudenko and of Roudenko and Zhang, who also worked with similar equations in spaces outside of compact objects. We successfully extend their research to account for objects that are not necessarily compact in a way that is consistent with their approach. Furthermore, this work also addresses a related equation, specifically the Gross-Pitaevskii equation, to analyze explosion solutions outside of compact objects. To analyze these solutions, we develop a new method of calculating the action functional of a specific type of manifold and prove several key properties about its behavior. Specifically, we establish that it is subcoercive and uniformly convex. This enables us to apply Taylor's theorem with Nijenhuis and Fornasini to analyze its properties near critical points. We leverage these properties, along with other tools, to establish the necessary properties about the solutions themselves. Additionally, we utilize a previously established connection between the solutions of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation and the solutions of the Gross-Pitaevskii equation to derive new insights about the behavior of the latter. To analyze these solutions, we ask whether there exist globally defined, explosive solutions with a specific type of decay. By modifying the condition on the nonlinearity so that it meets a specific equation, we find explosive solutions of much greater magnitude than those in free space. This extends earlier research by Lin and Zhang, who also worked with similar equations in spaces outside of compact objects. Nevertheless, we find that by modifying the condition on the nonlinearity so that it meets a specific type of perturbation, we can develop new insights about the explosion solutions outside of compact objects. Physics-informed neural networks offer an innovative solution for partial differential equations that combines adaptability and efficient use of data. The effectiveness of physics-informed neural networks depends heavily on a versatile function approximation technique known as adaptive grid refinement. By dividing the input space into discrete points and allowing the network to choose its outputs freely, adaptive grid refinement can be implemented. However, this approach has several drawbacks: it struggles to capture complex solutions, requires extensive points for accurate results, and lacks order of convergence. In response to these limitations, we introduce a new technique that modifies the output space instead of the input space. Our method, residual-based adaptive vertex creation, uses a network to predict residual errors at existing points and selects new points where these errors are highest. When evaluated on benchmark tests and a real-world example, this approach outperformed traditional physics-informed neural networks in accuracy and convergence. Additionally, it eliminated issues associated with previous adaptive methods. Code for this method is available at https://github.com/fatemehkarim/RANG. Femina. Femina is a Python package that provides an easy-to-use interface for implementing the RANG method in 1D, 2D, and 3D scenarios. It also includes a range of useful features and interfaces that make it easy to integrate RANG into existing physics-informed neural network frameworks. With its high performance and ease of use, RANG has the potential to become a widely adopted method in the physics-informed neural networks community. Evaluation of the approach on high-precision arithmetic revealed that it is capable of delivering even more accurate results, making it a highly competitive technique. In particular, it was found that increasing the precision of the arithmetic used to train the network can improve the overall performance and accuracy of the approach. Furthermore, it was observed that enhancing the robustness of the network through weight clipping can help to generalize the results and improve the overall efficiency of the approach. In particular, it was discovered that incorporating this modification allowed the network to achieve its full potential for sample efficiency and performance, making it an important consideration for training physics-informed neural networks. In conclusion, we introduced a new adaptive method for approximating solutions to partial differential equations that outperformed previous approaches and achieved its full potential for sample efficiency and performance. This method, which relies on predicting residual errors and selecting new points where these errors are highest, has been shown to be more accurate and efficient than traditional physics-informed neural networks and can deliver even more precise results when using high-precision arithmetic and robust training techniques. This study examines how the formation of ferroelectric domains in Field Effect Transistors affects their performance and energy consumption. Through computational modeling and analysis of experimental data, it's discovered that domain walls within the ferroelectric material significantly contribute to an undesirable capacitance that hinders the transition of electrical signals. The existence of these domain walls is inevitable in finite crystalline materials, and their impact must be considered during the design of ferroelectric technologies. To improve the reliability and efficiency of ferroelectric devices, it's crucial to develop methods that minimize domain-related issues and ensure stable, uniform performance. Simulation methods such as mult-domain finite-element simulation and atomistic strain-based models can aid in designing ideal ferroelectric materials with reduced defects. Conversely, these models can also identify whether observed issues are caused by the device's design or inherent defects in the material. By distinguishing between these factors, avenues for improving device performance and mitigating problematic defects can be identified. Various methods to control domain formation and minimize disruptions are discussed, and it's proposed that different interface types - including metal, oxide, and semiconductor interfaces - require distinct design strategies to achieve optimal results. By factoring in the unique characteristics of these interfaces, barriers can be designed to facilitate stable domain transitions and reduce the influence of domain walls on the device's performance. Ultimately, this research aims to provide a theoretical framework for developing ideal ferroelectric devices with high performance and efficiency. Potential research topics and challenges related to ferroelectric technology development are also discussed. Key considerations for designing ferroelectric Schottky barriers are explored, and it's examined how transition metal barriers can be designed to achieve high switching speeds. Various applications of ferroelectric technology are discussed, and it's proposed that ferroelectric Schottky barriers can enable the development of advanced, high-performance microelectronic and nanoelectronic devices. To facilitate this, research is needed to overcome existing challenges and design robust ferroelectric systems. By drawing insights from advanced theoretical models and incorporating experimental data, the feasibility and limitations of ferroelectric technology can be evaluated, and the road to developing high-performance ferroelectric devices can be mapped out. To achieve this, research must address fundamental problems such as domain control and energy loss, and design solutions such as domain engineering and transition metal optimizations must be explored. By combining these designs, the development of high-performance ferroelectric Schottky barriers with excellent switching performance and robust resistance properties may be enabled. The accuracy of predictions for the mass and size of terrestrial exoplanets relies heavily on the properties of their parent star, with considerations of stellar metallicity and age being most relevant. However, the relationship between these characteristics and planetary mass and size is complicated by factors such as the star's chemical composition, angular momentum transfer during formation, and the type of planets that are retained versus those that are lost or escaped. Determining the interior composition of these planets requires a detailed analysis of the star's elemental abundance pattern, which in turn affects the planetary mass and size predictions. We investigated these relationships using theoretical models and data from the Kepler-10 and Kepler-37 star-planet systems, focusing on the planetary interior compositions and using extensive stellar spectroscopy to constrain the models. The results show that the planetary size is more sensitive to changes in metallicity than in age, and that a decrease in metallicity leads to smaller planets, with the extent of the change increasing with planet size. Additionally, the critical age threshold for these changes to occur is around 4.6 billion years. The correlation between metallicity and planetary size is consistent for both giant and terrestrial planets, and this phenomenon is not unique to the Kepler-10 system, as similar patterns have been observed in other exoplanet datasets. Therefore, the relationship between metallicity and planetary size is a significant phenomenon that needs to be taken into account in planetary demography, and it is also a potential indicator of planetary internal composition and life-supporting habitability. Further studies are needed to verify that this trend is present in the Kepler dataset as a whole and to determine its effects on planetary internal composition and habitability. The proposed method of using stellar spectroscopy to constrain planetary demography can be an invaluable tool in achieving this goal. Finally, the accuracy of stellar metallicity as a demographic predictor for terrestrial planets can be supplemented by other factors, such as the escape velocity of the planets, and it is necessary to determine the stellar metallicity and age to understand planetary internal composition and habitability. Moreover, the necessary conditions for planets like Kepler-10e and Kepler-37e to form and survive around older stars need to be further investigated. The critical age threshold for these planets is around 4.6 billion years, and it is related to the radius at which these planets transition from rocky to rocky super-Earth structure. Therefore, the stellar demographic analysis of terrestrial planets and their internal compositions is an essential tool for understanding the planetary internal structure and the possible conditions for life to exist in these planets. In cubic bipartite graphs, a robust edge-tinting involves coloring the edges with two different colors such that every face is monochromatic. A special case is when the graph is a complete bipartite graph, allowing for a robust coloring with a specific constraint applied. However, we've found an example that contradicts the hypothesis: there is no universal lower bound for the robust coloring in all cubic bipartite graphs - the lower bound can be set to zero. Additionally, this applies to cubic planar bipartite graphs. Furthermore, this also sets a limit on the robust coloring in all cubic bipartite graphs: the upper limit is two. Finally, we've found an example that specifically contradicts the hypothesis for the complete bipartite graph case, revealing an alternative coloring scheme that satisfies the robust coloring condition with a limit of two. This resolves an open problem first posed by Mohar and Shalom.

The mechanical properties also varied greatly, with the optimal temperature for Martian samples ranging from 20-60 degrees Celsius and 20-40 degrees Celsius for Lunar samples. These findings indicate that ambient temperatures significantly affect the final properties of materials produced through a specific technique and must be considered when choosing processing temperatures. We further describe the action of the braid group and develop a conjectured basis for the type II quantum subgroups in the categories $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$. This is achieved by identifying a specific pattern in the braiding of the regional modules $(\Delta V^{(i)})_{\mathrm{reg}}$. This pattern allows us to propose a general structure for the type II quantum subgroups in the categories $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1},k)$. This proposal is further validated by considering its application to specific values of $r$, where we demonstrate that it yields the known type II quantum subgroups in the categories $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sl}_{3},k)$. Moreover, we show that our results can be extended to the categories $\mathcal{C}(\mathfrak{sp}_{2n},k)$. This is accomplished by realizing that the $\mathfrak{sp}_{2n}$-modules can be expressed in terms of the $\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1}$-modules, where $r$ is an integer greater than or equal to $n$. A median-driven analysis led to the development of two non-statistical methods: the median-based sequencing method and the median-driven resequencing method. When employed in conjunction with a neural speech synthesis model, the median-driven resequencing method demonstrated the ability to generate synthetic speech of varied lengths. A subsequent human evaluation revealed that the synthetic speech produced by this new approach was indistinguishable from naturally spoken sentences in terms of its overall quality. Additionally, the study found that the median-driven resequencing method was successful in creating synthetic speech of longer lengths, achieving a maximum extension of 300% above the original sample. However, despite considerable effort, no interactive system has been developed that utilizes deep learning for melanoma classification based on dermatopathology images. The main obstacles have been the small size of training datasets and the diverse range of clinical settings in which skin biopsies are sectioned. To overcome these challenges, our team employed data augmentation and interactively classified histopathological images from diverse angles. To enhance the accuracy of cosmological distance measurements, we've developed a deep learning model that automatically extracts meaningful features from type Ia supernovae spectra. The proposed stochastic autoencoder, comprising two interconnected layers, can pinpoint and eliminate unessential data and capture subtle variations in spectra. By utilizing a tailored sampling method, we've effectively mitigated the impact of noise and obtained an internal regularization technique. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that the proposed model surpasses its deterministic counterpart and yields superior noise reduction capabilities. Moreover, we've found that the learned latent space is ideal for distance modulation, yielding improved results compared to existing methods. Our findings indicate that deep learning can be utilized to develop sophisticated, specialized applications for the analysis of SN Ia spectral data. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ArashDarmanin/SAAE. Additionally, the reconstructed spectra and latent space can be accessed via https://arashdarmanin.github.io/reconstructed_spectra_and_latent_space.html. Our team also welcomes collaborations at arash.darmanin@gmail.com. All model-trained supernovae data can be obtained via https://arashdarmanin.githubio/sae-trained-sn1a-data.html. This work was supported by Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC) under grant number R30591007. The formation of galaxies during early universe periods is primarily driven by the rapid conversion of molecular gas into stellar material. However, a significant issue arises from the observed prevalence of neutral gas resonances in galaxies both today and in the early universe, which suggests that a substantial portion of this gas is not directly interacting with stars. Through high-resolution observations of a dusty, star-forming galaxy at a z=2.09, we identify multiple signals of neutral gas egressing from the galaxy. Notably, the gas in this galaxy is found to be transitioning from a neutral to an ionized state as it moves further away from the galaxy's central core. Our research suggests the presence of a theory-limited outflow rate of approximately 8.5 M$_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$, which may be accountable for the rapid removal of gas from the galaxy, thereby regulating both star-formation and gas accumulation. This outflow rate is primarily driven by the movement of gas through winds rather than the more extensive, but slower, gas dynamics governing the galaxy's overall disk. Our findings present a resolved glimpse into the ionization and outflow dynamics of a specific galaxy at a z=2.09, while also hinting at significant challenges for the growth of galaxies during early universe periods.

We investigate the process of incorporation of solid particles into thermal plumes rising from below a heated surface in a fluid. The study focuses on the interplay between the fluid's buoyant updraft and the self-similar turbulent flow that surrounds it as it rises. The incorporation process is examined using high-resolution numerical simulations, incorporating both particle size and surface properties into the analysis. The results indicate that the particle's size has a significant impact on its chances of being captured by the plume. For larger particles, the probability of incorporation decreases, and this decline is more pronounced when the plume's velocity is higher. Additionally, the study finds that particles with rough surfaces are less likely to be captured than those with smooth surfaces of the same size. The research also identifies distinct incorporation mechanisms based on the particle's location relative to the plume and offers insights into the role of turbulence in this process. The findings can inform models of incorporation that aim to quantify the rates at which solid particles accumulate in volcanic and oceanic mudflows. The research also sheds light on similar processes occurring in other types of geophysical and environmental flows. Understanding the spread of epidemics within networks, such as contact graphs, reveals patterns of disease transmission. However, assuming only pair-based interactions oversimplifies the complex human interactions seen in everyday life, neglecting the role of group meetings in disease spread. To address this shortfall, we introduce a more comprehensive model, exploring disease transmission on hypergraphs, a type of network that accounts for interactions among groups of individuals. Focusing on the transmission of diseases that spread quickly at the outset but slowly thereafter, we investigate the boundaries of extinction and highlight the importance of considering multi-person interactions in understanding epidemic transmission. Utilizing extremal hypergraph theories, we establish precise limits of extinction, revealing that even without assuming full connectivity, the boundaries of extinction are similarly determined as in contact graphs, largely due to the inherent transmission characteristics of the disease. This study provides a foundation for further research into more general types of diseases, and we apply our results to the analysis of two particular diseases, yielding predictions that align with real-world epidemiological data. Moreover, we develop a new method for determining disease extinction thresholds, and our analysis sheds light on the critical role of disease virulence in understanding epidemic transmission. To facilitate applications, we introduce an extensible software package for calculating extinction thresholds on hypergraphs, and our approach offers a new framework for tackling problems in mathematical epidemiology. As a result, the correlation between rotational velocity and latitude becomes more pronounced, mirroring a reverse process compared to the T Tauri phase. Studies of solar-type stars have revealed that these complex rotational patterns hold crucial implications for 3D dynamos, especially regarding the uncertainty surrounding early stages of rotation.

To explore how early, anti-solar differential rotation influences magnetic activity in low-to-medium rotating solar-type stars, researchers used the mean-field approximation to the MFDynAst code. It represents a numerical version of the stellar evolution code ASTEC, originally developed by J.D. Hubbard and J.P. Zahn. Within this framework, the Ohmic diffusion regime was always dominant, whereas the hybrid regime showed slight deviations. Consequently, the results primarily considered the Ohmic diffusion regime.

Key observations from these simulations include:

  - A sharp increase in magnetic activity and the strength of the toroidal magnetic field in the convection zone when considering anti-solar differential rotation.
  - A significant reduction in the timescale of magnetic cycles.
  - A decline in the maximum torque applied to the star.
  - A slight drop in the average luminosity.

Notably, incorporating anti-solar differential rotation has both positive and negative effects, leading to enhanced magnetic activity but also causing a decline in the potential for starspot modulation. Developing an effective deep learning framework for K-fan recognition across multiple modalities remains challenging. Research has focused on designing datasets for K-fan, but a universal, effective model has yet to be established. Existing multimodal deep learning models deal with individual modalities separately, ignoring potential interactions and using shared representations may be impractical given the diversity of modalities. This paper introduces a new deep learning model that can recognize K-fan shapes using multiple modalities and provides a universal, effective solution. This model employs a novel network architecture that allows different modalities to interact and incorporates a shared representation, demonstrating improved performance on K-fan recognition. Experimental results confirm the proposed model's effectiveness across various modalities. Notably, the proposed model achieves 5-10% better accuracy compared to state-of-the-art models, with source code available at https://github.com/pkumar52/Universal-K-fan-Recognition. Systematic evaluations using 15 datasets based on different geometric parameters further validate the model's reliability and show its potential to recognize K-fan shapes in other modalities. With a reliability score of 92%, this model outperforms other deep learning models. Impressive performance was also seen on challenging datasets, with the proposed model achieving 90% accuracy on complex datasets. This robust model is envisioned to enable accurate K-fan recognition in real-world applications. Developing reliable high-performance multicore software is increasingly difficult due to the intricacies of thread interactions and potential deadlocks. In this research, we present McMini, a innovative and versatile model checking tool designed to validate safety properties in multithreaded programs. Leveraging DPOR, the largest state space reducer among thread-based model checking techniques, McMini is capable of detecting a wide range of errors, including data races, deadlocks, and synchronization issues. Furthermore, McMini offers a range of features that enhance model checking efficiency, such as a highly configurable thread schedule and multiple optimization techniques. To achieve maximum flexibility, McMini presents a modular design. The paper showcases McMini's effectiveness through performance evaluations using open-source libraries and the MiniML language. Notably, McMini successfully identifies all data races in the OpenTTD train simulator, highlighting its practical usefulness. Comprehensive experimental results demonstrate that McMini's flexibility, variations in thread schedule, and optimization techniques significantly improve its performance. Crucially, McMini's research contributions are twofold: the detection of data races in MiniML and the validation of safety properties in multithreaded programs. McMini's codebase is freely accessible for research purposes. The rapid dissemination of information through social media can facilitate the spread of misinformation. In response, WhatsApp introduced limitations on message forwarding to slow down the dissemination of certain texts. Our study aims to assess the effectiveness of these limitations in reducing the spread of misinformation. We developed a simple theoretical model that simulates how misinformation spreads among users who interact sequentially, assuming that the quality of the information being shared depends on the sender's level of knowledge. Our results from testing this model under WhatsApp's forwarding limitations reveal two critical findings. Firstly, restricting forwarding to fewer users can actually increase the total number of interactions involved in spreading the information, thus potentially amplifying the spread of misinformation among a broader group of people. Secondly, such limitations tend to have a limited impact on the ultimate number of users who become aware of the misinformation, but can potentially delay the time it takes for those users to receive the information. Based on these findings, we conclude that WhatsApp's limitations may not be an effective solution to combating misinformation and propose alternative strategies that could be more successful. These alternatives include educating users, promoting media literacy, and adopting AI-driven systems for detecting misinformation, as well as incorporating neural networks as a simulated model of misinformation spread. Additionally, we suggest that WhatsApp could explore the potential of utilizing neural networks to model misinformation spread to develop more targeted and effective strategies to combat it. Furthermore, we demonstrate how an AI-driven neural network can be an effective method for detecting misinformation without relying on user-forwarding limitations. Our study shows that a neural network can learn to distinguish high-quality and low-quality information without the need for user interactions, thus enabling targeted removal of misinformation from conversations without affecting other messages. Our theoretical model and results provide a roadmap for detecting misinformation at scale, ultimately enabling more effective countermeasures to combat its spread. Keywords: WhatsApp, misinformation, forwarding limitation, neural network, misinfo classification, social media, information spread. We analyze a general branching population where individual lifetimes are independent and identically distributed, and individuals give birth to new ones at random times, also sharing the same distribution. This population is considered to be critically growing on average. Utilizing a branching random walk framework, we investigate the long-term, high-frequency characteristics of the population's allele frequency spectrum. Through an approximation method, we demonstrate that the observed frequency distribution of alleles in the population converges to a power law as the population size (or the number of generations) increases. This frequency distribution is represented by the formula $f(x)=Ax^{-1-\alpha}1_{(1/\theta <x <\infty)} + B\delta_{x-1/\theta}$. Notably, the dominant term follows a power law, implying that the distribution of allele frequencies declines at a rate of $x^{-1-\alpha}$, and the exponent $\alpha$ is directly linked to the offspring distribution's characteristics. This study provides the first theoretical estimation of the allele frequency spectrum's decline rate and explains the spectral shift at the lowest frequency end, thereby resolving prior seeming disparities between different models. Additionally, the spectral shift at the lowest frequency end is attributed to gene copies that are still retained in the population over extended periods, and these retained gene copies give rise to new individuals who will inherit these gene copies, thereby producing the observed spectral shift. Lastly, the nature of the spectral shift at the lowest frequency end is distinct from that resulting from the combination of multiple alleles, and varying the rate at which individuals produce new offspring can alter the decline rate of the observed frequency distribution. Furthermore, for an offspring distribution with distinct phases, we demonstrate that the frequency distribution of alleles in the population is characterized by two distinct power law declines with different exponents, and the nature of these exponents depends solely on the characteristics of the offspring distribution, and not on type of population growth. Moreover, the frequency distribution of alleles in the population is not solely characterized by a power law, but also by a Dirac mass that represents the persistence of certain gene copies in the population over extended periods. This persistence gives rise to the observed frequency distribution of alleles in the population. Lastly, for an offspring distribution with distinct phases, the frequency distribution of alleles in the population is represented by two distinct power law declines, and a Dirac mass that represents the observed frequency distribution of alleles in the population. Activating the learning process with the correct activation function is a low-level task that is typically taken care of. However, in the context of deep neural networks, this simple step holds significant importance. In the context of speaker verification and anti-spoofing systems, we discover that utilizing ReLU as the activation function hinders the learning process. We introduce an alternative activation function, dubbed the Vigilant ReLU (VR), which acts as a more precise version of its traditional counterpart. Through our research, we establish that substituting VR into existing systems enhances their performance and training efficiency compared to using ReLU. We also demonstrate that systems trained without VR on our proposed Vigilant ReLU variant exhibit improved end-to-end spoofing countermeasure performance. Notably, our method is versatile and can be applied to various tasks beyond speaker verification and anti-spoofing. We provide open-source code for others to utilize. Experimental results show that substituting VR leads to a mean average precision increase of 5.46% on the VoiceBank dataset and 4.53% on the Triplet-VR dataset at a fixed false acceptance rate of 0.1. Additionally, substituting VR reduced the 50% error rate by 1.03% on the VoiceBank dataset. These findings are summarized in Table 1. We also explored substituting VR in least-sufficient-component-energies ReLU and rectified linear units but found the results to be inconsistent. Consequently, we recommend the cautious adoption of VR in speaker verification and anti-spoofing systems, along with thorough testing of its effects. We also provide an open-source Python implementation of our research at https://github.com/ezzoz/Vigilant-ReLU. Furthermore, it is shown that the collection of all Borel subsets with a singular cardinality is countable. A related finding shows that the collection of all Borel subsets with an infinite cardinality is countably many. These outcomes remain effective in contexts where the underlying sets are restricted to either upper sets or intervals. The methods employed build on ideas from the presssing concerns of cardinal tree embeddings and a combinatorial partition theorem, leading to additional applications and implications. Finally, a question is posed about the cardinality of covers formed by sets with specific cardinalities. Specifically, under the assumption of choice, it is proposed that the collection of all Borel subsets with a singular cardinality is not countably infinite. Conversely, a demonstration shows that this assumption is not implied solely by the continuum hypothesis. Nevertheless, it is observed that the hypothesis would imply the existence of distinct, infinite sets with singular cardinalities. Lastly, a notable property is noted, where the cardinality of some Borel subsets with a singular cardinality contains uncountable sets. 

Keywords: Borel sets, real numbers, cardinality, counting theorem, tree embeddings, infinitary combinatorics.

Researchers have been using a statistical method called Protocol Identification through Anomaly Detection (PIAD) to accurately detect network security breaches in dynamic network environments. Recent advancements in PIAD have led to the development of a scalable and robust technique that can effectively detect security threats, measuring breach frequencies in units of megabytes. To further enhance PIAD, researchers have explored the potential of incorporating flow-size information into the protocol classification process. A recent PIAD technique incorporating flow-size information, denoted as PIAD-LS, has demonstrated significant improvements in breach detection rates and accuracy. PIAD-LS achieves these improvements by estimating packet sizes based on time-to-live values, thus requiring only two unique ports for breach frequency monitoring. A comprehensive vulnerability study was conducted to assess the robustness of PIAD-LS and PIAD protocols across various network communication patterns. Our investigation involved eight distinct attack scenarios using five modern operating systems and 14 various network communication patterns, examining how PIAD-LS and PIAD protocols classify traffic for 16 different system processes and 7 distinct network protocols. Our test revealed that both PIAD-LS and PIAD protocols exhibit minimal to no breach frequency deviations for legitimate system processes and regularly update their traffic patterns. In contrast, assault strategies targeting dynamic network environments cause significant inaccuracies in breach frequency monitoring, leading to inaccurate or misleading breach breach-frequency estimates. Our findings emphasize the need for Breach-Assessment Monitors to scrutinize traffic data when classifying breaches to prevent false security alerts. A breach frequency monitor must also be deployed to accurately monitor every system process and measure breach frequencies systematically. Our research further suggests that PIAD-LS is more susceptible to assault strategies than PIAD, as flow-size information can be manipulated to induce false security breaches. Ultimately, our investigation stresses the importance of validating network monitoring systems against comprehensive assault strategies to prevent assault tactics that could compromise dynamic network breach-frequency monitoring. For instance, an assault strategy targeting traffic amendments caused significant breach-frequency monitoring inaccuracies for PIAD-LS, as changes to flow sizes and system processes led to incorrect or misleading breach frequencies. Our investigation highlights the potential effectiveness of various assault strategies that could deceive dynamic network monitoring systems. Consequently, we recommend that researchers incorporate PIAD-LS and PIAD into the design of robust network security systems, including breach-frequency monitors that account for flow sizes and dynamic system processes to prevent false security breaches. This study analyzes how COVID news coverage varied across U.S. regions from March to December 2020 and explores the correlations between news coverage, COVID cases and deaths, and population demographics. Using data from the Media Cloud platform on articles about COVID published by major newspapers in 12 U.S. regions, researchers discovered significant differences in COVID news coverage, with the Northeast receiving the most coverage and the South the least. Notably, there was a substantial disparity in COVID-related coverage between liberal and conservative news sources. The team also discovered that news coverage of COVID was closely linked to regional COVID death rates but showed weaker correlations with cases and deaths. Interestingly, places with higher COVID news coverage experienced lower death rates, suggesting a potential 'watched pot' effect where increased monitoring leads to earlier mitigation efforts. Further, population demographics were found to influence COVID news coverage, with populations that received more coverage being largely white, urban, and affluent. Based on these findings, researchers conclude that regional characteristics determined the intensity and tone of COVID news coverage, which in turn had an impact on COVID death rates. These results may have implications for understanding the dissemination of health information and the mitigation of epidemics. To comprehend how humans learn to count, we designed a cognitive model that leverages a type of recurrent neural network called the Echo State Network. This model initiates a sequential task where a virtual agent learns to produce specific output patterns based on increasing numerical inputs. Our findings indicate that ESNs can master counting up to ten, but struggle with higher numbers. However, when we enhanced our model with a sophisticated training technique called Replays, it successfully learned to count as high as twenty. Additionally, our research demonstrates that the Replays method enables complex internal patterns to develop within the ESN, significantly boosting its counting capabilities. Interestingly, our model's ability to count is most effective when it is trained using a mix of increasing and decreasing numerical inputs. Ultimately, our cognitive model provides a valuable tool for simulating the cognitive processes involved in learning to count. Furthermore, its behavior is reminiscent of the renowned Feigenson system, which proposes the existence of a complex internal numerical representation, and our results suggest that such a system could be achieved through the use of sophisticated machine learning algorithms. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/pmnurtdinova/counting-cognitive-model. Additionally, the web page with the model's interactive demos is available at https://pmnurtdinova.github.io/cognitive-models-of-counting.

Bloom filters provide efficient memory-based approximations for predicting
membership in sets. Despite their effectiveness, they generate false positives at
a rate that may be unacceptable in certain applications. An alternative, Bloom
and Cuckoo filters, the CBF family, has been introduced with an improved false
positive rate. However, optimizing for space usage often results in prolonged
filtering times or vice versa. A new proposal, the Xor Filter Minimized
Bloom Filter (XFB), addresses these concerns by offering a compact and quick
alternative to CBF. Compared to CBF, XFB exhibits faster setup times and
similar or improved performance in terms of bandwidth usage, false positive
rates, and scalability. Moreover, integrating two XFB filters outperforms CBF in
terms of all these metrics while achieving comparable space usage. Furthermore,
an integrated solution, the Integrated Xor Filter Minimized Bloom Filter (IXFB),
is proposed, which combines the efficiency of two XFB filters into a single
component with even better performance. This work presents a thorough
investigation of the recently introduced XFB and its variations, comparing their
performance to existing solutions through experimentation. Additionally, an
open-source software framework, named IXFB, is made available for public use. 
It is based on the CBF library and supports both XFB and IXFB filters, as well as
integration of these structures into Bloom and Cuckoo filters.

This note explores the connection between two distinct conceptual frameworks: convex topology, developed by M.M. Pepe and M. Matviychuk, and complex geometry, rooted in R. Bott's work. We re-examine the topological definition of a complex from Matviychuk and Pepe's studies on convex structures, establishing a correspondence with Gromov's non-positive curvature theory. Furthermore, we establish a correspondence between convex circles and pluripolar sets in complex structures. Our analysis builds upon Bott's theorem, relating a complex with non-compact K\"ahler singularity to a bundle of Riemann surfaces. We hypothesize that a complex with this type of singularity is equivalent to a convex topological complex with a particular type of singularity, an idea inspired by Chern-Moser theory. If true, this relationship may enable the application of Chern-Moser's theorem to establish a bundle isomorphism between two complexes of this type. If a certain set in a complex with this type of singularity is empty, this would imply that a certain type of convex topological complex with a particular type of singularity is also non-existent. We also investigate the covering spaces of these complexes, establishing a correspondence between their properties and the properties of the original complex. We propose an extension of Gromov's theory to the realm of convex topology, as well as an analogue of Hilbert's Satz 2 for convex circles. Finally, we explore the connection between convex topology and the theory of complex singularities, establishing a correspondence between two frameworks and proposing an extension of the theory of complex singularities to the realm of convex topology. Our technique enabled an autonomous vehicle to navigate a complex 3D world resembling a real-world setting, after only being trained in a simulated environment using Unity. Significant advancements in deep learning technology have enabled the creation of highly convincing deepfakes that can fool the majority of people. Consequently, there is a growing need for effective deepfake detection tools. Although significant progress has been made, detecting deepfakes from real-world video still poses significant challenges. Specifically, detecting deepfakes in videos that contain facial makeup presents a difficult problem. To address this issue, we have developed a novel unconstrained deepfake detection technique, effectively handling videos with facial makeup and addressing the lack of comprehensive facial makeup datasets. Additionally, we created the MakeUp Face Uncovering dataset, comprising 3000 unconstrained videos with makeup. Utilizing this dataset, we introduced two innovative methods for detecting deepfakes with makeup, and our results demonstrate superior performance compared to the current best approaches. The implemented deepfake detection models are available on GitHub, and the MakeUp Face Uncovering dataset can be accessed via our website at universitelemaine.com. Keywords: deepfake detection, unconstrained videos, facial makeup, make up face uncovering dataset.

The presence of a liquid envelope layer around a gas giant planet has no hidden oceans, as its properties can be predicted through thermodynamic equilibrium with the atmosphere above it. In contrast, the low-pressure behavior of water on smaller, rocky planets with thin atmospheres may involve multiple phases of water, influenced by the temperature and chemical composition. This can result in the formation of a subsurface liquid water layer, which may be overlaid by an atmosphere that does not reflect the composition of the liquid below a certain pressure. Typically, the water vapor in the atmosphere does not contain enough dissolved water for the liquid phase to be represented by an ideal solution. However, if the pressure is relatively low, the water vapor in the atmosphere is in equilibrium with a shallow subsurface liquid water layer rather than the atmosphere's composition. This can lead to significant differences in the expected thermal pressure or composition of the atmosphere above such a hidden ocean layer compared to a layer influenced by ideal solution behavior. As a result, the low-pressure behavior of water, governed by solubility balances rather than thermodynamic equilibrium, may be preferred for detecting hidden oceans around small, rocky exoplanets through atmospheric analysis or transit experiments. We develop a spiking neural network for sequence learning tasks, drawing inspiration from brain mechanisms. The model utilizes synaptic plasticity based on a competitive learning principle, enabling it to detect underlying patterns in sequence data. Experiment results demonstrate that our competitive learning Spiking Neural Network (CL-SNN) is capable of accurately learning and memorizing long sequences, a capability comparable to deep learning models, yet doing so in a biologically plausible manner. What's more, CL-SNN exhibits robust performance even in the presence of noise, showcasing its efficacy for real-world applications. To evaluate its biological feasibility, we analyze and visualize the network's weight dynamics, finding that CL-SNN can efficiently utilize synaptic connections to optimize sequence learning. Additionally, CL-SNN requires less synaptic connections compared to a traditional Neural Network, thus we conclude that CL-SNN is a feasible model of brain function. The source code of our study is publicly available on GitHub. Furthermore, the simulation results can be reproduced using the JNN simulator, a Python package developed by our team to simulate large-scale spiking neural networks. The JNN simulator is also openly sourced at GitHub. The parameter configurations for reproducing our results can be found at this repository. Furthermore, we employed the HPC resources at VTT's Valtori data center to carry out the large-scale simulations needed for our research. The computational power provided by Valtori enabled us to test the robustness of our model across a wide range of sequence lengths. The CL-SNN framework holds promise for inspiring novel chip designs, with potential applications in computer vision and natural language processing, fields where learning from long sequences plays a crucial role. Both prompt-only and prompt with parsing data models were effective, with the best model achieving a comparable performance level when evaluated on both seen and unseen data. The obtained results indicated a significant advancement in parsing datasets that were collected through crowdsourcing and the utilization of pre-trained language models. This report seeks to document the challenge's execution, present the parsed datasets, and analyze the submission results. Additionally, we investigate potential methods for overcoming the out-of-context challenge through data augmentation and pre-training using irrelevant contexts. These exploratory studies may provide valuable insights for future research in natural language understanding. Ultimately, the primary aim of the out-of-context challenge is to stimulate the development of more robust language models that can generalize effectively across various domains. We've developed a novel approach to studying dwarf galaxies based on their chemical compositions and the histories of star formation and evolution. This method leverages detailed analyses of the chemical abundances of multiple elements within distant, low-mass galaxies. By employing simulations using the high-resolution astrochemical code ALCHEMI, we examine how the distribution of chemical abundances within low-mass galaxies develops over time. Furthermore, we utilize an automatic clustering model to analyze this distribution, effectively identifying distinct stages in the star formation history of a galaxy. Its chemical composition is determined solely by these episodes. We apply this method to the dwarf galaxy NGC 3109, using spectroscopic data and assuming a linear relationship between metal enrichment throughout the galaxy's history. The model envisions two stages of star formation: an initial stage that mirrors solar metallicity patterns and a later stage characterized by significantly lower metal levels. The model is set apart from other theories on dwarf galaxy evolution, suggesting that the galaxy's low-mass stars are the result of a suppression of low-mass star formation events. The proposed approach may serve as a valuable tool for studying dwarf galaxies based on chemical compositions and star evolution histories, even in cases where star formation events are difficult to trace. This method's primary advantage is its reliance on chemical compositions rather than parametric star formation history models. It uses chemical data to construct the history of a galaxy's star formation, effectively eliminating uncertainties related to model assumptions. Ultimately, this approach enables us to treat both the star formation history and the chemical enrichment history of a galaxy simultaneously, effectively merging the paradigms of galaxy formation theory and chemical evolution theory. The proposed model is expected to enhance our comprehension of the early universe and low-mass galaxies based on their chemical compositions. The code is based on Python 2.7 and is available at https://github.com/lll1337/dwarf_alchemy. A corresponding package for the analysis of spectroscopic data has also been released. Specifically, pack_ong3109_2.0.py contains the necessary tools for examining the dwarf galaxy NGC 3109, while other packages can be developed for the study of other galaxies. We define a homotopy invariant of finite homotopy theory for profinite groups by leveraging a previous extension of homotopy theory to compact monoids. A new action spectrum functor is created as a result, which assigns a sequential spectrum to each profinite group. This functor establishes a connection between the homotopy theory of profinite groups and that of actions on sequential spectra, preserving key properties like universality and distributivity. This framework leads to a method for constructing a universal profinite group representing a given homotopy type, and it also enables a generalization of a previous result showing that profinite groups can be embedded in a universal space. Additionally, a method based on simplicial presheaves is used to compute the homotopy groups of a profinite group's action spectrum, and it is demonstrated that these groups contain relevant information about the group's topology. A key example is provided to show that these homotopy groups can be more complex than initially anticipated. This new theory is applied to study the fundamental group of a space constructed from a profinite group's classifying space for torsors. Moreover, a method based on a generalization of a concept known as "pro-resolution" is devised to compute the total homotopy group of a profinite group's action spectrum, and it is shown that this construction generalizes a concept known as "pro-automorphic" action. Finally, a method based on a theory known as "non-abelian cohomology in homotopy groups" is used to study the second homotopy group of a profinite group's action spectrum and to establish connections between these groups and non-abelian cohomology classes. A key example is provided to show that these connections can lead to interesting topological invariants of the group. A future work will utilize these ideas to study the Galois group of a fundamental field. A preliminary version of these results was presented at a meeting of the London Algebraic Topology Seminar, specifically in sessions 54 and 55. In particular, theorem 0.1 was announced under the title "a universal profinite group for a given homotopy type" in session 54. Furthermore, a related concept known as "pro-finite homotopy theory" was introduced, which is a more general theory that encompasses both "pro-finite groups" and "pro-finite homotopy theory as a theory for compact monoids", and the relationship between these theories was also discussed in session 55. Document analysis, a vital component of automation and a foundation for digital transformation, has been hindered by the visual richness of documents, making them difficult to process automatically and label. To circumvent the high costs associated with data labeling, we've developed a cutting-edge, efficient approach for automatically annotating a diverse range of documents. Leveraging our advanced understanding of document structure, we've created a custom data preparation technique, independent of domain knowledge, to rapidly generate high-quality training data. Compared to existing labeling methods, our approach yields comparable results while significantly reducing annotation expenses. For example, while manual labeling takes around 20 minutes per image, our automated technique completes the labeling process in about 4 minutes, a similar time to fine-tuning a learning model. Additionally, our approach allows for greater scalability, enabling more training data to be prepared in an hour than traditional methods can be labeled in a day. To facilitate widespread adoption, we've made our data preparation technique and a comprehensive dataset of visually rich documents, consisting of over 300,000 documents and 45,000 categories, openly available. Furthermore, we've developed a flexible layout analysis toolkit that can be applied to various document types. This toolkit is based on a hierarchical model of documents and is composed of modular components that can be used for advanced research and development. It includes high-quality datasets covering multiple scenarios and a flexible layout analysis toolkit, enabling efficient annotation and enhancing the robustness of layout analysis models. To ensure fairness and consistency in labeling, our approach incorporates rules and ensures that annotators do not perform both labeling and training, preventing the model from becoming too dependent on individual annotators. Moreover, to mitigate technical biases during annotation, we've established a set of reference labels, demonstrating typical labeling outcomes and providing context for model evaluation. To facilitate adoption and ensure the quality of annotations, we've established a process for reviewing and addressing questions and concerns related to annotations. Lastly, to make our dataset more comprehensive, we've developed a tool for generating hypothetical documents based on existing categories, expanding the dataset and facilitating research into visually rich documents. This tool can also be used to create training data for automatic document analysis models. A refined hierarchy of Borel Wadge classes is proposed with enhanced distinctions between classes. The traditional Borel Wadge system suffers from a limitation where classes like $\text{Borel}$ and $\text{continuous Borel}$ are not effectively separated. Similarly, $\text{intersection Borel}$ and $\text{union Borel}$ classes are also difficult to distinguish. Our new system overcomes these limitations and consists of an extension of the Borel Wadge quantifier with added efficiency, enabling greater control over the complexity of formed sets. The modified quantifier employs a strategy to balance the finer and coarser classes in a manner analogous to Lusin's theorem. As a direct consequence, our classes exhibit better separation efficiency. Furthermore, our new system includes an efficient categorization of analytic Wadge classes, overcoming a related limitation. A key tool for achieving these results involves developing more efficient continuous Borel Wadge quantifiers using a novel application of fundamental sequences. Finally, our study includes an examination of the computational complexity associated with each Borel Wadge class. The additional efficiency achieved through quantifier optimization leads to a surprise: we demonstrate that optimal computability is not achievable for certain classes, thereby resolving a long-standing open problem. Specifically, we show that the $\text{Borel}$ quantifier is not computationally optimal, thereby answering question 2.61 in the Introduction to the Wadge Basel Problem Book. This new direction in research is referred to as the computationally optimal Wadge problem. To facilitate our analysis, we develop a concept called 'quantifier complexity'. This allows us to generalize about the computational properties of sets formed using specific types of quantifiers, as well as to apply findings from computability theory. Lastly, we broaden our study to apply it to a related system known as Sacks system, which consists of the Borel Wadge classes applied to Polish topological spaces. The efficient separation of Sacks classes has also been a subject of research for decades, but our results enable us to generalize our findings from Borel Wadge classes to obtain a partially efficient separation of Sacks classes. Nonetheless, the general Sacks Wadge problem remains largely unresolved. Actor-critic reinforcement learning is widely employed in robotics and intelligent control due to its high success rate. Despite this, actor-critic reinforcement learning can suffer from poor exploration of the state space and a slow convergence rate. To address these challenges, a novel approach based on Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) has been developed to optimize the critic actor-critic (CAC) algorithm. HMC utilizes Hamiltonian Dynamics to gradientlessly sample from a targeted probability distribution, and our proposed HMC-CAC algorithm incorporates this sampling method to improve the actor's policy exploration. Experimental results demonstrate that the HMC-CAC algorithm leads to a more efficient exploration of the state space and achieves higher cumulative rewards compared to the traditional HMC-CAC algorithm. Additionally, our proposed HMC-CAC algorithm demonstrates a higher success rate in comparison to the traditional HMC-CAC algorithm. A significant improvement in performance was observed in cartpole swing-up, inverted double pendulum, and robot arm navigation tasks using the proposed HMC-CAC algorithm. Furthermore, the computational efficiency of the proposed HMC-CAK algorithm was evaluated in comparison to the traditional HMC-CAC algorithm, and the findings indicate that the proposed HMC-CAK algorithm achieves a notable enhancement in performance with a minimal increase in computational workload. These models can be linked to a universal $U(1)_X$ force, and we identify the relevant fermion interaction operators under the $SU(4)$ and $\bar{E}_6$ groups. Subsequently, we introduce possible fermion mass matrices that are consistent with the universal $U(1)_X$ symmetry. Ultimately, we examine the characteristics of the $\bar{E}_6$ model, including the anomaly cancellation condition, and any constraints it imposes on the universal $U(1)_X$ model. Specifically, we investigate a scenario with right-handed up-type fermions and investigate the characteristics of this model in comparison to the $\bar{E}_6$ model. We also discuss a universal $U(1)_X$ model derived from the $SU(4)$ $\Delta S_2$ scenario, along with two additional $\Delta S_1$ and $\Delta S_3$ scenarios that result in distinct fermion mass matrices and interaction operators. We derive the LEP bound on the $Z-X$ mixing angle for each of these three scenarios. Lastly, we discuss two additional scenarios, one derived from the $\bar{E}_6$ model and an $SU(4)$ scenario with left-handed up-type fermions, yielding distinct universal $U(1)_X$ models. We also examine a universal $U(1)_X$ model derived from the $\bar{E}_6$ scenario with left-handed up-type fermions in two-Higgs-doublet models. We consider Bayesian optimization problems with uncertain costs and constraints governed by probability distributions that can be represented using probabilistic circuits (PCs). Given a Bayesian optimization problem formulated through a PC-based model, our framework provides a method to establish a quantitative relationship between the optimal solution obtained by relaxing a PC-based optimization problem and the optimal Bayesian optimizer. This relationship holds specifically in scenarios where the optimal solution within the relaxed optimization problem is feasible in the original Bayesian optimizer problem. We construct PC-based models for various problems, including max-linear, matrix p-norm, and matrix p-row rank optimization problems, to demonstrate the efficacy of our approach. Furthermore, our method is not limited to optimization problems; we also discuss its application in defining a reliable predictor or classifier. We introduce a metric called constraint relaxation ratio (CRR) to measure the ratio of probabilistic constraints relaxed in our framework to those present in the original Bayesian optimizer problem. We establish lower bounds on CRR for several problem types and evaluate their practical implications, notably finding that CRR is capped at a value greater than 1. We also discover that our approach yields an optimal solution with a restricted form of input data and provide guidelines on how to utilize our approach in conjunction with existing optimization techniques, including gradient descent and cutting plane methods. We evaluate the performance of our approach on a set of well-established machine learning problems, including regression, classification, and matrix p-row rank optimization problems. The developed code for these experiments is publicly available at this GitHub address: https://github.com/asharivar/credal_bayesian_optimizer.asharivar/credal_bayesian_optimizer.

Developing an understanding of electron dynamics in response to intense light from x-ray free-electron lasers requires detailed explanations of how matter responds. We present a simple rate-based model that describes how an electron population in an atom or molecule changes over time after being exposed to an intense x-ray flux from an x-ray free-electron laser. This model considers non-linear interactions with multiple electronic states. We apply it to explain high-fluence x-ray absorption fine-structure and edge changes observed previously. We use it to demonstrate how an initial ionization and subsequent population of excited states affects the x-ray absorption spectrum and superimposes an initial bleaching phase. We also utilize it to explain the autoionizing state behavior of small molecules like nitrogen and oxygen. This model can be utilized for interpreting experimental data or as a starting point for more in-depth computational simulations. It is also accessible as a web-based tool at http://xray-rate.org. We utilize an analytical approach to derive key model parameters through fits of x-ray absorption spectra. We simulate x-ray coherent short-wavelength spectroscopy experiments to provide insight into how electron dynamics influences matter's response to intense x-rays. We explore how an accurate description of nonlinear interactions affects the transition from linear to nonlinear x-ray interaction. Utilizing our model, we explain observed delays, differences and similarities between linear and nonlinear x-ray absorption spectra and propose this model as a standard tool for the x-ray research community. This paper introduces a highly sensitive and accurate on-chip temperature sensor, featuring a ultra-low power design that allows it to function within a voltage range of 0.6V to 1.8V. The temperature sensor was fabricated using a 0.5$\mu$m CMOS process and has a tiny area of 0.023$mm^2. The device achieves a remarkable resolution of 0.24°C and a error margin of only 1.4°C, all while consuming a low power budget of 1.06nJ per conversion at 20fA, making it an ideal solution for controlling temperature-related issues in complex mixed-signal systems. To put this into perspective, a detailed analysis reveals that even when power consumption increases to 30nW, the corresponding area exhibits exponential growth and exceeds 100$\mu$m. Furthermore, a comprehensive study across four CMOS processes reveals that the proposed design features notably improved performance metrics, including reduced power consumption, increased resolution, and reduced area requirements. Crucially, the design's reliability was evaluated under various real-world conditions, and the results showed that it could function effectively in harsh environments for an extended period of time. Specifically, the tests confirmed that the device could operate within a temperature range of -30°C to 90°C and a voltage range of 0.6V to 1.8V without exhibiting any significant errors. To demonstrate its reliability, a prototype integrated circuit incorporating the temperature sensor was fabricated and thoroughly tested, verifying that it could convert temperature information into easily readable digital code. Detailed analysis and comparison with commercially available temperature sensors showed that the proposed design outperforms even the highest-end commercial solutions in nearly every key performance metric, earning up to a 35% improvement in resolution, a 2x improvement in conversion speed, and a 1000x improvement in power efficiency. Overall, the impressive balance of performance and energy efficiency exhibited by this temperature sensor make it an attractive solution for a wide range of temperature monitoring applications. Specifically, the design's low power requirements make it particularly well-suited for use in healthcare equipment and telecommunications systems. Additionally, the sensor's exceptional accuracy and reliability features make it a great choice for controlling temperature-related issues in precision scientific instruments and high-end automotive navigation systems. Finally, the design's compact size and simple binary output make it a great choice for a wide range of general-purpose embedded system applications. present. Our approach introduces a novel technique for generating entangled

photon in a dual-channel setup modulated by an entanglement gap. This Heralded

noise on entanglement creation. Our analysis includes a study of the effect of

convergence speed in the context of quantum key distribution. This method
demonstrates a promising means of producing entangled states and is relevant to
research in quantum physics. Additionally, this method is suitable for research
in single-photon quantum computing and other related fields. Our research may be
helpful to researchers focusing on the heralding of entangled states and key

A virtual spanner of a graph is a subgraph with increased edge lengths that maintains certain distance ratios between all pairs of vertices. In this research, we extend and simplify previous findings on virtual spanners with Euclidean distance metrics in higher-dimensional spaces. By applying techniques from approximate algebraic geometry, we demonstrate the existence of tight virtual Euclidean spanners in dimensions of $d \geq 3$. For scenarios where all distances are based on the Euclidean $d$-norm, our methods yield sublinear and weakly-tight solutions. In particular, for $d$-dimensional Euclidean space, our techniques result in virtual upper bounds with a factor of $O(\log d)$. To achieve these bounds, we also develop tight and weakly-tight approximate local spanners in Euclidean spaces of any dimension. These local spanners, which are based on Delaunay triangulations, allow for the efficient reconfiguration of existing closeness relationships into distance ratios among all pairs of vertices' neighbors. To generalize these findings, we define and conceptually study the idea of 'virtuality' as an graph theory property. In this research, we also explore the relationship between the concepts of Euclidean spanners and'shadow graphs'. By applying the concept of shadow graphs, we demonstrate that certain graphs do not have exact or tight approximate Euclidean spanners. Finally, based on the research, we study and generalize the idea of 'virtually tight' graphs. By applying techniques from approximate algebraic geometry, we maintain and generalize previously established findings on virtually tight graphs in dimensions of $d \geq 3$. To conclude the research, we explore new approaches for achieving tight and weakly-tight approximate algebraic geometry in dimensions of $d \geq 3$. This work addresses the challenge of efficient feature extraction for machine learning model training on limited IoT devices, including low-power computers like Raspberry Pi. A new method, called AutoFE, leverages autoencoders to both select relevant features and train the rest of the model, thereby optimizing the use of these devices for classification tasks. Compared to other feature selection and feature extraction techniques, AutoFE achieves comparable or better performance while significantly reducing the memory and computation requirements, thus enabling classification tasks to be run on IoT devices more effectively. This research evaluates AutoFE on three real-world datasets and provides a comprehensive evaluation of its efficiency, indicating its potential to enable a wide range of machine learning applications on IoT devices. The source code for this research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/SaeedAboudi/AutoFE. The project website can be accessed at https://saeedaboudi.github.io/Project_FES.

We conducted the first comprehensive simulations of Primordial Black Hole Dark Energy (PBHDE) models, leveraging the high-performance cosmological simulator PopSyCLE. Specifically, we ran 275 PBHDE simulations across three primary scenarios, all within the Lambda-CDM cosmological framework. Our PBHDE models generated through 11 distinct halo mass patterns, resulting in a total of 825 simulated dark matter density paths. These simulations enabled us to extract precise statistics, including rare event predictions, and to analyze how PBHDE affects the late-time cosmological behavior. Furthermore, we explored how suppressing early-time matter-radiation equality impacted the late-time cosmological behavior. Our findings were then compared to the constraints of PBHDE theories imposed by gamma-ray observations of microlensing and black hole masses formed through collapse of small perturbations. Our research demonstrates that high-resolution PBHDE simulations, enabled by PopSyCLE, allow us to accurately quantify the late-time cosmological effects of these theories, while also facilitating the exploration of late-time dark energy behaviour and the potential impact of primordial black holes on late-time dark energy dynamics. Our simulation data is publicly available at https://github.com/CSDC-observatory/PBHDE-simulations. Our code is also available at https://github.com/CESB-Project/popSyCLE-codes. We're investigating a system where solid balls occupy a one-dimensional row, forming a tower that falls into a stage of stability when the ratio of the number of balls to the width of the tower is maximized. This paper explores how this stage of stability changes when the tower's structure becomes irregular, caused by introducing certain types of motions. Using advanced computer modeling, we identify various stages of stability that can emerge in such a scenario and examine how its width and stability are interconnected. Additionally, we investigate how these stages of stability change when the rate at which the tower's structure becomes disordered increases. Notably, these distributions exhibit a double-peaked structure, consisting of a closer initial burst and a distant larger peak. Previous studies assumed this pattern resulted from superimposed Gaussian distributions, but this assumption lacks clear evidence. Conversely, research on solar eruptions and other spatially isolated events demonstrates a two-part structure consisting of a initial intense spot and subsequent spike, more accurately modeled using a cascade of nonlinear interactions. Here, we apply a different approach to analyze data from the Big Bear Observatory and the Big Bear Vector Observatory, matching the peak frequencies of the distant larger peak from faculae and granulation plots. The results show faculae and granulation peak frequencies align, providing observational evidence for a similar double-peaked structure model representing solar bright spots. Furthermore, we observe that the overall brightness of the larger peak from faculae distributions is higher than that of the smaller initial peak, in contrast, the brightness of the larger peak from granulation distributions is lower than that of the smaller initial peak. This disparity in brightness may be attributed to differing temperatures corresponding to the peaks. Moreover, we demonstrate that the distribution shapes and patterns can be identical, yet the peaks can be interpreted differently, highlighting the importance of consideration and context in analysis.
